researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
LifeBridge Surrogacy Overview
LifeBridge Surrogacy is a U.S.-based gestational surrogacy agency that supports gestational surrogates
throughout the surrogacy process, from the initial application through pregnancy and delivery.
LifeBridge describes itself as a female-owned and operated agency built around compassion, trust, and
lived experience. Its model is surrogate-focused and designed to provide prospective and current
surrogates with ongoing guidance while coordinating the different professionals involved in a
gestational surrogacy journey.
The agency advertises:
•   A dedicated, surrogate-focused support team.
•   24/7 access to experienced surrogacy professionals.
•   Access to legal professionals who help protect surrogate rights.
•   Relationships with IVF clinics involved in screening and treatment.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
•   Assistance coordinating the surrogate journey from application through delivery.
•   Ongoing communication and check-ins throughout pregnancy.
•   A relatively quick matching process compared with some traditional agency timelines.
LifeBridge has advertised matching in approximately four weeks in some materials. However,
matching time is not guaranteed and can vary substantially according to the surrogate, intended parents,
preferences, screening, availability, and other circumstances.
General Surrogate Qualifications
LifeBridge’s general eligibility criteria include several demographic, reproductive, and health-related
requirements.
Prospective gestational surrogates are generally expected to:
•   Be approximately 21–40 years old.
•   Reside in the United States.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
•   Meet the agency’s BMI or height-to-weight requirements, with a BMI generally under 32.
•   Have experienced at least one prior uncomplicated pregnancy.
•   Have had no more than approximately five total deliveries.
•   Have had no more than approximately two cesarean deliveries.
A history of miscarriage does not necessarily automatically exclude a prospective surrogate. According
to the agency information represented in these materials, an applicant may remain eligible when she has
subsequently experienced at least one healthy birth.
These criteria function as preliminary qualifications rather than final medical clearance. Meeting the
general requirements does not guarantee acceptance as a gestational carrier because medical,
psychological, reproductive, and other screening occurs later in the process.
Additional Health and Pregnancy-History Considerations
LifeBridge also considers a prospective surrogate’s broader medical and obstetric history.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
The agency materials identify factors such as:
•   No history of preterm labor or preterm delivery.
•   No history of gestational hypertension.
•   No history of gestational diabetes.
•   Generally good overall health.
•   Non-smoking status.
•   Medication use compatible with pregnancy and the requirements established by the treating fertility
clinic.
A prospective surrogate’s medical history is reviewed as part of screening rather than relying
exclusively on a short eligibility checklist.
Medication use may also require individualized evaluation. Certain medications can be incompatible
with pregnancy or fertility-treatment protocols, but medication use should not be treated as a blanket

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
exclusion without evaluation by the appropriate medical professionals.
Psychological Screening
Gestational surrogacy involves psychological screening in addition to physical and reproductive-health
screening.
Psychological evaluation is conducted by qualified professionals and helps determine whether the
prospective gestational carrier is appropriately prepared for the emotional, relational, and practical
demands associated with surrogacy.
Psychological screening can examine areas such as:
•   Understanding of the surrogacy arrangement.
•   Expectations surrounding pregnancy and delivery.
•   Emotional readiness.
•   Support systems.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
•   Communication and relationship expectations.
•   Understanding of relinquishment and intended-parent relationships.
•   Relevant mental-health history.
•   Current psychological well-being.
•   Ability to provide informed consent.
Mental-health history should be evaluated individually by qualified professionals. A history of a
psychological condition or psychotropic medication use is not appropriately interpreted without
considering diagnosis, stability, treatment, medication safety, fertility-clinic requirements, and
professional evaluation.
Application and Matching
The surrogacy journey begins with an application and eligibility review.
An initial application review may take approximately 1–3 days, although timelines can vary.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
If preliminary requirements are satisfied, the prospective surrogate can progress toward matching with
intended parents.
Matching may involve:
•   Review of surrogate and intended-parent profiles.
•   Consideration of preferences and expectations.
•   Communication between the parties.
•   A video meeting or other introductory conversation.
•   Determining whether both parties feel comfortable proceeding with the match.
LifeBridge has promoted relatively quick matching, including approximately four-week matching in
some materials. A broader estimate represented in the process materials is approximately 4–8 weeks for
matching and the associated meeting process.
These figures should be treated as estimates rather than guarantees.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
Medical Screening
After an appropriate match is established, the gestational carrier undergoes medical screening through
the fertility/IVF clinic.
The IVF clinic—not LifeBridge itself—provides the clinical fertility care and determines whether
the prospective carrier satisfies its medical requirements.
Medical screening may include:
•   Review of previous pregnancy and delivery records.
•   Medical-history review.
•   Bloodwork.
•   Infectious-disease testing.
•   Uterine evaluation.
•   Assessment of reproductive health.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
•   Additional testing required by the treating fertility clinic.
The materials indicate that medical screening may require travel to California depending upon the
clinic and arrangement.
An estimated medical and psychological screening period of approximately 4–6 weeks is provided,
although actual timing varies.
Importantly, agency eligibility and medical clearance are not identical. A person can satisfy an
agency’s preliminary qualifications but still require—and potentially not receive—final medical
clearance from the fertility clinic.
Who Handles What?
Gestational surrogacy involves several separate professional roles.
LifeBridge / the surrogacy agency
LifeBridge coordinates much of the overall journey and assists with:

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
•   Applications.
•   Preliminary eligibility.
•   Matching.
•   Communication.
•   Coordination between participants and professionals.
•   Surrogate support.
•   Ongoing check-ins.
IVF / fertility clinic
The fertility clinic is responsible for medical components of the assisted-reproduction process,
including appropriate medical screening and fertility treatment.
Licensed medical providers may conduct:
•   Bloodwork.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
•   Uterine evaluation.
•   Medical screening.
•   Medication management.
•   Embryo-transfer preparation.
•   Embryo transfer.
•   Pregnancy-related medical confirmation as appropriate.
Psychological professionals
Qualified psychological professionals conduct the psychological evaluation required during the
surrogacy process.
Attorneys
Experienced reproductive or surrogacy attorneys handle the legal agreements and advise the parties
regarding their respective legal rights and obligations.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
These roles should remain distinct. The agency coordinates the journey, while licensed clinicians
provide medical care and attorneys provide legal advice and representation.
Estimated Surrogacy Timeline
The materials provide approximate timelines for several stages of the process:
•   Application review: approximately 1–3 days.
•   Matching and video meeting: approximately 4–8 weeks.
•   Medical and psychological screening: approximately 4–6 weeks.
•   Legal contract process: approximately 2–3 weeks.
•   Embryo transfer and confirmation: approximately 4–8 weeks.
These estimates should not be interpreted as guaranteed timelines.
Actual timing can be affected by factors including:
•   Availability of intended-parent matches.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
•   Compatibility between the parties.
•   Medical-record collection.
•   Clinic scheduling.
•   Screening results.
•   Travel.
•   Psychological evaluation.
•   Legal negotiations.
•   Medication protocols.
•   Embryo-transfer scheduling.
•   Embryo-transfer outcomes.
The overall process is therefore better understood as a sequence of stages than as a fixed countdown.
Compensation

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
LifeBridge’s promotional materials describe surrogate compensation beginning at approximately
$50,000, with additional benefits potentially adding $10,000 or more.
Promotional compensation ranges may reach approximately $120,000, depending on factors such as
previous surrogate experience and the specific compensation package.
These figures should not be interpreted as a guarantee that every surrogate will receive the maximum
advertised amount.
Actual compensation depends on the individual arrangement and ultimately should be documented in
the applicable legal agreement.
Additional Compensation Details
The materials describe several additional compensation-related provisions.
These include:
•   Base compensation beginning after heartbeat confirmation, according to the represented agency

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
materials.
•   A $1,000 bonus for each embryo transfer.
•   A monthly allowance beginning after contract signing.
•   Final compensation being paid following delivery according to the applicable compensation
arrangement.
•   Compensation amounts, reimbursements, allowances, benefits, and other financial provisions being
established and protected through the legal contract.
Because individual arrangements can differ, the signed gestational-carrier agreement is the controlling
source for the actual compensation schedule, benefits, reimbursements, contingencies, and payment
terms applicable to a particular surrogate.
Legal Care and Contracts
Legal representation is a central component of gestational surrogacy.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
The materials indicate that legal contracts are completed before medical procedures associated with
the surrogacy arrangement proceed.
Gestational-carrier agreements are designed to establish and protect the rights and responsibilities of the
surrogate and intended parents.
The contract can address matters such as:
•   Compensation.
•   Allowances.
•   Reimbursements.
•   Medical expenses.
•   Insurance.
•   Travel.
•   Lost wages where applicable.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
•   Pregnancy-related expectations.
•   Medical decision-making.
•   Communication.
•   Risks and contingencies.
•   Delivery.
•   Parentage procedures.
•   Responsibilities of the surrogate.
•   Responsibilities of the intended parents.
Compensation is governed by the legal agreement rather than merely by promotional materials or
preliminary discussions.
Because surrogacy law varies by jurisdiction and individual circumstances, each party should receive
appropriate independent legal guidance regarding the agreement and applicable law.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
Ongoing Surrogate Support
LifeBridge describes support as continuing beyond matching and conception.
The surrogate can receive dedicated agency support from application through delivery, including
ongoing communication and check-ins during the pregnancy.
Support can be particularly important because gestational surrogacy requires coordination among
numerous parties, including:
•   The surrogate.
•   Intended parents.
•   Agency staff.
•   Fertility-clinic personnel.
•   Obstetric providers.
•   Mental-health professionals.

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
•   Attorneys.
•   Other relevant professionals.
The agency’s role is therefore not limited to finding a match. It also acts as a coordinator and support
resource throughout the broader journey.
Important Takeaways
LifeBridge’s eligibility checklist represents only the beginning of the screening process. Prospective
surrogates undergo a more extensive, multi-step process before embryo transfer.
General eligibility does not equal final medical approval.
Medical screening and IVF treatment are handled by fertility clinics and licensed medical professionals
rather than by LifeBridge itself.
Psychological screening is performed by qualified professionals.
Legal agreements are handled by attorneys and establish the parties’ rights, responsibilities, and

researchNoteChunks.heading: LifeBridge Surrogacy: Agency Overview, Qualifications, Process, Compensation, Support & Legal Care
researchNoteChunks.text:
compensation arrangements.
Advertised compensation and timelines are useful for understanding the general structure of the
program, but they should be treated as estimates or promotional ranges rather than guarantees.
The exact requirements, screening decisions, compensation package, medical protocol, legal
obligations, and timeline can vary by individual case.

the steps:
1.     initial discussion w/ match specialist: process begins with intended parents
meeting with a match specialist to discuss their preferences and expectations for a
surrogate. this includes qualities they are looking for, a preferred location, and the
desired level of communication.
2.     surrogate pre-screening: surrogacy agency conducts a rigorous screening
process for all surrogate candidates. this includes reviewing their applications, having
conversations to understand their motivation and support systems, and performing

researchNoteChunks.heading: matching process – finding the right fit
researchNoteChunks.text:
background checks, living environment assessments, and psychological evaluations.
this pre-screening ensures that only candidates who meet the highest standards are
considered for matching.
3.      video/in person match meeting: once a potential match is identified, a video
or in person meeting is arranged by the coordinator. this provides an opportunity for
the intended parents and the surrogate to meet and get to know each other.
4.     finalizing the match: after the meeting, the coordinator checks in with both
parties to ensure they feel comfortable and ready to move forward. if all parties agree,
the match is officially made, and the legal and medical processes can begin.

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking common surrogacy myths (e.g. surrogates = paid to give up their own baby)
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      opening line: so, let’s be real. the topic of surrogacy is widely discussed in the
media & it’s like a game of telephone–certain details are either left out of the picture or
completely misconstrued as the discussion endures. let’s delve into some common
misconceptions, and the actual truths!
•      myth #1: surrogacy is only for the wealthy / celebrities
•      this is FALSE. while the cost can be high, it is not indeterminable. the total cost
depends on factors such as agency fees, whether an egg donor is used, and the
intended parents' insurance coverage. some insurance policies may cover part of the
process, while others may require an additional policy.
•      myth #2: a woman will choose surrogacy to save her figure or avoid pregnancy.
•      this is FALSE. surrogacy is typically an expensive and emotional last resort for
women who have had multiple failed attempts to conceive or carry a baby. the

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking common surrogacy myths (e.g. surrogates = paid to give up their own baby)
researchNoteChunks.text:
decision is made out of a desire for parenthood, not a concern for physical
appearance.
•      myth #3: the gestational surrogate might try to take parental custody of the
child.
•      this is a FALSE. most surrogates (and majority these days are gestational not
traditional) and intended parents undergo a psychological evaluation before entering
into an agreement. legal contracts and state laws are in place to ensure that the
intended parents are recognized as the legal parents, and surrogates are aware from
the start that they will not have parental rights.
•      myth #4: intended parents will have trouble bonding w/ their baby.
•      this is FALSE. the bonding process begins after the child is born and is
immediately handed over to the intended parents, who will nurture and care for the

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking common surrogacy myths (e.g. surrogates = paid to give up their own baby)
researchNoteChunks.text: baby.

researchNoteChunks.heading: science behind IVF – how does it work?
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      have you ever wondered what really goes into IVF? well worry not, because it’s
all here!
•      what is IVF? : a medical procedure that helps individuals or couples become
pregnant. it’s a type of assisted reproductive technology (ART) where eggs are
collected from the ovaries and fertilized with sperm in a laboratory, outside of the
body. the resulting embryos are then transferred to the uterus.
•      Steps ( full IVF cycle typically takes about two to three weeks and involves five
main steps ) :
1.     ovarian stimulation : to get the ovaries to produce multiple eggs instead of just
one. a combination of medications are used:
•      to stimulate follicle growth : follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and human
menopausal gonadotropin (hMG) [stimulates ovaries to produce eggs].

researchNoteChunks.heading: science behind IVF – how does it work?
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      to prevent premature ovulation : gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)
[hormone that stimulates pituitary gland to make follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) &
luteinizing hormone (LH) → release of estrogen & progesterone [needed for ovulation])
agonists, GnRH antagonists, and progestins.
•      to trigger ovulation : human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) and/or GnRH
agonists are used once the eggs are mature.
2.     egg retrieval : about 36 hours after the final medication, the eggs are retrieved
in a minor surgical procedure → doctor uses ultrasound to guide a needle through the
vagina to the ovaries, removing eggs from each follicle; procedure is quick, typically
lasting 15 to 30 minutes, and is done under anesthesia.
3.     fertilization : in the lab, the retrieved eggs are fertilized with sperm [ejaculated
sperm is collected via masturbation into a sterile container, while surgical retrieval

researchNoteChunks.heading: science behind IVF – how does it work?
researchNoteChunks.text:
involves procedures like PESA (percutaneous epididymal sperm aspiration), TESA
(testicular sperm aspiration), or TESE (testicular sperm extraction)].
•      eggs & sperm = mixed in a petri dish
•      intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) may be used, where a single sperm is
injected directly into the egg to improve the chances of fertilization.
4.     embryo culture: the fertilized eggs, now embryos, are monitored and grown in a
laboratory for two to five days.
5.     embryo transfer: the final step is placing the selected embryo(s) into the uterus
•      a doctor inserts a thin tube called a catheter through the cervix into the uterus.
•      embryos can be transferred immediately (fresh transfer) or frozen for later use
(frozen embryo transfer or FET), which is a common practice to reduce the risk of
complications and allow for genetic testing.

researchNoteChunks.heading: science behind IVF – how does it work?
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      to increase the chances of success, more than one embryo can be transferred,
but this also increases the risk of multiple births (twins, triplets, etc.) → it is generally
recommended to transfer only one embryo during an IVF cycle, a practice known as
elective single embryo transfer (eSET).
•      success rates:
•      under 35: 40% to 55%
•      35 to 37: 30% to 40%
•      38 to 40: 20% to 30%
•      over 40: Less than 20% (with rates decreasing significantly after age 42).

researchNoteChunks.heading: genetics of surrogacy (baby is NOT related to gestational surrogate)
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      in gestational surrogacy, the baby is not genetically related to the woman who
carries the pregnancy.
•      the baby's genetic material (DNA) comes solely from the egg and sperm used
to create the embryo through in vitro fertilization (IVF).
•      the gestational carrier's role is to provide the uterine environment for the
embryo to grow and develop. She does not contribute any of her own genetic
material to the child.
•     this is the primary difference from traditional surrogacy, where the surrogate's
own egg is used, making her the genetic mother of the child.

researchNoteChunks.heading: surrogacy timeline (how long?)
researchNoteChunks.text:
•       the timeline of a gestational surrogacy journey can be lengthy (but rewarding!
:)), with the process from start to finish typically taking 18 to 24 months. the timeline
can vary depending on various factors, but a general breakdown includes several key
stages:
1.      pre-screening: to ensure candidates meet initial criteria before being matched
(e.g. age requirement, previous healthy pregnancy, etc.)
you fill it out you are set!!! :)
2.      matching: the process of the IPs finding a suitable gestational carrier and
getting to know her. this can take anywhere from 1 to 6 months.
3.       COMPREHENSIVE legal & medical screening: a crucial phase where the
intended parents and surrogate undergo legal and medical screenings to ensure
everyone is healthy and the legal contract is in place. this stage typically takes 1 to 2

researchNoteChunks.heading: surrogacy timeline (how long?)
researchNoteChunks.text:
months.
4.       embryo transfer: once all parties are medically and legally cleared, the IVF
clinic can proceed with the embryo transfer. the surrogate prepares her body for the
transfer, which takes 1 to 1.5 months.
5.       pregnancy & post-birth: the longest part of the timeline is the pregnancy
itself, which is typically 9 months. after the birth, the legal process to establish
parental rights is finalized, which can take an additional 1.5 to 3 months.

researchNoteChunks.heading: role of embryo transfer in IVF process
researchNoteChunks.text:
•       the role of embryo transfer is to place the embryo into the uterine cavity at the
precise moment it has the highest chance of implantation. this is a delicate process
guided by science:
•       timing: the transfer is timed to coincide with the "implantation window," a
period when the uterine lining (endometrium) is most receptive to an embryo. this is
typically done on day 3 (cleavage stage) or day 5 (blastocyst stage)--states of
development of embryo–after fertilization.
•       procedure: a thin, flexible tube called a catheter is loaded with the embryo and
gently guided through the cervix into the uterus. the entire procedure is performed
under ultrasound guidance to ensure the embryo is placed at the optimal location
within the uterine cavity.
•       embryo quality: the highest-quality embryos are selected for transfer, as they

researchNoteChunks.heading: role of embryo transfer in IVF process
researchNoteChunks.text:
have a greater potential for survival and implantation. embryologists assess factors
like cell division rates and overall morphology.
•     uterine receptivity: before the transfer, the patient's uterine lining is prepared
with hormonal support, primarily progesterone, to ensure it is thick and ready to
receive the embryo.

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
(ALL ARTICLES COMBINED)
Overview of Surrogacy in Assisted Reproduction
•     Surrogacy is a reproductive arrangement where a woman carries a
pregnancy for intended parents
•     Two main types exist:
– Traditional surrogacy
•     surrogate provides the egg
•     surrogate is genetically related to the child
– Gestational surrogacy
•     embryo created using egg and sperm from intended parents or
donors
•     surrogate has no genetic relationship to the baby

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
•     Gestational surrogacy is the most common modern form
•     Surrogacy has increased due to advances in assisted reproductive
technologies (ART) and IVF
– in 2022, approximately 4.7% of embryo transfer cycles in the U.S. used
gestational carriers
Why People Use Surrogacy
Common indications for gestational surrogacy include:
– absence of uterus
– uterine malformations
– prior hysterectomy
– medical conditions making pregnancy dangerous
– recurrent pregnancy loss

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
– multiple failed IVF attempts
Specific medical reasons reported include:
•    severe cardiac disease
•    systemic lupus
•    pulmonary hypertension
•    genetic disorders
•    Turner syndrome
•    CAIS syndrome
•    severe endometriosis
In many cases, surrogacy allows individuals to have genetically related children when
pregnancy would otherwise be impossible or unsafe.
Selection Criteria for Surrogate Mothers

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
Guidelines from reproductive medicine organizations recommend surrogates:
– age typically between 21–45 years
– have at least one prior healthy pregnancy
– have no history of obstetric complications
– have no significant psychiatric conditions
– live in a stable support environment
Additional screening includes:
– psychological evaluation
– infectious disease testing
– uterine anatomy assessment
– legal contracts and counseling
These extensive screening processes contribute significantly to positive outcomes.

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
Study Population and Sample Characteristics
One major study examined:
•     95 surrogate mothers
•     128 babies delivered
Breakdown:
– 65 singleton births
– 27 twin pregnancies
– 2 triplet pregnancies
Average ages:
•     Surrogates: ~30 years
•     Intended mothers: ~38 years
Surrogates are typically younger and have proven fertility, which supports healthy

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
pregnancy outcomes.
Pregnancy Success Rates
Across studies:
•      Pregnancy rates: ~24%–61%
•      Live birth rates: ~15.8%–55.5%
Factors influencing success:
– embryo quality
– surrogate health
– egg donor age
– IVF protocol
Research shows:
•     similar success rates for fresh and frozen embryo transfers

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
•     no major differences between donor eggs and intended mother eggs
Overall, gestational surrogacy shows strong success rates comparable to or better
than standard IVF.
When Surrogacy Cycles Do Not Result in Pregnancy
Not every embryo transfer results in pregnancy, which is common in all IVF
treatments, including surrogacy.
Possible reasons include:
– embryo does not implant
– embryo stops developing early
– chromosomal abnormalities in the embryo
– uterine environment not receptive during that cycle
Important context:

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
• implantation failure is one of the most common reasons IVF cycles fail, regardless
of who carries the pregnancy.
Many intended parents undergo multiple embryo transfers before achieving
pregnancy.
Early Pregnancy Loss and Failed Implantation
Some pregnancies end very early after embryo transfer.
Examples include:
– biochemical pregnancy (very early miscarriage detected only by hormone testing)
– early miscarriage during the first trimester
These events occur in IVF pregnancies generally, not specifically because of
surrogacy.
Most studies show miscarriage rates in surrogate pregnancies are similar to typical

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
IVF pregnancies.
Key biological reason:
• many early losses are caused by chromosomal abnormalities in embryos, which
occur naturally during reproduction.
Embryo-Related Risks Before Pregnancy
Research examining embryos in surrogacy programs identified several factors
affecting success:
– embryo quality is one of the strongest predictors of pregnancy success
– embryos with chromosomal abnormalities may fail to implant or stop developing
Modern fertility clinics often use:
– preimplantation genetic testing (PGT)
– improved embryo culture systems

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
These advances help increase success rates and reduce failed implantation.
Embryo Transfer Practices
Historically:
•       multiple embryos were transferred
Example:
– average 4 embryos per transfer in earlier programs
This sometimes produced multiple pregnancies.
Current recommendations:
– single embryo transfer (SET)
Reason:
•       reduces risk of preterm birth
•       reduces neonatal complications

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
•       reduces cesarean delivery rates
Gestational Age and Delivery Timing
Average gestational ages reported:
– Singletons: ~38.7 weeks
– Twins: ~36.2 weeks
– Triplets: ~35.5 weeks
This pattern is consistent with natural pregnancies where multiples tend to deliver
earlier.
Birth Weight Outcomes
Average birth weights:
– Singletons: ~3.5 kg
– Twins: ~2.7 kg

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
Low birth weight rates:
– Singletons: ~3.3%
– Twins: ~29.6%
– Triplets: ~33.3%
Important observation:
•      singleton babies born through surrogacy tend to have healthy birth
weights
Most risks are associated with multiple pregnancies rather than surrogacy itself.
Preterm Birth
Preterm delivery (<36 weeks):
– Singletons: ~11.5%
– Twins: ~20.4%

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
Comparison with standard IVF pregnancies:
•     prematurity rates were often lower in surrogacy pregnancies
Reason:
•    surrogates typically have healthy uterine environments and prior
pregnancies
Neonatal Health Outcomes
Most infants were:
– appropriate for gestational age (AGA)
Examples:
•     94% of twins
•     83% of triplets
Neonatal ICU admissions:

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
•     17 infants required NICU care
•     typically short stays (4–30 days)
Important finding:
•       no perinatal mortality reported
Congenital Malformations
Studies found:
•     rates of birth defects similar to the general population
Examples reported:
– cleft lip/palate
– gastrointestinal atresia
All affected infants:
•     successfully treated with surgery

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
•     developed normally afterwards
These rates are consistent with typical population statistics.
Maternal Health Outcomes (Surrogate Mothers)
Major pregnancy complications were relatively uncommon.
Rates reported:
– Pregnancy-induced hypertension: ~4.9%
– Gestational diabetes: ~1.6%
– Placental complications: ~4.9%
These rates were:
•      lower than those reported in some IVF pregnancies carried by
infertile patients
Possible explanation:

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
•     surrogates are medically screened and have proven fertility
Mode of Delivery
Cesarean delivery rates:
– Singletons: ~21%
– Twins: ~59%
This pattern reflects typical obstetric practice:
•      multiples often require surgical delivery
Singleton cesarean rates were:
•     similar to the general U.S. population
Postpartum Outcomes
Postpartum complications occurred in:
•     ~6.3% of surrogate pregnancies

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
Examples:
– postpartum bleeding
– infection
Most complications were minor and treatable.
Psychological Outcomes
Studies reported:
•     very low rates of postpartum depression
Contributing factors:
– rigorous psychological screening
– support systems for surrogates
– strong motivation to help intended parents
Some women experienced:

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
– temporary emotional adjustment (“maternal blues”)
These were short-lived and resolved naturally.
Comparisons With Standard IVF Pregnancies
Surrogacy pregnancies sometimes show equal or better outcomes compared with
IVF pregnancies carried by infertile patients.
Examples:
– lower rates of hypertension
– lower placental complications
– lower low-birth-weight incidence for singleton births
Possible reasons:
•     healthier surrogate uterine environment
•     prior successful pregnancies

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
Key Factors That Improve Outcomes
Research highlights several protective factors:
– healthy surrogate selection
– prior successful pregnancies
– extensive medical screening
– single embryo transfer
– high-quality IVF protocols
These factors help produce strong maternal and neonatal outcomes.
Overall Conclusion from the Literature
Major research findings consistently show:
•     gestational surrogacy is generally associated with favorable
pregnancy outcomes

researchNoteChunks.heading: Surrogacy Outcomes
researchNoteChunks.text:
•     most risks relate to multiple pregnancies rather than surrogacy itself
•     singleton surrogate pregnancies show outcomes comparable to
natural pregnancies
Overall conclusion of the main study:
•      results provide reassurance regarding obstetric and neonatal
outcomes for families pursuing IVF-surrogacy

Types of Surrogacy
Traditional (Partial) Surrogacy
•     The surrogate’s own egg is used.
•     This means the surrogate is genetically related to the child.

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
•     This type was more common in earlier surrogacy practices.
Gestational Surrogacy
•     The egg comes from the intended mother or an egg donor.
•     The surrogate has no genetic connection to the child.
•     Gestational surrogacy is now the most common type.
Altruistic vs Commercial Surrogacy
Altruistic surrogacy
•      The surrogate receives no payment beyond expenses.
Commercial surrogacy
•    The surrogate receives financial compensation.
•    Different countries regulate these forms differently.
Growth of Surrogacy Research

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
•     Research on surrogacy has increased significantly in recent years.
•     However:
– there are still relatively few high-quality review studies
– relational aspects of surrogacy remain understudied
•     The article analyzed 39 qualitative studies based on:
– interviews with surrogates and intended parents
– ethnographic research
– narratives of lived experience
Countries Represented in the Research
Studies examined surrogacy in many contexts including:
– USA
– UK

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
– India
– Israel
– Ukraine
– Russia
– Canada
– Australia
– Mexico
– Greece
•      This diversity helps researchers understand how cultural and legal
contexts influence surrogacy experiences.
Medical and Psychological Outcomes
Previous reviews of surrogacy outcomes found:

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
•     no significant medical or obstetric differences between:
– surrogacy pregnancies
– typical pregnancies
•      Psychological outcomes for families are also generally positive.
Key findings from earlier research:
•     Surrogates rarely experience difficulty relinquishing the child.
•     Relationships between surrogates and intended parents are often
satisfying.
•     Altruistic motivations are common among surrogates.
•     Many surrogates report feeling proud of helping another family.
Common Motivations for Becoming a Surrogate
Research consistently shows several motivations:

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
Altruism
•     Many surrogates report a desire to help others build families.
•     Surrogacy is often described as “giving the gift of life.”
Empathy for Infertility
•     Surrogates frequently say they want to help people who cannot have
children themselves.
Personal Fulfillment
•    Some surrogates describe the experience as emotionally meaningful
and rewarding.
Financial Compensation
•      In commercial surrogacy, payment may also play a role.
•      However, research shows compensation often coexists with altruistic

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
motivation.
Relational Justice in Surrogacy
The article introduces the concept of relational justice.
Relational Justice
•     Surrogacy ethics should consider the relationships between all parties
involved, including:
– surrogate
– intended parents
– child
•    Ethical evaluation should ensure:
– fairness
– respect for autonomy

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
– well-being of all participants
Reproductive Justice Framework
•     Reproductive justice focuses on ensuring that people can:
– make healthy reproductive decisions
– build families safely and ethically
•     This includes considering:
– economic conditions
– cultural context
– social inequalities
•      Surrogacy itself is not inherently ethical or unethical.
•      Instead, ethical outcomes depend on:
– how relationships and rights are managed

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
Relational Ethics
•    Relational ethics emphasizes that individuals make decisions within
relationships and social contexts.
•    Surrogacy involves mutual responsibilities and interactions.
•     Ethical evaluation must therefore consider:
– communication between parties
– expectations during pregnancy
– relationships after birth
Key Themes Identified in Surrogacy Relationships
Researchers found four major themes influencing surrogacy relationships:
1.    Bonding and emotional distance
2.    Kinship language and identity

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
3.    Cultural expectations
4.    Financial vs altruistic exchange
Bonding Between Surrogates and Intended Parents
Relationships between surrogates and intended parents vary widely.
Close Relationships
•     In many cases:
– intended parents attend prenatal appointments
– both parties maintain regular communication
•     Some intended mothers report experiencing “pseudopregnancy”
symptoms such as:
– weight gain
– emotional involvement

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
•     These experiences reflect strong emotional engagement with the
pregnancy.
Distance in Some Arrangements
•     In other cases, relationships are more distant, especially when:
– intended parents live in another country
•    Communication may occur through:
– phone calls
– video calls
– online messaging
•     Some parents deliberately choose geographical distance to maintain
clear family boundaries.
Strategies Surrogates Use to Avoid Emotional Attachment

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
Research shows surrogates often mentally frame the pregnancy differently.
Common strategies include describing themselves as:
– “an oven”
– “a babysitter”
– “a caretaker”
•     These mental frameworks help surrogates maintain emotional clarity
about the child’s parentage.
Kinship Language and Identity
Different cultures use different language to describe relationships.
Examples include:
– “tummy mommy”
– “auntie”

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
– “like family”
•     These terms reflect varied interpretations of the surrogate’s role.
•     However, most surrogates emphasize that the intended parents are the
true parents.
Expectations and Emotional Experiences
Surrogacy experiences are influenced by expectations about the relationship.
When expectations match reality:
– satisfaction is high
When expectations differ:
– disappointment may occur
Example situations:
– surrogates expecting long-term contact

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
– intended parents expecting a more transactional relationship
Gift vs Transaction Narrative
Surrogacy is often framed in two ways.
Gift Narrative
•     Surrogacy described as a meaningful act of helping another family.
•     Emotional language such as “gift of life” is common.
Transactional Narrative
•     Surrogacy viewed as a compensated form of reproductive labor.
•     Some surrogates emphasize professional boundaries.
•     Both perspectives often coexist.
Four Types of Surrogacy Relationships
The article identifies four relationship models.

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
1. Open Relationships
Characteristics:
•      Frequent communication
•      Strong emotional connection
•     mutual respect
Examples:
– regular visits
– ongoing friendship
– contact after birth
Outcomes:
– high satisfaction for both parties
2. Restricted Relationships

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
Characteristics:
•      little or no contact
•      communication mostly through agencies
Focus:
– primarily financial exchange
Possible challenges:
– surrogates may feel unsupported emotionally
3. Structured Relationships
Characteristics:
•      communication defined by contracts
Examples:
– scheduled updates

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
– occasional post-birth contact
Outcomes:
– expectations often clearly defined and fulfilled
4. Enmeshed Relationships
Characteristics:
•      very intense emotional involvement
Possible challenges:
– mismatched expectations
– emotional complexity
Overall Findings on Surrogacy Outcomes
Across many studies:
•    Most surrogates do not view themselves as the child’s mother.

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
•    Many surrogates prefer continued contact with families, though not
always.
•    Positive relationships are common when expectations are aligned.
•    Emotional satisfaction is highest when:
– communication is clear
– respect is mutual
– roles are well defined
Importance of Long-Term Relationships
Research suggests ongoing contact between families and surrogates can:
– improve emotional well-being
– strengthen positive experiences
•    Many surrogates report that maintaining contact helps them feel

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
valued and appreciated.
Policy and Ethical Implications
Effective surrogacy frameworks should ensure:
– fair treatment of surrogates
– clear expectations between parties
– respect for reproductive rights
Policies should consider:
– emotional relationships
– cultural norms
– economic conditions
Key Takeaway
•    Surrogacy is a complex but often positive collaborative reproductive

researchNoteChunks.heading: SURROGACY OUTCOMES — GESTATIONAL
researchNoteChunks.text:
arrangement.
•    Successful outcomes depend on:
– communication
– mutual respect
– clear expectations
•     Ethical frameworks should support healthy relationships between
surrogates, intended parents, and children.
Citation
Gunnarsson Payne, J., Korolczuk, E., & Mezinska, S. (2020). Surrogacy relationships:
a critical interpretative review. Upsala journal of medical sciences, 125(2), 183–191.
https://doi.org/10.1080/03009734.2020.1725935

researchNoteChunks.heading: study overview
researchNoteChunks.text:
– purpose: examine how 16 weeks of different exercise programs affect female
body composition and anthropometric measures
– design: longitudinal, quasi-experimental study with repeated measurements
– sample: 89 adult women, ages 25–55 (mean age 41.42 ± 9.23 years)
– groups:
– strength training group (SG): n = 25
– dance group (DG): n = 18
– hydrogymnastics group (HG): n = 21
– sedentary control group (CG): n = 25
main hypothesis
– hypothesis: adult women can improve body composition and anthropometric
dimensions after 16 weeks of strength training, dance, or hydrogymnastics

researchNoteChunks.heading: study overview
researchNoteChunks.text:
participant characteristics
– age range: 25–55 years
– location: northeastern Brazil
– marital status: 60% married, 27% single, 12% divorced
– inclusion criteria:
– participation in assigned exercise sessions
– no infectious disease, chronic disease, or musculoskeletal disorder
– beginner or active for ≤12 months
– negative on physical activity readiness screening
exercise protocols
– strength training
– frequency: 3x/week

researchNoteChunks.heading: study overview
researchNoteChunks.text:
– intensity: 60–70% of 1RM
– volume: 3 sets of 8–12 reps
– rest: 2–3 min between sets
– session length: 50–60 min
– used machines, free weights, and resistance equipment
– dance
– frequency: 3x/week
– intensity: 60–85% of max heart rate
– session length: 50–60 min
– continuous whole-body movement with popular dance + aerobics rhythms
– music cadence: 100–160 bpm
– hydrogymnastics

researchNoteChunks.heading: study overview
researchNoteChunks.text:
– frequency: 3x/week
– intensity: 60–85% of max heart rate
– session length: 45–55 min
– included cardiorespiratory work + muscular endurance in water
– used aquatic equipment like dumbbells, shin pads, bars, plates, floats
measurements collected
– body mass
– height
– circumferences: chest, waist, abdomen, hip, thighs, calves
– skinfolds: triceps, suprailiac, thigh
– derived variables:
– BMI

researchNoteChunks.heading: study overview
researchNoteChunks.text:
– fat percentage (F%)
– fat mass (FM)
– lean mass (LM)

measurement timeline
– time 1: before training began

statistics used

researchNoteChunks.heading: study overview
researchNoteChunks.text:
– effect size: η²
– small > 0.01, medium > 0.06, large > 0.14
baseline findings

– important note: education level was not significantly related to the anthropometric

researchNoteChunks.heading: study overview
researchNoteChunks.text:
outcomes, so it was not used as a covariate

body mass results
– interaction effect for time × group was significant
– time effect was also significant
– group effect alone was not significant
– interpretation: body mass changed over time somewhat differently across groups,

researchNoteChunks.heading: study overview
researchNoteChunks.text:

hip circumference results

researchNoteChunks.heading: study overview

waist-hip ratio (WHR) results

main conclusion

outcomes than sedentary women

researchNoteChunks.heading: study overview

why hydrogymnastics may have looked less favorable at baseline

researchNoteChunks.heading: study overview

study limitations

researchNoteChunks.heading: study overview
researchNoteChunks.text:

practical takeaway
– for adult women, 16 weeks of consistent exercise can improve body composition

– hydrogymnastics can also be very effective, especially for women who prefer low-

researchNoteChunks.heading: stress impact on hormonal health
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      sometimes, you gotta take a chill pill! ^___^ stress can have more detrimental
effects than you think.
•      when your body perceives stress (psychological, physical, emotional), it
activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. the hypothalamus releases
corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), which signals the pituitary to release
adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which in turn prompts the adrenal glands to
secrete cortisol (the “stress hormone”). high or chronic cortisol levels feed back to
suppress or dysregulate other hormone systems.
•      cortisol and CRH suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis. in
the female reproductive system, this interference can lead to reduced Gonadotropin-
Releasing Hormone (GnRH) pulses, which in turn blunt the luteinizing hormone (LH)
and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) release needed for normal ovarian function.

researchNoteChunks.heading: stress impact on hormonal health
researchNoteChunks.text:
over time, this suppression can lead to menstrual irregularities or anovulation.
•       effects on reproductive hormones & ovulation
•       a study of healthy women measuring daily stress found that higher recent stress
was associated with lower estradiol (E2), lower LH, lower luteal progesterone, and
higher FSH. importantly, elevated stress increased odds of sporadic anovulation
(failure to ovulate).
•       chronic stress also can disrupt the release of kisspeptin, which is a
neuropeptide that stimulates GnRH secretion. when stress or metabolic signals (low
energy, starvation) reduce kisspeptin activity, ovulation can be suppressed — a
mechanism implicated in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA).
•       broader hormonal disruptions & health effects
•       stress impacts many hormone systems beyond reproductive ones:

researchNoteChunks.heading: stress impact on hormonal health
researchNoteChunks.text:
glucocorticoids, catecholamines, growth hormone, prolactin, thyroid hormones, etc.
over time, this can lead to endocrine dysregulation, metabolic disturbances (insulin
resistance, weight gain), and reproductive dysfunction (ovarian, thyroid, adrenal)
•       dysregulation of the HPA axis—especially when chronic stress leads to
“allostatic load” (wear and tear on regulatory systems)—can lead to mismatches
between neural and hormonal stress responses, further worsening endocrine balance.
•       fluctuations in estrogen and stress interact: periods of lower estrogen may
render women more vulnerable to the psychological impacts of stress (mood,
anxiety). estrogen also modulates brain circuits involved in stress responses, so
hormonal shifts can make stress more impactful.
•       women experiencing high chronic stress may notice irregular or absent periods,
heavier or lighter bleeding, or more painful cycles.

researchNoteChunks.heading: stress impact on hormonal health
researchNoteChunks.text:
•       fertility can be impacted: suppressed ovulation, luteal phase defects
(insufficient progesterone), or poor hormonal support of implantation.
•       women under stress may show lower reproductive hormone levels, altered
menstrual cycle length, and increased risk of anovulatory cycles.
•       over long periods, hormonal imbalance from stress may contribute to
conditions like functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, worsening of PCOS, or
exacerbation of menstrual disorders.

were minimized. effective self-advocacy helps ensure your voice is heard, that your
symptoms are taken seriously, and that you play an active role in decision-making
about your health. studies of self-advocacy strategies (communication, preparation,
persistence) show they can improve patient outcomes, satisfaction, and the quality of
the patient–provider relationship.
•     key strategies & tactics for advocating for yourself
1.    research ahead of time! : before your appointment, gather credible information
about your symptoms, possible diagnoses, and treatment options. knowing at least
the basics helps you ask informed questions, spot red flags, and catch gaps in what

researchNoteChunks.heading: tips for advocating for yourself in doctor’s office
researchNoteChunks.text:
your provider says.
2.    prioritize & make an agenda : write down your main concerns, symptoms (with
onset, duration, intensity), medications/supplements, family history, and what you
hope to get from the visit (e.g., diagnosis, treatment plan, referral). order your
questions so that the most important ones get addressed first — just so you are
mindful of your doctor’s time :).
3.     bring a support person & take notes : having someone accompany you can
lighten the cognitive load (they can ask questions, take notes). meanwhile, write down
your provider’s explanations, diagnoses, prescriptions, and next steps. if anything is
unclear, ask them to rephrase or repeat in simpler terms.
4.     speak clearly & assertively:
your voice matters. use statements like:

researchNoteChunks.heading: tips for advocating for yourself in doctor’s office
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      “what i’m experiencing is …” (describe symptoms in concrete terms)
•      “can you explain why you think this approach is best?”
•      “what are the alternatives, and what are the pros/cons?”
•      “i’m concerned about _______ (side effect, cost, invasiveness); how can we
mitigate that?”if your concerns are brushed aside, you can say: “i feel my concern
wasn’t fully addressed — can we explore this further?”
5.     ask clarifying questions until you understand
•      don’t leave confusion unaddressed. you have the right to know exactly what a
test, diagnosis, or treatment means for you. use phrasing like: “so just to confirm,
what you’re saying is…?” or “could you explain that again in simpler terms?”
6.     know your rights as a patient: informed consent, access to your records,
refusal of treatment, second opinions. if you feel a provider is not listening, not

researchNoteChunks.heading: tips for advocating for yourself in doctor’s office
researchNoteChunks.text:
respecting you, or missing something, it’s okay to ask for a second opinion or switch
to a clinician you trust.
7.     follow up! : medical appointments can be overwhelming, and sometimes you’ll
think of things after you’ve left. keep a journal of symptoms, side effects, questions
that arise, and be ready to bring them up in the next visit. if test results came back
after your appointment, follow up to go over them.
•      challenges / barriers
•      power dynamics & hierarchical structures: patients often feel intimidated or
deferential to doctors.
•      implicit bias, discrimination, or dismissal: women, people of color, and
marginalized groups often report being disbelieved or having their pain minimized.
•      time constraints: short appointment slots make it harder to raise everything.

researchNoteChunks.heading: how to track menstrual cycle naturally
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      when you’re tracking naturally (without meds or devices), paying attention to
multiple body signals gives you the best picture. key signs include:
•      start date of bleeding: day 1 is the first day you see full flow (not spotting).
tracking this every month is foundational.
•      length of your cycle: count from the first day of one period to the day before the
next one begins. over several cycles, you start to see the average, and the range of
your shortest vs longest cycle. this helps you predict fertile windows, possible
irregularities.
•      basal body temperature (bbt): measuring your temperature first thing in the
morning (before getting up, doing anything) each day. after ovulation, progesterone
pushes temperature slightly higher. when you see a pattern (rise + three higher
readings), you can confirm that ovulation likely occurred.

researchNoteChunks.heading: how to track menstrual cycle naturally
researchNoteChunks.text:
•       cervical mucus / cervical fluid changes: as you approach ovulation, mucus often
becomes wetter, clearer, slippery (“egg-white” texture). after ovulation, under
progesterone influence, it usually becomes thicker, sticky, or drier. this change gives
clues to fertile days.
•       other symptoms: ovulation pain (mittelschmerz), breast tenderness, changes in
libido, mood/energy changes, cervical position (some people track softness/openness
of the cervix). also, noting how heavy or long your periods are, how regular, how you
feel (cramping, mood, fluid retention) can help see patterns.
•       methods you can employ:
•       calendar / rhythm method: just tracking bleeding dates for many cycles to
estimate when ovulation is likely. best for regular cycles. less accurate if cycles are
irregular.

researchNoteChunks.heading: how to track menstrual cycle naturally
researchNoteChunks.text:
•       fertility awareness-based methods (fabms): these combine multiple signs —
calendar + bbt + cervical mucus + sometimes urinary hormone tests. they can be
used to identify fertile windows (for trying to conceive) or avoid pregnancy.
•       basal body temperature method: as above; confirms ovulation has happened.
it’s retrospective (you see the rise after ovulation) so it’s more useful for knowing
when not fertile rather than precisely predicting ahead.
•       cervical mucus method: observing fluid daily, noting texture, wetness, etc. very
helpful especially when combined with bbt or calendar. gives you an ongoing clue of
approaching ovulation.
•       why tracking helps:
•       predict fertile window: if you’re trying to conceive or avoid pregnancy, knowing
when you’re fertile is a BIG plus.

researchNoteChunks.heading: how to track menstrual cycle naturally
researchNoteChunks.text:
•       spot irregularities: irregular cycles, long luteal phases, skipped ovulation, or
symptoms like spotting between cycles can signal health issues (thyroid, pcos,
hormonal imbalance).
•       plan for symptoms: if you know patterns (e.g. premenstrual mood shifts, pms,
cramping, energy dips), you can schedule around them, manage proactively.
•       general hormone health insight: patterns over time can show if hormone cycles
are stable—or if something is off and might warrant checking with a doctor.
•       limitations & things to be aware of
•       if you have irregular cycles, predictive methods are less reliable. cycle length
variation makes calendar predictions trickier.
•       bbt can be affected by external factors: illness, lack of good sleep, alcohol,
inconsistent waking time. these can distort the temperature pattern.

researchNoteChunks.heading: how to track menstrual cycle naturally
researchNoteChunks.text:
•       tracking takes consistency and patience — you often need multiple cycles (3-
6+) to see meaningful patterns.
•       some apps or trackers may oversimplify or assume regularity; always take them
with caution, especially if using for contraception or fertility.
•       natural methods don’t protect against sexually transmitted infections.

researchNoteChunks.heading: science behind menstrual cramps & what actually helps
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      “menstrual cramps” are medically called dysmenorrhea. there are two main
types:
•      primary dysmenorrhea: pain from menstrual cycles without an underlying
pathological cause (NO fibroids, endometriosis, etc.).
•      secondary dysmenorrhea: pain due to another condition; abnormal tissue
growth (endometriosis, uterine fibroids, ovarian tumors, adenomyosis, pelvic
inflammatory disease, etc.).
•      key physiological mechanisms (primary dysmenorrhea)
1.     prostaglandins & uterine contractions
•      toward the end of the menstrual cycle (after progesterone drops), the lining of
the uterus (endometrium) releases prostaglandins (especially PGF2α, PGE2).
•      these molecules cause the uterine muscle (myometrium) to contract more

researchNoteChunks.heading: science behind menstrual cramps & what actually helps
researchNoteChunks.text:
strongly and frequently. they also cause vasoconstriction (narrowing of blood vessels)
in the uterus.
2.     ischemia & anaerobic metabolites
•      strong contractions compress blood vessels → reduced blood flow (ischemia)
in uterine tissue.
•      reduced oxygen leads to accumulation of anaerobic metabolites (e.g. lactic
acid) which irritate nerves and contribute to pain.
3.     sensitization of pain nerves
•      the nerves in the uterus become sensitized: signals from uterine contractions
and chemical mediators evoke greater pain perception. over time, women with more
severe dysmenorrhea may have increased baseline sensitivity to pain, even outside of
menstruation.

researchNoteChunks.heading: science behind menstrual cramps & what actually helps
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      there may also be involvement of prostaglandins and leukotrienes in sensitizing
pain fibers (making them more reactive).
4.     other hormonal & inflammatory mediators
•      vasopressin (a hormone) may play a role in heightening uterine contraction and
reducing local uterine blood flow.
•      inflammation is central: increased inflammatory mediators accompany high
prostaglandin levels.
5.     risk factors / features that make it worse
•      early age at menarche (like if you got your period at an early age), heavy or
prolonged menstrual flow, obesity, smoking, family history
•      psychological factors: stress and mood may worsen pain perception, so try to
do things to help you relax. sleep quality and overall health also matter.

researchNoteChunks.heading: gut health + hormonal balance link
researchNoteChunks.text:
•     a key concept is the “estrobolome”, the collection of gut bacterial genes
(especially those producing β-glucuronidase) that can deconjugate (reactivate)
estrogens excreted into the gut, allowing them to be reabsorbed into circulation.
when gut microbial diversity is reduced (dysbiosis), β-glucuronidase activity can drop,
leading to more estrogens being excreted rather than recycled — lowering active
estrogen levels. thus, gut dysbiosis can contribute to hormonal imbalances,
especially estrogen deficiency or altered estrogen metabolism.
•     sex hormones also play a role! the relationship is bidirectional: estrogen,
progesterone, and androgens influence gut microbiome composition, function, and
diversity. fluctuations in sex hormones (e.g. across menstrual cycle, pregnancy,
menopause) change gut environment, which may favor or disfavor certain bacteria.
for example, menopause is associated with lower microbial diversity, shifts toward a

researchNoteChunks.heading: gut health + hormonal balance link
researchNoteChunks.text:
more “male‐like” gut microbiome composition, and declines in beneficial bacteria
such as lactobacillus and bifidobacteria
•     as for your metabolism & your immune system, gut bacteria produce short-
chain fatty acids (SCFAs), bile acid metabolites, and other signaling molecules that
impact systemic metabolism, insulin sensitivity, inflammation, and immune regulation
— all of which influence hormone pathways (e.g. insulin hormonal regulation, adrenal
hormone balance). through effects on gut barrier integrity and inflammatory
pathways, gut dysbiosis can lead to “leaky gut,” systemic endotoxin exposure, and
low-grade chronic inflammation, which disrupt endocrine signaling (e.g. affecting the
hypothalamic-pituitary axes).
•     reproductive & ovarian impacts – animal and human studies show links
between gut microbiota profiles and reproductive hormone levels, ovarian function,

researchNoteChunks.heading: gut health + hormonal balance link
researchNoteChunks.text:
and conditions like pcos, endometriosis, and infertility. for instance, certain bacterial
taxa correlate with insulin, testosterone, LH/FSH levels, and ovarian morphology. in
experimental models, transferring gut microbiota from individuals with pcos into mice
induced metabolic and reproductive dysfunction in the recipients.
•     clinical / practical implications!
•     women with gut dysbiosis (e.g. due to poor diet, antibiotics, chronic gi
conditions) may be more prone to hormonal irregularities — erratic cycles, estrogen
withdrawal symptoms, insulin resistance, etc.
•     during hormonal transitions (perimenopause, menopause), gut changes may
exacerbate symptoms (hot flashes, metabolic shifts) via reduced microbial diversity
and altered estrogen recycling.
•      interventions aimed at improving gut diversity (fiber, prebiotics, probiotics,

researchNoteChunks.heading: how to deal w/ body image & self- esteem issues as a woman
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      body image and self-esteem are influenced by biological, psychological, and
sociocultural factors. for women, societal pressures (e.g. social media and depictions
of the “hourglass” figure), hormonal fluctuations, and personal experiences can
contribute to negative body image and low self-esteem.
•      neurobiology: brain regions such as the insula and amygdala are involved in
self-perception and emotional evaluation of one’s body, and overactivation can
contribute to body dissatisfaction.
1.     menstrual cycle effects
•      follicular phase (days 1–14): rising estrogen can improve mood and body
satisfaction.
•      ovulatory phase (around day 14): peak estrogen and testosterone may
temporarily boost confidence.

researchNoteChunks.heading: how to deal w/ body image & self- esteem issues as a woman
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      luteal phase (days 15–28): progesterone rise can increase emotional sensitivity
and body dissatisfaction.
•      pregnancy & postpartum: rapid hormonal changes can cause body image
anxiety; up to 60% of postpartum women report negative feelings about appearance.
•      perimenopause & menopause: declining estrogen may reduce skin elasticity,
change fat distribution, and affect self-esteem.
•      brain chemistry: low serotonin levels, influenced by hormones and stress, can
exacerbate negative self-talk about appearance.
2.     sociocultural & environmental pressures
•      social media exposure: viewing idealized bodies on instagram or tiktok
increases self-objectification, shame, and comparisons. limit exposure to <30
minutes/day or unfollow accounts that trigger body dissatisfaction.

researchNoteChunks.heading: how to deal w/ body image & self- esteem issues as a woman
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      family & peer influence: negative comments about weight, appearance, or
dieting during adolescence correlate with persistent low self-esteem in adulthood.
•      cultural factors: beauty standards differ across cultures (e.g. thin figure in east
asian cultures; “slim thick” figure in african cultures); understanding personal identity
and embracing diversity can buffer against societal pressure.
3.     psychological strategies
•      cognitive behavioral techniques (cbt):
•      identify “body-negative thoughts” (e.g., “i’m too fat”) and reframe with factual,
neutral statements (“my body is healthy and functional”).
•      behavioral experiments: wear clothing that makes you feel confident and note
the difference in self-perception.
•      mindfulness & self-compassion:

researchNoteChunks.heading: how to deal w/ body image & self- esteem issues as a woman
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      practice daily 5–10 minute meditation focusing on body acceptance.
•      journaling prompt: “name three things my body did for me today.”
•      exposure therapy for mirror anxiety: gradually increasing mirror exposure while
focusing on function, not flaws.
4.     lifestyle interventions for improved self-esteem
•      exercise for strength & function, not appearance:
•      weight lifting 2–3x/week improves mood, bone density, and body appreciation.
•      yoga or pilates improves mind-body awareness and reduces stress.
•      nutrition & balanced eating:
•      avoid extreme dieting; focus on whole foods, protein, fiber, and micronutrients.
•      adequate iron, vitamin d, omega-3s support mood and cognitive function,
indirectly boosting self-esteem.

researchNoteChunks.heading: how to deal w/ body image & self- esteem issues as a woman
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      sleep hygiene: 7–9 hours/night reduces cortisol spikes that can exacerbate
body dissatisfaction.
5.     practical daily strategies
•      media literacy: Critically analyze images online; remember most are edited and
unrealistic.
•      support network: Discuss body image concerns with friends or a therapist to
normalize experiences. (can rant in the comment section below too ^___^!)
•      positive reinforcement: daily affirmations focusing on strength, resilience, and
health, not appearance.
•      persistent negative body image or avoidance behaviors, or disordered eating
patterns, warrant professional evaluation. evidence-based treatments include CBT,
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), and group therapy programs.

– pregnancy sickness

– nausea

– frequency varies by country
– example reported values
– Japan ≈ 84%
– United States ≈ 64%
– India ≈ 35%
– overall range across studies

researchNoteChunks.text:
– 11% – 100% of pregnancies
– thus, morning sickness is extremely common worldwide.
When Morning Sickness Occurs During Pregnancy
Time of day
– symptoms occur throughout waking hours
– nausea appears most frequently during daytime
– symptoms are much less common during sleep hours.
Time during pregnancy
– symptoms begin around
– week 4 of pregnancy
– symptoms increase rapidly and peak around
– weeks 9–14

researchNoteChunks.text:
– symptoms then gradually decline

Relationship to Embryonic Development
– morning sickness peaks during the period when the embryo is most vulnerable to
toxins.
– the most sensitive developmental period occurs during
– weeks 6–12 of pregnancy
– during this time
– organ systems are forming (organogenesis)

– therefore the embryo is highly vulnerable to chemical disruption.
Key implication
– the timing of nausea and vomiting closely matches the embryo’s most
sensitive developmental stage.
Proposed Evolutionary Purpose
Embryo-protection hypothesis
– morning sickness may function to protect the embryo from harmful substances.
– nausea and vomiting cause pregnant women to
– expel potentially harmful foods
– develop aversions to dangerous foods
– these foods may contain

– morning sickness may have a heritable component.

Researchers considered other explanations for morning sickness.
Hormonal byproduct hypothesis
– morning sickness may simply be a side effect of pregnancy hormones.

Signaling pregnancy hypothesis

– the data best support the idea that morning sickness is adaptive.

researchNoteChunks.heading: herbal remedies safe for pregnancy (& those to avoid)

•     consultation: always consult with your doctor before starting a new exercise

researchNoteChunks.text:

•      pelvic tilts: strengthens core muscles and stabilizes the pelvis. can be done
while reclining, sitting, or standing.
reclined (first trimester): lie on your back with knees bent and feet on the floor. exhale
and contract your abdominal muscles, rotating your pelvis upward. hold for 3-5
seconds, then relax. repeat 10 times.

distributed through your feet or stand with feet hip-width apart. follow the same steps
as the reclined version.

researchNoteChunks.text:

toward the ceiling while your head falls gently toward your chest. hold for 10-15
seconds and return to the starting position. repeat 10 times.
•      bird dog: improves core strength, balance, and stability.
start on your hands and knees with shoulders over your hands and hips over your
knees. engage your abdominal muscles and keep your spine straight.

stand with feet slightly apart and knees slightly bent.

researchNoteChunks.text:

researchNoteChunks.heading: pregnancy discomfort solutions
researchNoteChunks.text:
•     overview of pregnancy discomforts
•      discomforts vary by trimester
•      1st = sharp hormonal changes → fatigue, nausea, moodiness.
•      2nd = brings about relief from earlier symptoms, but new aches, swelling, and
pain can occur as the body grows.
•      3rd = most uncomfortable due to added weight of the fetus – strains joints &
puts pressure on organs which can lead to issues like heartburn & shortness of
breath.
•      normal vs. serious – while minor discomforts are normal, knowing the signs of
a more serious issue is crucial. it recommends consulting a healthcare provider for
severe or persistent symptoms, such as severe vomiting (which could be hyperemesis
gravidarum) or sudden, severe swelling (which could be preeclampsia).

researchNoteChunks.heading: pregnancy discomfort solutions
researchNoteChunks.text:
•      common discomforts & recommended solutions
1.     fatigue : feeling exhausted is a normal response to the body's increased work,
especially in the first and third trimesters.
•      maintain a regular sleep schedule, take short naps before 3 p.m., and engage in
safe daily exercise. also advised to get a blood test to check for anemia, a potential
cause of fatigue.
2.      headaches : common in the first trimester due to hormonal changes, increased
blood volume, and stress.
•      apply ice packs, drink plenty of water (10-12 glasses daily), and rest in a dimly
lit room. it’s crucial to consult a provider before taking any medication, as common
NSAIDs are not always safe during pregnancy. acetaminophen may be
recommended by a doctor.

researchNoteChunks.heading: pregnancy discomfort solutions
researchNoteChunks.text:
3.      nausea & vomiting (morning sickness) : Can happen at any time of day and
affects up to 70% of pregnant women in the first trimester.
•      eat bland foods (the BRAT diet of bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast), sip
non-caffeinated fluids throughout the day, and eat small meals frequently. suggested
to try supplements like vitamin B6 and ginger extract.
4.      physical aches & pain : hormones loosen ligaments to prepare for birth, and
the added weight strains muscles and joints. this can cause round ligament pain, leg
cramps, and backaches.
•      use a lumbar pillow or maternity belt for support, get massages, use heating
pads, and wear comfortable, low-heeled shoes. gentle exercise, proper body
mechanics, and a prenatal vitamin rich in calcium and electrolytes are also advised.
5.     swelling & varicose veins : increased pressure on blood vessels can cause fluid

researchNoteChunks.heading: pregnancy discomfort solutions
researchNoteChunks.text:
retention and swelling, particularly in the legs and feet.
•      wear comfortable shoes and compression socks, stay hydrated, and elevate
your legs and feet whenever possible.
6.      bladder problems : increased urination and incontinence [loss of bladder
control] are common, especially in the third trimester, due to the growing fetus putting
pressure on the bladder.
•       practicing kegel exercises where you contract the muscles you would use to
stop urine midstream / prevent passing gas [avoid practicing while urinating; don’t
hold contraction from too long to avoid straining] to strengthen pelvic floor muscles
and help with bladder control. It also advises to stay hydrated and be on the lookout
for signs of a UTI (pain / burning during urination, frequent urination, foul-smelling or
cloudy urine, blood in urine).

researchNoteChunks.heading: pregnancy discomfort solutions
researchNoteChunks.text:
7.     heartburn & constipation : the added weight of the fetus and hormonal changes
can slow down digestion, leading to heartburn and constipation.
•      eat small, frequent meals, avoid spicy and greasy foods, and don’t lie down for
two to three hours after eating. for constipation, increase your intake of fiber (e.g.
dried fruits) and fluids.
8.      skin changes: hormones and skin stretching can lead to stretch marks,
melasma ("mask of pregnancy”; brown to gray brown patches on skin), a dark line on
the abdomen (linea nigra), and acne.
•      maintain a good skincare routine with gentle cleansers and moisturizers. wear
sunscreen and stay hydrated. avoid using most acne medications (e.g. isotretinoin)
during pregnancy.
9.     trouble sleeping : many discomforts contribute to insomnia, especially in the

researchNoteChunks.heading: pregnancy discomfort solutions
researchNoteChunks.text:
third trimester.
•      adjust your sleep position by using C-shaped / wedge-shaped pillows for
support, and try light stretches & warm milk before bed. DO NOT take sleep
medications while pregnant.

researchNoteChunks.text:
•      postpartum recovery = a time of significant transition as the body heals from
pregnancy and delivery. here are the normal occurrences you can expect!
•      lochia is the vaginal discharge that occurs after birth. it’s a normal process for
the body to shed the extra blood and tissue built up in the uterus during pregnancy. it
typically lasts up to six weeks and progresses through three stages:
1.     lochia rubra: the first three to four days, the discharge is dark or bright red,
and heavy like a period, with small clots.
2.     lochia serosa: from day four to ten, the discharge becomes thinner and
pinkish-brown.
3.     lochia alba: from about day 12 and lasting up to six weeks, the discharge is
yellowish-white and light.

researchNoteChunks.text:
