researchNoteChunks.heading: sea moss benefits for women
researchNoteChunks.text:
what sea moss is
sea moss is a type of red algae commonly called Irish moss or Irish sea moss.
its scientific name is Chondrus crispus.
sea moss naturally grows in coastal ocean environments.
it absorbs minerals and other substances directly from the water around it.
sea moss contains carrageenan, a carbohydrate that gives it a thick, gel- like texture.
carrageenan is commonly used in foods as a thickener and stabilizer.
sea moss can be eaten raw or prepared as a gel.
it is also sold as powders, capsules, gummies, and blended supplements.
the composition of sea moss can vary depending on species, growing location, season, harvesting, drying,
and processing.
one sea moss product can therefore provide a very different amount of nutrients from another.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sea moss benefits for women
researchNoteChunks.text:
research on edible seaweeds overall is much larger than research specifically on sea moss.
findings involving another seaweed species cannot automatically be applied directly to sea moss.
sea moss can be a nutrient-containing food without being a proven treatment for disease.
many online health claims are currently stronger than the sea moss- specific human research behind them.
nutrients inside sea moss
sea moss can provide fiber.
sea moss can provide folate, also called vitamin B9.
sea moss can provide calcium.
sea moss can provide iodine.
sea moss can provide zinc.
sea moss can provide iron.
sea moss can also contain small amounts of protein and amino acids.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sea moss benefits for women
researchNoteChunks.text:
fiber supports normal bowel function and can contribute to fullness.
folate participates in DNA formation and normal cell division.
calcium helps maintain bones and participates in muscle and nerve function.
iodine is required for normal thyroid-hormone production.
zinc contributes to immune function, wound healing, and many cellular processes.
iron is required to form hemoglobin and transport oxygen.
sea moss also contains taurine, an amino acid involved in normal muscle function.
the presence of a nutrient does not mean a typical serving supplies enough to correct a deficiency.
nutrient amounts are not standardized across sea moss gels, powders, capsules, or gummies.
supplement labels should be checked instead of assuming every sea moss product has the same nutritional
profile.
potential digestive benefits

researchNoteChunks.heading: sea moss benefits for women
researchNoteChunks.text:
fiber is one of the clearest reasons sea moss is discussed for digestive health.
fiber adds bulk to stool and helps support regular bowel movements.
fiber can help people feel full for longer after eating.
seaweed also contains polysaccharides that can interact with microorganisms in the digestive tract.
some algae are being studied for possible prebiotic effects.
beneficial gut microorganisms participate in digestion, metabolism, and immune function.
sea moss is often promoted online for gas, bloating, constipation, diarrhea, and heartburn.
those specific symptom claims go beyond the strongest sea moss- specific evidence available.
persistent constipation can have dietary, medication, pelvic-floor, hormonal, or medical causes.
persistent diarrhea can cause dehydration and may reflect infection or gastrointestinal disease.
persistent bloating can occur with food intolerances, constipation, gastrointestinal disorders, and other
conditions.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sea moss benefits for women
researchNoteChunks.text:
sea moss should not be used to delay evaluation of persistent digestive symptoms.
“contains fiber” and “treats digestive disease” are not the same statement.
potential heart and metabolic benefits
fiber can contribute to cardiovascular and metabolic health within an overall nutritious eating pattern.
dietary fiber can support healthier cholesterol patterns.
fiber can help slow digestion and support steadier blood sugar responses.
fiber also contributes to fullness and appetite regulation.
seaweed research has explored possible effects on cholesterol, blood pressure, and metabolic markers.
the amount and type of seaweed matter when interpreting those findings.
broader seaweed findings do not prove that a sea moss gummy lowers cholesterol.
sea moss does not replace medication for high cholesterol.
sea moss does not replace treatment for high blood pressure.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sea moss benefits for women
researchNoteChunks.text:
sea moss does not replace treatment for diabetes.
cardiovascular health also depends on overall nutrition, physical activity, sleep, smoking exposure,
medications, genetics, and other factors.
a sea moss supplement cannot compensate for an otherwise poor- quality dietary pattern.
sea moss fits more accurately as one optional nutrient-containing food.
thyroid health and iodine
the thyroid gland requires iodine to make thyroid hormones.
the major thyroid hormones include thyroxine, or T4, and triiodothyronine, or T3.
the body cannot manufacture iodine.
iodine therefore has to come from foods or supplements.
common iodine sources include iodized salt, dairy foods, eggs, seafood, and seaweed.
sea moss can provide iodine.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sea moss benefits for women
researchNoteChunks.text:
insufficient iodine can interfere with normal thyroid-hormone production.
excess iodine can also interfere with normal thyroid function.
seaweed iodine concentrations vary widely across species.
growing location, season, processing, preparation, and serving size can also change iodine exposure.
sea moss is therefore not a predictable thyroid supplement.
people with hypothyroidism may be sensitive to unnecessary iodine supplementation.
people with hyperthyroidism may also experience problems from excess iodine.
excess iodine can contribute to thyroid dysfunction in susceptible people.
combining sea moss with kelp, bladderwrack, prenatal vitamins, or other iodine-containing supplements can
increase total iodine exposure.
more iodine does not mean better thyroid function.
sea moss should not be used to self-treat Hashimoto’s disease, Graves’ disease, hypothyroidism,

researchNoteChunks.text:
hyperthyroidism, thyroid nodules, or another thyroid disorder.
fatigue, unexplained weight changes, palpitations, heat intolerance, or cold intolerance deserve medical
evaluation rather than self-treatment with sea moss.
women’s health and bone health
calcium is one sea moss nutrient that can be relevant to women’s health.
calcium is required for normal bone mineralization.
estrogen also helps maintain bone density.
estrogen levels decline during perimenopause and menopause.
declining estrogen can accelerate bone loss.
this contributes to the increased risk of osteoporosis after menopause.
sea moss can contribute some calcium.
the amount of calcium varies between products and serving sizes.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sea moss benefits for women
researchNoteChunks.text:
sea moss should not be treated as a complete bone-health strategy.
bone health also depends on adequate vitamin D.
adequate protein supports both muscles and bones.
weight-bearing physical activity helps maintain bone.
resistance exercise can support muscle and bone strength.
smoking, alcohol, age, family history, and certain medications can influence osteoporosis risk.
people at increased risk for osteoporosis may need screening or treatment.
sea moss cannot replace evidence-based osteoporosis prevention or care.
hormone, period, and fertility claims
sea moss is frequently promoted online as a “hormone-balancing” supplement.
sea moss does contain nutrients involved in normal physiological function.
nutrition can influence reproductive and metabolic health.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sea moss benefits for women
researchNoteChunks.text:
that does not establish sea moss as a hormone treatment.
sea moss has not been established as treatment for PCOS.
sea moss has not been established as treatment for endometriosis.
sea moss has not been established as treatment for irregular periods.
sea moss has not been established as a fertility treatment.
sea moss has not been established as treatment for menopause symptoms.
fertility depends on age, ovulation, ovarian function, sperm factors, uterine factors, medications, health
conditions, and many other variables.
persistent irregular periods deserve evaluation for their actual cause.
very heavy bleeding also deserves medical evaluation.
fertility concerns deserve appropriate reproductive assessment instead of reliance on one supplement.
a nutrient-containing food and a proven reproductive treatment are two different things.

researchNoteChunks.text:
heavy metals and environmental contaminants
seaweed absorbs substances directly from the surrounding seawater.
this helps explain why seaweed can contain useful minerals.
it also creates the possibility of accumulating environmental contaminants.
sea moss can contain arsenic.
sea moss can contain lead.
sea moss can contain cadmium.
sea moss can contain mercury.
concentrations can differ according to growing location and seaweed species.

dose, frequency, duration, and total exposure all matter.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sea moss benefits for women
researchNoteChunks.text:
repeated daily intake makes product quality especially important.
“natural” does not mean contaminant-free.
“wildcrafted” does not prove that a product is safer.
“organic” does not automatically mean heavy-metal-free.
transparent contaminant testing can provide more useful information than marketing language.
cadmium specifically
cadmium is a naturally occurring environmental metal.
industrial activity can also contribute to environmental cadmium.
plants and aquatic foods can absorb cadmium from soil or water.
food is an important route of cadmium exposure for the general population.
cadmium can accumulate in the body over time.
long-term excessive exposure can affect kidney health.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sea moss benefits for women
researchNoteChunks.text:
excessive long-term exposure can also affect bone health.
risk depends on total exposure rather than simply detecting any amount.
finding trace cadmium does not automatically mean acute poisoning will occur.
reducing unnecessary repeated exposure is the more practical concern.
product-quality testing becomes especially relevant when a supplement is consumed frequently.
pregnancy considerations
adequate iodine is particularly important during pregnancy.
maternal thyroid hormones contribute to fetal growth and neurological development.

researchNoteChunks.text:
this makes concentrated seaweed products a less predictable iodine source.

diet may also provide iodine through iodized salt, dairy foods, eggs, and seafood.

sea moss should not replace thyroid treatment during pregnancy.

professional.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sea moss benefits for women
researchNoteChunks.text:
normal infant thyroid function is important for growth and neurological development.
sea moss may also contain arsenic, lead, cadmium, and mercury.
iodine and contaminant concentrations can differ substantially between products.
direct information about sea moss concentrations in human milk is limited.
direct information about infant exposure after maternal sea moss use is limited.

how to use sea moss more safely
sea moss can be treated as an optional food instead of a medicinal cure.
sea moss gel can be mixed into smoothies.

researchNoteChunks.text:
it can be stirred into oatmeal.

powders can be mixed into foods or drinks.
capsules and gummies function more like concentrated supplements.
one studied amount discussed in the research was 4 grams daily.

look for transparent testing for heavy metals.

someone who dislikes sea moss does not need it for adequate nutrition.

researchNoteChunks.heading: seed cycling
researchNoteChunks.text:
what seed cycling is
seed cycling is a dietary wellness practice that rotates four seeds across different menstrual-cycle phases.
flaxseed and pumpkin seeds are usually eaten during the follicular phase.
sesame seeds and sunflower seeds are usually eaten during the luteal phase.
the routine is promoted as a way to influence estrogen and progesterone patterns.
the proposed explanations involve lignans, unsaturated fats, vitamin E, minerals, fiber, and other plant
compounds.
all four seeds are nutrient-dense foods regardless of menstrual timing.
the nutritional value of the seeds is better established than the claim that specific cycle-day timing is
necessary.
studies of an individual seed do not automatically prove that the entire seed-cycling protocol works.
emerging research has begun examining combinations of these seeds in women with menstrual concerns

researchNoteChunks.heading: seed cycling
researchNoteChunks.text:
and PCOS.
research protocols remain variable.
seed cycling can therefore be viewed as an emerging food-based practice instead of proven hormone
therapy.
how the menstrual cycle fits into the routine
the menstrual cycle begins on the first day of menstrual bleeding.
the follicular phase begins on the first day of the period.
follicles inside the ovary develop during this phase.
estrogen generally rises as a dominant follicle develops.
ovulation occurs when an egg is released from the ovary.

researchNoteChunks.heading: endometriosis awareness
researchNoteChunks.text: - endometriosis is a chronic gynecological condition where tissue similar to the endometrium (the lining of the uterus) grows outside the uterus, most commonly on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, pelvic lining, and in rare cases, beyond the pelvic region. it affects an estimated 10% of reproductive-age women worldwide, making it one of the leading causes of chronic pelvic pain and infertility. it is common but severely underdiagnosed.

researchNoteChunks.text: - pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea: severe menstrual cramps that don’t improve with standard pain relief.

researchNoteChunks.heading: endometriosis awareness
researchNoteChunks.text: - dyspareunia: pain during or after sex.

researchNoteChunks.heading: endometriosis awareness
researchNoteChunks.text: - chronic pelvic pain: pain unrelated to periods, persisting throughout the cycle.

researchNoteChunks.heading: endometriosis awareness
researchNoteChunks.text: - infertility: endometriosis is present in up to 50% of women with infertility issues.

researchNoteChunks.text: - other symptoms: pain with bowel movements or urination, bloating (“endo belly”), fatigue, nausea, and heavy or irregular menstrual bleeding.

researchNoteChunks.heading: link between fibroids & fertility (esp on black women)
researchNoteChunks.text: - uterine fibroids (also called leiomyomas) are among the most common benign tumors in women of reproductive age. they are tumors made of smooth muscle cells and fibrous connective tissue that develop in the uterus. studies estimate that 5–10% of infertile women have fibroids, and in 1–2.4% of infertility cases, fibroids may be the only identifiable cause

researchNoteChunks.heading: link between fibroids & fertility (esp on black women)
researchNoteChunks.text: - black women are particularly affected: they tend to develop fibroids earlier, with greater number, size, and symptom severity, compared to white women. because of more aggressive disease, the impact on fertility and pregnancy outcomes is often more pronounced.

researchNoteChunks.text: - fibroids in black women & fertility: disparities & amplified impacts

researchNoteChunks.text: - earlier, more aggressive onset: black women often develop fibroids at younger ages and tend to have more severe disease earlier in reproductive years, increasing the cumulative burden and risk of fertility impairment over time.

researchNoteChunks.text: - despite being disproportionately affected, black women are underrepresented in fibroid and fertility outcome studies. thus, many clinical recommendations are based mostly on data from white women, limiting the understanding of how fibroids uniquely affect fertility in black populations.

researchNoteChunks.text: - black women with fibroids often experience more complications, more invasive interventions, higher recurrence, longer recovery, and greater progression of disease. these compounded burdens can further impair fertility options and outcomes.

researchNoteChunks.heading: link between fibroids & fertility (esp on black women)
researchNoteChunks.text: - social determinants like access to quality care, delayed diagnosis, biases in health care, greater environmental exposures (e.g. hormone-disrupting chemicals [EDCs]), vitamin D deficiency, stress, and systemic racism contribute to both the heavier fibroid burden and worse reproductive outcomes in black women. :(

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates
researchNoteChunks.text: - maternal mortality has been rising in the u.s. in recent years, with the burden overwhelmingly borne by women of color, as american indian / alaska native (ai/an) and non-hispanic black women have had the highest aggregated pregnancy-related mortality rates. this disparity is stark: in 2022, the maternal mortality rate for black women was 49.5 deaths per 100,000 live births, which is roughly 3 to 3.5 times greater than the rate for white women (19.0), hispanic women (16.9), or asian women (13.2). disparities are even more extreme for certain causes, such as the risk of dying from eclampsia,

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates
researchNoteChunks.text: preeclampsia, or postpartum cardiomyopathy, which is about 5x greater for black women compared to white women, and these already elevated rates for complications like hemorrhage, embolism, and hypertensive disorders were further intensified by the covid-19 pandemic.

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates
researchNoteChunks.text: - black, ai/an, and some hispanic communities have higher prevalence of chronic conditions like hypertension, diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular disease. these raise risks during pregnancy and postpartum.

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates
researchNoteChunks.text: - many women of racial/ethnic minorities live in areas with fewer high-quality obstetric services, fewer specialists, or under-resourced hospitals. delays in diagnosis or treatment, fragmented prenatal or postpartum care, and lack of continuity exacerbate risk.

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates
researchNoteChunks.text: - studies and qualitative reports show that racism—both overt and subtle—affects how women are listened to, how symptoms are taken seriously, how aggressively treatments are pursued, and how care teams interact. black women report being dismissed or having their concerns downplayed.

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates
researchNoteChunks.text: - conditions such as housing instability, food insecurity, transportation barriers, environmental stressors, socioeconomic inequality, and lack of insurance coverage all disproportionately affect marginalized racial groups and make it harder to access preventive and emergent care.

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates
researchNoteChunks.text: - a substantial proportion of maternal deaths occur after delivery (within 42 days to 1 year postpartum). minority women are more likely to die in this “late maternal” period, especially from cardiomyopathy, embolism, and cardiovascular causes.

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates
researchNoteChunks.text: - over 60-80% of pregnancy-related deaths are considered preventable. many deaths result from failures at multiple levels: patient (delayed care seeking), provider (missed warning signs), facility (lack of protocols, poor escalation), and system (lack of resources, policies).

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates
researchNoteChunks.text: - black / non-hispanic black women suffer the largest absolute and relative disparity in maternal mortality.

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates
researchNoteChunks.text: - american indian / alaska native (ai/an) women show the highest rates in some time periods, especially when adjusted for age and across states.

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates
researchNoteChunks.text: - hispanic women historically had rates closer to or lower than white women, but during the pandemic their mortality ratios spiked (for a time surpassing white women in some settings).

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates
researchNoteChunks.text: - asian american / pacific islander women often have lower maternal mortality rates overall, though subgroups may experience risk depending on region and specific health profiles.

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates

researchNoteChunks.heading: racial disparities in maternal mortality rates

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: understanding female reproductive anatomy is key to empowerment, sexual health, and overall wellness. many myths persist, so here’s what the science actually says:

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: - myth: women’s reproductive organs are hard to locate or understand.

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: - fact: the vulva, clitoris, vagina, cervix, uterus, and ovaries are all identifiable and functionally interlinked. the clitoris alone has an internal structure nearly 9 cm long, extending alongside the vaginal canal (baskin et al., 1998). understanding these structures helps in sexual health, fertility awareness, and self-exams.

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: - myth: frequent douching or special washes are required.

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: - fact: the vagina maintains its own microbiome, dominated by lactobacillus species, which produce lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide to prevent infections (borges et al., 2014). over-washing or using fragranced products can disrupt this balance and increase the risk of bacterial vaginosis and yeast infections.

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: - myth: period blood is dirty or harmful if it touches skin

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: - fact: menstrual blood is composed of blood, endometrial tissue, and cervical mucus. it’s not toxic. good hygiene is about changing pads/tampons/cups regularly, not about “sterilizing” the vagina.

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: - myth: uterus is a passive organ

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: - fact: the uterus undergoes dynamic cycles—thickening, shedding, and contracting in response to hormonal signals (estradiol, progesterone). these contractions help with menstruation and support embryo implantation during fertility.

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: - myth: there’s one standard “shape or size” for vaginas, labia, or ovaries.

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: - fact: female anatomy varies widely across individuals. labia size, clitoral length, and vaginal canal depth can all differ naturally. these variations are normal and healthy, contrary to unrealistic media portrayals.

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: - myth: female sexual pleasure is just vaginal penetration.

researchNoteChunks.heading: debunking misconceptions about female reproductive anatomy
researchNoteChunks.text: - fact: the clitoris has extensive internal anatomy; orgasmic response can involve clitoral, vaginal, cervical, and even psychological stimulation. recognizing the internal clitoral network is important for comprehensive sexual health education.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sexual health + STIs (w/o stigma)
researchNoteChunks.text: - high prevalence, often asymptomatic: many STIs, such as chlamydia and gonorrhea, often show no symptoms in women, making routine screening crucial. untreated infections can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), infertility, and chronic pelvic pain.

researchNoteChunks.text: - viral vs. bacterial

researchNoteChunks.text: - abstinence (the obvious answer lol).

researchNoteChunks.heading: sexual health + STIs (w/o stigma)
researchNoteChunks.text: - barrier methods: consistent use of condoms and dental dams reduces STI transmission.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sexual health + STIs (w/o stigma)
researchNoteChunks.text: - vaccinations: HPV vaccines protect against cervical cancer and genital warts. Hepatitis B vaccine protects liver health.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sexual health + STIs (w/o stigma)
researchNoteChunks.text: - routine screening: CDC guidelines recommend sexually active women under 25 get screened for chlamydia and gonorrhea annually, or older women with risk factors. pap smears and HPV testing are essential for cervical cancer prevention.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sexual health + STIs (w/o stigma)
researchNoteChunks.text: - emphasize routine screening as part of overall wellness, not as a judgment of behavior.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sexual health + STIs (w/o stigma)
researchNoteChunks.text: - encourage open communication with partners regarding sexual history and testing.

researchNoteChunks.text: 4. supporting vaginal & reproductive health

researchNoteChunks.heading: sexual health + STIs (w/o stigma)
researchNoteChunks.text: - maintain a vaginal microbiome with gentle hygiene and probiotics (e.g., yogurt with live cultures).

researchNoteChunks.heading: sexual health + STIs (w/o stigma)
researchNoteChunks.text: - avoid scented douches or washes that can disrupt natural flora.

researchNoteChunks.text: - awareness of asymptomatic STIs, vaccination, and routine screening empowers women to take control of their reproductive health.

researchNoteChunks.heading: sexual health + STIs (w/o stigma)
researchNoteChunks.text: - educate yourself on early warning signs: unusual discharge, pain during urination, pelvic pain, or lesions, and seek care promptly.

researchNoteChunks.text: - sexual health and libido: testosterone (primary sex steroid hormone in both men & women; produced in adrenal glands & ovaries in women) contributes to sexual desire and arousal. low levels may result in reduced libido, while excessively high levels can cause symptoms like acne or hirsutism.

researchNoteChunks.text: - bone health: testosterone supports bone density by stimulating osteoblast activity, helping prevent osteoporosis in combination with estrogen.

researchNoteChunks.heading: testosterone in women (its role, the right amount, etc.)

researchNoteChunks.heading: testosterone in women (its role, the right amount, etc.)
researchNoteChunks.text: - mood & cognition: optimal testosterone levels are associated with better mood, energy, and cognitive function, including memory and focus.

researchNoteChunks.heading: testosterone in women (its role, the right amount, etc.)
researchNoteChunks.text: - metabolic health: testosterone influences fat distribution, insulin sensitivity, and energy metabolism.

researchNoteChunks.heading: history of reproductive justice + relevance today
researchNoteChunks.text: - reproductive justice is a framework that extends beyond what most “reproductive rights” discourse covers. it includes the right to have children, the right not to have children, and the right to parent children in safe, healthy, sustainable environments. it emphasizes bodily autonomy, parenthood, and social justice

researchNoteChunks.heading: history of reproductive justice + relevance today
researchNoteChunks.text: - term “reproductive justice” was coined in 1994 by a group of black women associated with sistersong and others during a meeting in chicago that was focused on universal health care and concerns about how health reform proposals ignored or marginalized the needs of black and brown women.

researchNoteChunks.heading: history of reproductive justice + relevance today
researchNoteChunks.text: - arose from critiques of mainstream feminist/reproductive rights movements that focused mostly on legal access to abortion and contraception, but often ignored intersectional factors like race, class, disability, immigration status, environment, economic barriers, and systemic inequalities [the reproductive rights framework is seen by RJ advocates as too narrow, often centering white, middle-class women].

researchNoteChunks.heading: history of reproductive justice + relevance today
researchNoteChunks.text: - key moments in history!

researchNoteChunks.heading: history of reproductive justice + relevance today
researchNoteChunks.text: - forced sterilization and eugenics: in the 20th century, many states in the u.s. passed eugenics policies targeting poor, black, latina, indigenous, disabled individuals. coerced sterilizations continued well into the 1970s and beyond.

researchNoteChunks.heading: history of reproductive justice + relevance today
researchNoteChunks.text: - madrigal v. quilligan (1978) was a case involving latina women in los angeles coerced into sterilization without adequate informed consent

researchNoteChunks.heading: history of reproductive justice + relevance today
researchNoteChunks.text: - in peru, the forced sterilization program of the 1990s targeted indigenous and rural women under ostensibly family planning programs, causing long-term harm.

researchNoteChunks.text: - abortion rights milestones

researchNoteChunks.heading: history of reproductive justice + relevance today
researchNoteChunks.text: - roe v. wade (1973) in the U.S. established a constitutional right to abortion (later overturned june 24, 2022).

researchNoteChunks.text: - the dobbs v. jackson women’s health organization decision (2022) removed the federal constitutional protection of abortion, prompting renewed mobilization for rj

researchNoteChunks.heading: history of reproductive justice + relevance today
researchNoteChunks.text: - the 1994 cairo conference on population and development and the 1995 beijing conference on women shifted global focus toward reproductive health as a human rights issue — these provided some political opening for reproductive justice discourse.

Ethics Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine. (2023).
Consideration of the gestational carrier: An Ethics Committee opinion. Fertility and
Sterility, 119(4), 583–588.
How To Talk To Your Children About Becoming A Surrogate
- Becoming a surrogate can bring up a lot of family feelings, so one of the biggest
concerns many women have is how to explain surrogacy to their own children.
Start Small And Early
- Start introducing the idea early instead of dropping it on your child all at once.
- It can help to explain surrogacy first as a general concept before saying that it is
something you are planning to do.
- This gives your child a little room to process the idea without feeling like everything
is suddenly decided already.
- It may also make them more comfortable asking questions and sharing how they
feel.
Explain It In Age-Appropriate Terms
- The explanation should match your child’s age and personality.
- Some children are more sensitive, more anxious, or more easily frightened than
others, so the explanation should feel clear without feeling scary.
- One example the article gives is a babysitter-style explanation:
- the surrogate is caring for the baby until the baby is healthy and strong
- then the baby goes to the parents, who will take care of them
- This can help children understand that the baby is not staying with your family after
birth.
- Another possible framing is that your family is helping another family.
Keep The Conversation Open
- After explaining surrogacy, let your child ask questions.
- Do not treat it like one single conversation and then done forever.
- Check in throughout the pregnancy to see how your child is feeling, how they are
coping, and whether they have new questions.
All Emotions Are Acceptable
- Children can feel happy, sad, jealous, confused, or upset about surrogacy, and the
article says these are all normal emotions.
- Let them express those feelings freely instead of shutting them down.
- If a child feels upset that the baby will not stay with your family, that feeling should
be acknowledged rather than minimized.
- You can still remind them that the baby is going to a loving family without dismissing
what they feel.
Big Takeaway
- The article frames surrogacy as something that affects the whole family, not just the
surrogate herself.
- So the goal is not only to explain the process.
- The goal is also to help your child feel included, informed, and emotionally
supported throughout it.
݁

becoming a surrogate. https://www.worldwidesurrogacy.org/blog/how-to-talk-to-

sources.title:
Mothers with higher adherence to this pattern had:
– higher MUFA in milk
– higher ALA in milk
– lower saturated fatty acids (SFA) in milk
This suggests maternal diet may affect whether breast milk has more unsaturated fats
vs more saturated fats.
Animal-Protein / Saturated-Fat Pattern
“Proteins and fatty acids with legs” pattern
Dominant nutrients in this pattern included:
– animal protein
– saturated fat (SFA)
– cholesterol
– calcium
– phosphorus
– zinc
– riboflavin
Foods correlated with this pattern included:
– milk
– cheese
– white meat
– processed meat
– red meat
– butter
This pattern was associated with:
– higher SFA in milk
– higher ω-6 in milk
– lower MUFA in milk
So diets heavier in animal products and saturated fats may shift milk toward a less
favorable fat profile compared with the more vegetable/fish-rich patterns.
Starch / Vegetable Protein Pattern
“Starch and vegetable proteins” pattern
Dominant nutrients included:
– starch
– vegetable protein
– sodium
Foods correlated with this pattern included:
– refined grain bread
– plain pasta
– pasta with meat
– soups
This pattern showed:
– only a weak positive association with lactose
Overall, it did not show major associations with milk fat quality like the other patterns.
What Foods Seemed Helpful in This Study
Based on the patterns associated with a more favorable milk fatty acid profile, the
study supports diets that include more of the following:
– fish
– olive oil
– raw vegetables
– cooked vegetables
– fruit
– soups
– fiber-rich foods
– vitamin- and mineral-rich foods
Especially important for milk composition were patterns linked to:
– omega-3 intake
– plant-rich diets
– fish-rich diets
What This Article Suggests About Breastfeeding Nutrition

mother but also because it may affect the nutrient quality of breast milk.

sources.title:
The strongest message is not “eat more calories” or “eat a perfect diet.”
It is more:
– overall dietary patterns matter
– a balanced, nutrient-rich diet may improve the fatty acid quality of breast milk
– omega-3-related milk components seem especially influenced by maternal diet
What This Article Did NOT Show
This study did not show that maternal diet strongly changes:
– milk protein
– total milk fat amount
– milk energy
– major milk macronutrients overall
So the paper does not support the idea that every aspect of milk changes
dramatically based on what a mother eats.
Instead, the stronger evidence here is for:
– milk fatty acid composition, especially omega-3-related fats
Simple Practical Summary
If you turn this paper into a practical breastfeeding nutrition takeaway, it would be:

                  @fruitsoflife.xo’s Ultimate Guide!   🍋‍🟩🍍🍅🍇 . ˖

Hello there! ( ´ ▽ ` )ﾉ Before we delve into all of the tips & tricks, I just wanted
to sincerely thank you for supporting @fruitsoflife.xo. Your support truly means
the world to me! I created this guide with love to offer soft, research-based
education (based on my social media posts) for anyone navigating pregnancy,
postpartum recovery, and women’s wellness more broadly. My hope is that you will
feel more informed, supported, and cared for along the way. Hope you enjoy it! ♡


Nurturing life, softly,
FruitsofLife.xo (⌒ ‿ ⌒)

        Chapter 1: Caring For Your Body

Key Vitamins & Minerals For Women
Vitamins, minerals, and everything in between! (￣︶￣) Before we get into specific
foods and nutrients, I want to start with one comforting truth: women do not
need perfect diets to properly support their bodies. What usually matters most
is building a steady, nourishing foundation over time! This section is here to help
you understand the core vitamins and minerals women hear about all the time, why
they matter, and what you can actually do with that information in daily life.


When people talk about women’s health, they often jump straight to hormones,
fertility, pregnancy, or aging. But underneath all of that is something simpler: your
body needs enough nutrients to function well. Those nutrients support energy,
blood health, bones, mood, skin, immunity, metabolism, reproduction, and recovery.
So yes, the topic is basic, but it is also very, very important!


And, as always, this section is for education only, not medical advice.

7


Main Content ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

A good place to begin is this: women’s nutrient needs are not totally different
from men’s, but there are certain nutrients that become especially crucial because
of menstruation, fertility, pregnancy, breastfeeding, bone health, thyroid health,
and aging. That is why it helps to think in terms of life stages, not just generic
nutrition advice.


      ☆ Think “Food First”, Not Fear First
            ​ A balanced diet with fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins,
             legumes, dairy or fortified alternatives, nuts, seeds, and healthy fats
             can cover a lot.
                    ​Actual meals are the prime focus! Those trendy drinks and
                    powders can be supplementary, but they should not replace
                    actual sustenance.
            ​You do not need to obsess over every nutrient every day.
                    ​ Follow through on patterns rather than trying to achieve the
                    picture-perfect diet. One imperfect week of eating is not the
                    end of the world—don’t worry! ( ◜ ‿ ◝ )♡
            ​If your intake is limited, you’re pregnant, postpartum, or dealing with
             any medical condition, it may be worth discussing labs or supplements
             with a provider.


The most important lesson from this section is “what is this nutrient and what does
it help me do?” That’ll make the information much easier to remember!
Additionally, attached below is a plate rich with target food group examples I
created for visualization purposes! \( ^ ᵕ ^ )/

8




    ☆ Vitamin A: The Growth, Vision, And Reproduction Helper!
         ​ Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, cellular growth, and
          reproduction. It is also a high-priority nutrient in pregnancy,
          especially because it plays a role in fetal development.
               ​ Food sources of preformed vitamin A include eggs, cheese,
                milk, liver, and oily fish like mackerel.
               ​ Food sources of beta-carotene include carrots, sweet potatoes,
                spinach, apricots, and mangoes.
                      ​So basically, if you want a “vitamin A support” addition to
                       your plate, think orange vegetables + dark leafy greens
                       + a protein source.

9

                 ​ Now, vitamin A matters, but in pregnancy especially, more is
                  not always better. High-dose vitamin A supplements or very
                  high intakes of preformed vitamin A can be harmful, so
                  supplementation should be discussed with a provider.
                       ​ This is why a food-first approach is usually gentler than
                        randomly supplementing.


    ☆ Vitamin E: The Antioxidant Beauty-And-Cell Protection Nutrient!
           ​ Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, which means it helps protect cells
           from damage. It also supports skin health and may help support
           immune function.
                 ​ Food sources include sunflower oil, rapeseed oil, grapeseed oil,
                  olive oil, almonds, sunflower seeds, and wheat germ.
                 ​Women who smoke or have conditions linked to higher oxidative
                  stress may especially benefit from paying attention to
                  antioxidant-rich foods!
                       ​Adding a handful of almonds, sunflower seeds, or a little
                        olive oil to meals can be a quick and efficient way to
                        bring more vitamin E into your routine. :-)


    ☆ Folate: One Of The Biggest Must-Knows For Women Of Reproductive
    Age!
           ​ Folate is one of the most significant nutrients for women who could
           become pregnant. It supports cell division and DNA production, and it
           helps prevent major birth defects of the brain and spine.
                 ​ Food sources include spinach, kale, broccoli, asparagus, peas,
                  beans, lentils, enriched breads, pastas, and cereals.
                 ​If you are in your reproductive years, it is smart to keep
                  folate-rich foods in regular rotation even if pregnancy is not
                  immediately on your mind!
                 ​Easy meal ideas:
                       ​Lentil soup + greens.
                       ​Bean bowl with broccoli.

10

                       ​Fortified cereal + fruit.
                       ​Pasta with spinach and peas.


     ☆ Vitamin D: The Bone, Immunity, And Hormone Support Nutrient!
          ​ Vitamin D helps with calcium absorption, which makes it especially
           important for bone health. It also supports immune function and may
           play a role in hormone regulation.
                ​ Sources include sunlight exposure, salmon, sardines, red meat,
                 egg yolks, fortified cereals, dairy milk, and fortified plant
                 milks.
                       ​If you don’t get much sun, do not eat much fish, or mostly
                          eat indoors, it is definitely worth paying attention to your
                          vitamin D intake!


     ☆ Vitamin B12: Especially Important For Blood, Nerves, And The Brain!
          ​ Vitamin B12 is essential for making red blood cells and supporting
           brain and nerve function.
                ​ Food sources include meat, fish, eggs, poultry, dairy, fortified
                 cereals, and nutritional yeast.
                ​ Women who are pregnant, vegetarian, vegan, or over 50 may be
                 at higher risk of not getting enough!
                ​ If someone is eating very little animal food, B12 becomes a
                 nutrient to consciously plan for (supplements may be needed).
                       ​ Fortified foods can help, but many women in higher-risk
                          groups may need to discuss additional support with a
                          provider!

     ☆ B-Complex Vitamins: The Subtle Workhorses Behind Energy, Skin,
     Nerves, And Mood!
          ​ Beyond B12 and folate, other B vitamins matter too! ( ´ ω ` ) These
           include B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, and biotin, and they help with energy
           metabolism, skin health, nervous system function, and mood regulation.
                ​ B1: peas and whole grains.
                ​ B2 (riboflavin): milk, eggs, leafy greens.

11

                   ​ B3 (niacin): meat, fish, nuts.
                   ​ B6 (pyridoxine): meat, poultry, fish, bananas, potatoes.
                          ​ Women especially should keep these in mind because
                          pregnancy, dietary restrictions, and changing needs
                          across life stages can all affect B-vitamin intake!
                          ​ If your diet is very limited or highly processed, B
                          vitamins are one of the first places to tighten things up.

      ☆ Vitamin C: For Collagen, Healing, And Iron Absorption (Not Just
      Immunity)!
            ​ Vitamin C is an antioxidant, but it is also central for wound healing,
             collagen formation, and helping the body absorb iron from plant foods.
                   ​ Food sources include oranges, grapefruit, kiwi, mangoes,
                   strawberries, peppers, broccoli, and tomatoes.
                   ​ Pairing plant-based iron foods with a vitamin C food increases
                   iron bioavailability and absorption!
                          ​Examples of this:
                                 ​Beans + bell peppers (like in a burrito bowl!).
                                 ​Lentils + tomatoes.
                                 ​Spinach + strawberries or citrus.
                                        ​ This is especially helpful for women who are
                                        trying to support iron status without relying
                                        entirely on meat.

      ☆ Choline: One Of The Most Underrated Nutrients For Women!
            ​ Choline helps with brain development, neurotransmitter production,
             cell membrane structure, and methylation. It is especially important
             during pregnancy and lactation!
                   ​ Food sources include egg yolks, meat, poultry, fish, dairy,
                   legumes, broccoli, and Brussels sprouts.


Once you understand the vitamins, the next big category is minerals. These are
worth paying attention to because they affect bones, blood, muscles, nerves,
thyroid function, and metabolism!（ * ＾ ＾ * )

12



     ☆ Calcium: One Of The Biggest Bone-Health Priorities For Women
     (Especially In The Face Of Osteoporosis… (゜ Д゜； ) )!
          ​ Calcium helps build and maintain strong bones and teeth! Because
           women face a higher risk of osteoporosis, especially after menopause,
           calcium deserves special attention.
                ​ Food sources include milk, cheese, yogurt, broccoli, kale, tofu,
                 sardines, and fortified plant milks.
                ​Examples of ways to build calcium into your routine:
                         ​ Yogurt at breakfast.
                         ​ Tofu in stir-fry.
                         ​ Fortified plant milk in smoothies.
                         ​ Leafy greens in meals.
                ​ Also, calcium works closely with vitamin D, so think of those
                 two together and you’re golden!

     ☆   Magnesium:      Your      Ride   Or   Die   When   It   Comes   To   Calming,
     Muscle-And-Nerve Support!
          ​ Magnesium is involved in hundreds of body processes, including muscle
           function, nerve function, blood glucose regulation, and blood pressure
           control. It often comes up in lots of discussions about stress &
           cramping.
                ​ Food sources include pumpkin seeds, almonds, cashews, spinach,
                 edamame, and legumes.


     ☆ Iodine: The Thyroid Support Material!
          ​ Iodine is needed to make thyroid hormones, which help regulate
           metabolism.
                ​ Food sources include fish, shellfish, milk, yogurt, and iodized
                 salt.
                         ​ Thyroid health encompasses energy, mood, metabolism,
                         and temperature regulation, so iodine is not a minor
                         detail.

13

Alright, now it’s time to delve into trace minerals! Although they are only needed
in small amounts, they still support major functions!

      ☆ Zinc:
            ​Supports immune function, wound healing, DNA synthesis, and may
             play a role in fertility.
                   ​ Food sources: oysters, red meat, poultry, eggs, dairy, nuts,
                    whole grains.


      ☆ Selenium:
            ​Helps with antioxidant defense and thyroid function.
                   ​ Food sources: fish, shellfish, red meat, grains, eggs, chicken,
                    garlic.


      ☆ Copper, Manganese, Molybdenum:
            ​These help with enzyme activity and metabolism.
                   ​ Food sources: legumes, nuts, whole grains, and organ meats.
                          ​ Now, trust me when I say that you do not need to obsess
                              over any of these nutrients! Eating a varied diet helps
                              cover them naturally. ♡

Okay, now that we’ve cleared up the individual nutrients, let’s zoom out and answer
a question we touched on earlier: which nutrients matter most at different
stages of life?

      ☆ For Women Of Reproductive Age (~15-49)
            ​ Folate is a big one!
            ​ Iron, which is especially relevant while you still have your period.
            ​ B12 matters, especially for women eating vegetarian or vegan diets.
            ​ Vitamin C helps with iron absorption.
            ​ Choline is worth knowing about early, not only once pregnant.


      ☆ During Pregnancy & Postpartum

14

            ​ Nutrients like folate, choline, B vitamins, zinc, and iron help support
            maternal health, fetal growth, neural development, and recovery!
            ​In the case of nausea, food aversions, anemia, or dietary restrictions,
            a provider can help individualize this! :-)


      ☆ During Perimenopause & Menopause
            ​ Calcium and vitamin D become especially important, as they relate to
            bone health & oxidative stress.
            ​ Estrogen decline can alter bone and metabolic patterns, so food
            choices have more of an impact!

      ☆ As Women Age
            ​ Absorption of B12 and vitamin D may decrease.
            ​Needs around bone support, protein, and antioxidant-rich foods
            become more crucial.


At the end of the day, nutrition for women is not about perfection. It is about
giving your body enough support to do all of the things it is constantly doing like
cycling, healing, adapting, carrying oxygen, protecting bones, managing hormones,
and getting you through everyday life!


1-week Nutrient-Rich Sample Meal Plan ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚
      ☆ How To Use This:
            ​ This is a sample framework, not a rigid prescription.
            ​Feel free to mix and match meals based on appetite, budget, culture,
            and preferences! :-)
            ​The goal is nutrient coverage across the week, not perfection in every
            single meal (because, let’s face it, that's extremely unrealistic
            (＃＞＜;) ).

Conclusion ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

If there is one takeaway from this section, let it be this: women’s nutrition is not
just about calories; it is about support. The right vitamins & minerals help your
body feel steadier, stronger, clearer, and more resilient across every stage of life.
You do not need to memorize everything at once (this isn’t an exam ( ⁀ ᗢ ⁀ )).
Start by noticing the big ones—folate, iron, vitamin D, calcium, B12, vitamin C,
magnesium, and choline—and focus on building a nourishing pattern over time. Add
a sprinkle of colour to your plate and you’re in tip-top shape! ( ⌒ ω ⌒ )☆

Weight Loss & S trength Training
Let’s make this feel a lot simpler and a lot less intimidating, shall we? <(￣︶￣)>
When women think about exercise for weight loss or toning, it is so easy to get
overwhelmed by all the options and all the “perfect” routines online. But in real life,
the best plan is usually the one that feels doable, sustainable, and matched to your
energy, age, and fitness level! One notably interesting thing from the cited
research here is that strength training stood out strongly for improving body
composition,   especially   when   it   came   to   lowering   body fat percentage.
Hydrogymnastics was another standout, which is a great reminder that low-impact
movement can still be very effective! Fun fact: because hydrogymnastics is
gentler on the joints, it may be especially appealing for older women or women who
want a more gentle-feeling entry into exercise! ( . ‿ . ) So, in short, you do not
need the hardest workout to make progress. You need the right one for you. This
section is here to help you figure out what that workout may look like!

Now, another thing to keep in mind is that modifying is not failing. It is actually

modified pushups! If balance feels shaky, hold onto something while doing
split-squats or single-leg work. If jumping bothers your joints, do regular squats
instead of jump squats. That is the goal, really: not to do the fanciest version, but
to do the version you can do well, safely, and consistently.


☆ Why A Caloric Deficit Can Help Even More


Exercise alone does not always create the same changes as exercise paired with
dietary weight loss. If your goal is fat loss or body recomposition, pairing exercise
with a gentle, realistic calorie deficit can be especially helpful. A calorie deficit
simply means eating slightly less energy than your body uses, so your body has
to pull from stored energy over time. It does not have to mean extreme dieting,
starving, or being downright miserable. In one study, cited below, women who lost
at least 5% of their starting body weight tended to see stronger improvements in
inflammation-related markers, meaning that even modest weight loss can matter!
With that said, here’s how a healthy calorie deficit can look in real life:


      ☆ Pairing strength training with more mindful portions.
      ☆ Building meals around protein, fiber, and whole foods.
      ☆ Reducing excess liquid calories or mindless snacking.
      ☆ Staying consistent enough to create a small deficit over time.

be such a useful tool for women because it supports muscle tone, body composition,
strength, and long-term health all at once. Whether your starting point is 2x/week
beginner or 4x/week intermediate, what matters most is choosing something that
feels realistic, safe, and sustainable for your body. Little by little, those
consistent choices really do add up. ( ´ ｖ ｀ ) So be gentle with yourself, stay

How S tress Affects Your Hormones
Stress is one of those things that can feel so normal that women forget how
deeply it can affect the body. But hormonally, it can be a pretty big deal! When
stress becomes frequent, intense, or long-lasting, it can affect other factors
beyond mood, such as ovulation, cycles, energy, metabolism, and even how
supported your body feels overall. So if you have ever noticed your period acting up
during a particularly hard season, or felt like your body was “off” when life dealt
you a bad hand, you are absolutely not imagining it.


The good news is that stress is not just something to “push through.” It is
something women can learn to notice, work with, and regulate. This section will
focus on both sides of that coin: how stress affects hormones, and what you can
actually do about it in real life! d(⌒ー⌒)


And, as always, this section is for education only, not medical advice.

34


Main Content ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

When your body perceives psychological, physical, or emotional stress, it activates
the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. In plain English, this is one of the
body’s main stress-response systems!


      ☆ What Happens During The Stress Response (In Simplest Terms):
           ​ The hypothalamus releases CRH (corticotropin-releasing hormone).
           ​ That signals the pituitary gland to release ACTH (adrenocorticotropic
            hormone).
           ​ ACTH then prompts the adrenal glands to release cortisol.
           ​ Cortisol is often called the stress hormone.


That response can be helpful in short bursts (like an adrenaline rush). The problem
is when stress becomes chronic. Then, instead of briefly helping you adapt, the
system can start interfering with other hormone pathways.


☆ How Stress Can Interfere With Ovulation


      ☆ Cortisol And CRH Can Suppress The HPG Axis.
           ​ This can reduce GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) pulses.
           ​Lower GnRH can blunt LH & FSH.
           ​LH and FSH are both needed for healthy ovarian function.
                  ​Over time, this can contribute to:
                        ​ Irregular periods.
                        ​ Missed ovulation.
                        ​ Anovulation.
                        ​ Cycle disruption.

35

In the cited study of healthy women tracking daily stress, higher recent stress
was linked to lower estradiol, lower LH, lower luteal progesterone, and higher FSH.
Importantly, higher stress also increased the odds of sporadic anovulation, which
means a cycle where ovulation does not happen. That is a big reminder that stress
can affect the cycle even when everything else seems “fine” on the outside.


      ☆ Another Important Pathway: Kisspeptin!
            ​ Kisspeptin is a neuropeptide that helps stimulate GnRH.
            ​Stress and low-energy states can reduce kisspeptin activity.
            ​This can suppress ovulation.
            ​ This    is   one   mechanism      involved   in   functional   hypothalamic
            amenorrhea (FHA).


This all goes to show that, yes, stress can show up hormonally in various tangible
ways—not just emotionally. And stress-related hormone disruption signs kind of
sneak up on you, as they are not always crystal clear at first! (             x   ＿ x )
Sometimes it starts with smaller shifts that are easy to brush off.


      ☆ Possible Signs Stress Is Affecting Hormonal Health:
            ​Irregular periods.
            ​ Missed periods.
            ​ Heavier or lighter bleeding.
            ​ More painful cycles.
            ​ Changes in cycle length.
            ​ Feeling like your cycle is suddenly less predictable.
            ​ Signs of weak ovulatory function.
            ​ Worsening of existing hormonal issues.


            ☆ Long-Term Chronic Stress May Contribute To / Worsen:
                     ​ Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.
                     ​ Ovulatory dysfunction.
                     ​ Luteal phase defects.
                     ​ Worsening of PCOS.
                     ​ More noticeable menstrual symptoms.

36

And that’s not all! Stress can affect multiple endocrine systems at once.

        ☆ Other Hormone Systems Stress Can Influence:
              ​Thyroid hormones.
              ​ Prolactin (hormone responsible for lactation).
              ​ Growth hormone.
              ​ Catecholamines    (molecules that are both neurotransmitters and
              hormones).
              ​ Broader adrenal and metabolic signaling.


This is why chronic stress can feel so “whole-body-ish” to women. Additionally, we
can notice changes in energy, blood sugar, weight, sleep, mood, and cycles all at
once.

☆ Why Some Hormonal Phases Can Feel Extra Sensitive

Hormones and stress are closely intertwined, kind of like a wildly dysfunctional
married couple where neither can stand the other, but they absolutely refuse to
get a divorce. (｀⌒´メ) Stress affects hormones, but hormone shifts can also
affect how stress feels. That helps explain why some women feel more anxious,
overwhelmed, or emotionally fragile at specific points in the cycle. It is not “just in
your head.” It’s biology!

        ☆ Periods of lower estrogen may make women more vulnerable to the
        psychological effects of stress.
        ☆ Estrogen helps influence brain circuits involved in stress response.
        ☆ When estrogen shifts, stress can feel more intense emotionally and
        physically.


☆ What To Actually Do When Stress Is Messing With Your Body

37

The best part of this section is that stress regulation does not have to be fancy.
According to one study, even short mindfulness exercises could measurably reduce
acute physiologic stress. That matters because sometimes women (and people for
that matter) need tools that work in five minutes, not a full wellness retreat!
( ￣ー ￣ ) The three exercises studied were:

         1.​ Grounding: When Your Thoughts Are Spiraling.
                  ​A mindfulness exercise that helps bring attention back to the
                  present moment. It stops your brain from jumping ten steps
                  ahead, thereby interrupting the stress loop before it escalates.
                        ​Grounding may help when you feel:
                              ​ Scattered.
                              ​ Overstimulated.
                              ​ Mentally overloaded.
                              ​ Stuck in anticipatory stress.
                              ​ Unable to stop overthinking.
                                       ​ How-to: Look around and name:
                                             ​ 5 things you see.
                                             ​ 4 things you feel.
                                             ​ 3 things you hear.
                                             ​ 2 things you smell.
                                             ​ 1 thing you taste.
                              ​Or go down the affirmation route & simply plant
                               your feet and say:
                                       ​ “I am here. I am safe. I can take this one
                                       step at a time.”
                        ​ Grounding is linked to signs of greater parasympathetic
                         activation,    which    is   the    body’s   more   restful,
                         recovery-oriented state.


         2.​ Deep Breathing: When Your Body Feels Rushed Or Activated.
                  ​One of the fastest ways to influence the nervous system. It
                  slows the body down and reduces automatic arousal.
                        ​ 4–7–8 breathing.

                          ​ Inhale for 4 seconds.
                          ​ Hold for 7 seconds.
                          ​ Exhale for 8 seconds.
                                ​Do 3–5 rounds before bed.
                                ​ Try   it before an appointment, difficult
                                 conversation, or stressful task (or when you
                                 notice you are a little more tense than
                                 usual).
     3.​ Body Scan: When Stress Feels Stored Physically.
             ​ This was the strongest exercise in the study. It is a slow
              check-in where you bring awareness to different parts of the

              judgment!
                   ​This is helpful when you feel fine mentally, but you feel

                          ​ How-to:
                                ​ Start at your forehead.
                                ​Move slowly through:
                                        ​Jaw.
                                        ​Neck.
                                        ​Shoulders.
                                        ​Chest.
                                        ​Stomach.
                                        ​Hips.
                                        ​Legs.
                                        ​Feet.

                                        ​“Am I holding tension here?”
                                        ​“Can I reduce that tension by even
                                           5%?”

The more often your body is stuck in fight-or-flight, the harder it is to support

The Importance of Regular Checkups
A doctor a day keeps the… yeah, I don’t know where I was going with that one
either. ┐(´～｀ˇ)┌ There is just something so empowering about simply being aware
of what is going on in your body. Regular checkups and screenings are not just
boring little calendar tasks sitting on your to-do list—they are actually one of the
kindest, smartest forms of self-care a woman can give herself! They help catch
problems that lurk in the corners before they start making a scene, create space
for important conversations, and make it easier to get support earlier rather than
later.


A lot of women mistakenly wait until something feels “really wrong” before booking
an appointment. But many important conditions do not start with obvious symptoms.
That is exactly why preventive care matters! The goal is to help you stay informed,
supported, and one step ahead without giving you a fright!


And, as always, this section is for education only, not medical advice.

Regular checkups and screenings can help detect health issues early, when they
are often easier to treat and less likely to cause bigger complications later! That
includes conditions like cancer, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, and
certain reproductive-health concerns. Preventive care is so important for a number
of reasons:
      ☆ Many screenable conditions can be present long before symptoms appear.
              ☆ Early detection → earlier treatment → higher chance of better
              outcomes.
      ☆ Preventive visits can also reduce the chance of needing more invasive or
      costly care later.
      ☆ Regular visits create a space to talk about things women often put off,

              ​Fertility concerns.
              ​Menopause.
              ​Intimate partner violence.
              ​Contraception.
              ​Reproductive planning.

a comprehensive check-in where your clinician helps guide screening decisions,
reviews your health history, and talks through risk factors or life-stage needs.

A lot of women realize a little too late that they should’ve paid attention in Sex

A lot of STIs are common, many are treatable, and many cause few or no early

48


Main Content ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

Sexual health is not about being “good” or “bad.” It is about being informed,
protected, and well-cared for. Routine sexual health habits can help women lower
risk, catch concerns earlier, and feel more confident having honest conversations
with partners and healthcare providers. Like jeez… a sexually transmitted
disease/infection is an illness, not a defining characteristic, and it should
definitely be treated as such. (｀_´) Here’s what sexual health really includes:
     ​Preventing sexually transmitted infections, or STIs.
     ​ Recognizing symptoms early when they do show up.
     ​Getting routine screening even when you feel completely fine.
     ​Protecting the vaginal and reproductive environment from unnecessary
      irritation & disruption.
     ​Communicating     clearly   with   partners   about   testing,   symptoms, and
      protection.


Part of why this matters is that many women are taught to only pay attention to
sexual health once something feels urgent, scary, or straight up embarrassing.
（＠´＿｀＠）In actuality, the healthiest approach is much more routine and far less
dramatic. Because, sometimes, STIs are almost too un-dramatic to be noticed!
     ​Many STIs, especially chlamydia and gonorrhea, are often asymptomatic in
      women.
     ​ “Asymptomatic” simply means there may be no obvious symptoms at all.
            ​ So, as a little tidbit for your awareness (not fear): a woman can feel
             normal and still have an infection!
     ​Untreated infections can sometimes lead to pelvic inflammatory disease,
      infertility, or chronic pelvic pain.

The body is wise, but in this department it’s not always the dramatic oversharer we
might want it to be! One of the biggest practical takeaways here is pretty simple:

because the female body doesn’t always ring an alarm bell on these things! Now,

     ​ Use condoms consistently, not just when it feels convenient.

Building Your Support System
“Clean this, cook this, take care of this….” There is something so naggingly
exhausting about always being the one who keeps everything afloat. So many women
are taught how to be dependable, nurturing, emotionally aware, and endlessly
available long before they are taught how to say, “Hey, I need help too.” That is
part of why this conversation matters so much. A support system is not just some
cherry on top of the sundae that is “real” health. It is part of health. A big part
at that! The people around you, the care available to you, and the spaces where you
feel safe all play a role in how well you cope, recover, rest, and keep going! Support
can protect mental health, reduce the effects of chronic stress, and make life’s
bumpy road feel less lonely and less scary. And thankfully, building support does
not require having a giant friend group or a perfect life! It simply means learning
how to create a network that is real, usable, and supportive in the ways you
actually need. (─ ‿ ─)

57

As always, this section is for education only, not medical advice. Care should
always be individualized, especially when mental health struggles are severe or
ongoing!


Main Content ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

A support system can be a protective factor against both physical and mental
health challenges. In very vivid ways, support acts like a buffer against disease and
stress, a psychological safety net, and a foundation for empowerment. Now, what is
a support system exactly?


      ☆ (˶ ˘ ³˘)ˆᵕ ˆ˶) Support System: The People, Spaces, And Relationships
      That Help Protect Your well-being!
            ​This can include friends, family, mentors, healthcare providers,
             therapists, professors, faith communities, neighbors, and community
             networks.
            ​ Alongside helping you emotionally, a good support system helps you
             function, recover, make decisions, and feel less alone.
                  ​Strong social ties → lower mortality, better immune function,
                   faster recovery from illness, and reduced stress-related
                   disease!


Support also comes in different forms, which is important because sometimes
women think, “But I do have people around me,” while still feeling unsupported.
Often, the issue is not that there is no one by your side. It is that the type of
support you need is missing!


☆ The Four Types Of Support And Their Impact


      ☆ Emotional Support
            ​Empathy, listening, comfort, and feeling understood.
            ​This might look like a friend who lets you vent, a sister who checks in,
             or a family member who can sit with your pain without rushing you.

58

           ​This type of support can help reduce anxiety and improve self-esteem.


      ☆ Instrumental Support
           ​Practical help; things like childcare, transportation, financial help,
            meals, errands, or hands-on assistance.
           ​ This kind of support can reduce burnout, especially for mothers,
            caregivers, and women juggling too many responsibilities at once.


      ☆ Informational Support
           ​Guidance that helps you make clearer decisions.
           ​This may come from healthcare providers, mentors, support groups,
            therapists, professors, or trusted educators.
           ​It improves decision-making and health literacy, meaning your ability
            to understand health information and actually use it in real life.


      ☆ Appraisal Support
           ​Honest feedback, grounded encouragement, and perspective.
           ​ This is the kind of support that helps you trust your judgment, cope
            better, and remember that you are capable.
           ​ It strengthens self-efficacy, which is defined as confidence in your
            ability to handle challenges.


Once you see support this way, the whole topic becomes way less obscure! You can
start noticing whether you are missing emotional comfort, practical help,
trustworthy guidance, or honest encouragement. Now that goes beyond just
“having people in your life.” And there’s more! As mentioned before, support
matters for both mental and physical health.


      ☆ Mental Health
           ​Lower risk of depression, anxiety, and PTSD.
                  ​This is especially important for women coping with trauma,
                  chronic illness, reproductive challenges, pregnancy stress,
                  miscarriage, infertility, or postpartum mental health struggles.

59

                   ​ Strengthens resilience, which is the capacity to adapt and
                    recover from stress.


        ☆ Physical Health
             ​Lower blood pressure, better cardiovascular health, and stronger
              immune response.
             ​ Can reduce some of the harmful physiological effects of chronic
              stress hormones such as cortisol.
                   ​Being supported can help the body carry stress with less wear
                    and tear.
             ​Also, consistent support makes women more likely to stick with
              medical treatments and maintain healthier habits!


Okay, if good support comes in so many fabulous shapes and sizes, and has so many
benefits, why does finding it feel like an endless treasure hunt? Let’s dive into
the plethora of answers to that question!


        ☆ We’ve normalized women being the ‘rock’ for everyone else, but we
        haven’t made it normal for women to have a rock of their own.
              ☆ Isolation is common among new mothers, older women, and women

              ☆   Cultural norms in some settings may discourage vulnerability,
