Easing Pregnancy Discomforts
Growing a human is a miraculous experience, but it does in fact come with a side of
“glitchy” physical discomforts that weren’t in the starter pack. One week it is
nausea, the next it is heartburn, leg cramps, swelling, back pain, or sleep that
disappears the second your head hits the pillow. Talk about a serious test of your
internal server capacity. So if your body feels a little out of whack right now, that
does not automatically mean anything is wrong. It could just mean your body is
doing a lot. ( －ω － ) 。oO

But, let’s try to see the glass half full! (づ˶˃⤙˂˶)づ Pregnancy discomforts are
common, manageable, and surprisingly responsive to small daily adjustments. This
section is here to help you distinguish between “normal-but-annoying” changes and
symptoms that deserve a call to your provider, while also giving you real-life
relief tips that can make this season feel a little less harsh.

As always, this section is for education only, not medical advice.

301


Main Content ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

Pregnancy discomforts tend to shift by trimester, which is part of why they can
feel so hectic! Just when you adjust to one thing, your body introduces another
little ( usually unpleasant (⁠T⁠﹏ ⁠T ⁠) ) surprise. Don’t we just love that?


☆ How Discomforts Change By Trimester
      ​First trimester: sharp hormonal changes can bring about fatigue, nausea,
      vomiting, headaches, and moodiness.
      ​Second trimester: some early symptoms may ease, but new aches, swelling,
      and pressure can start showing up as the body grows.
      ​Third trimester: the added weight of the fetus can strain joints, press on
      organs, and make symptoms like heartburn, shortness of breath, bladder
      pressure, and sleep problems more noticeable.

That said, common does not mean you should suffer silently through everything! If
that were the case, the human race would have been a limited-time-only event, if
we’re being for real. ( ─ ‿ ─ ) There’s a whole toolkit of ways to support your
body while pregnant. One of the most useful pregnancy skills is: not freaking out
over every twinge, but also not brushing off symptoms that are trying to tell
you something important.


      ☆ Normal Discomfort Vs. When To Call A Provider
            ​Many minor discomforts are a normal part of pregnancy.
            ​Severe or persistent symptoms deserve medical attention.
                   ​Severe vomiting could point to hyperemesis gravidarum rather
                    than ordinary morning sickness.
                          ​Sudden, severe swelling could be more serious and may
                           need urgent evaluation.
            ​Any symptom that feels intense, unusual, or rapidly worsening is worth
             checking with your provider.

302

Okay, enough with the preamble. ( . ^ ◡ ^ . ) Let’s talk symptoms, solutions, and how
to reclaim your comfort!

         1.​ Fatigue
            ​Feeling exhausted is common, especially in the first & third
             trimesters.
                  ​Your body is doing an enormous amount of behind-the-scenes
                   work, even when you are technically doing nothing.
            ​Fatigue can also be worsened by anemia, so a blood test may be useful
             if exhaustion feels especially heavy or persistent.


             ☆ Tips To Ease Pregnancy Fatigue
                  ​Keep a regular sleep schedule as much as possible.
                           ​Take short naps earlier in the day, ideally before 3 p.m.,
                           so they do not interfere with nighttime sleep.
                  ​Include safe daily exercise, because light movement can
                   sometimes improve energy more than inactivity.
                           ​Ask your provider whether you should be checked for
                           anemia if fatigue feels excessive!
         2.​ Headaches
                  ​Headaches are especially common in the first trimester.
                           ​Hormonal changes, increased blood volume, dehydration,
                           and stress can all play a role.
                  ​Pregnancy-safe medication decisions should always go through
                   your provider, since common pain relievers are not all equally
                   safe in pregnancy.

             ☆ Tips To Ease Pregnancy Headaches
                  ​Apply an ice pack or cool compress.
                  ​Drink plenty of water, with a goal of around 10 to 12 glasses
                   daily if your provider has not told you otherwise.
                           ​A   lot   of   pregnancy   headaches   are   worsened   by
                           dehydration and overstimulation, so upping your water
                           intake might just do the trick!

303

              ​Rest in a dimly lit, quiet room.
              ​Ask your provider before taking medication.
              ​If recommended by your provider, acetaminophen may be an
               option!


      3.​ Nausea And Vomiting
        ​Morning sickness can happen at any time of day, not just in the
         morning.
        ​It affects up to about 70% of pregnant women in the first trimester.
        ​Nausea and vomiting can range from mild and annoying to much more
         disruptive.

         ☆ Tips To Ease Nausea And Vomiting
              ​Eat bland foods such as bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast.
              ​Sip non-caffeinated fluids throughout the day instead of
               forcing large amounts at once.
                       ​Eat small, frequent meals rather than letting yourself get
                       overly hungry.
              ​Ask your provider whether vitamin B6 or ginger extract might
               be appropriate for you.
                       ​Reach out sooner rather than later if vomiting becomes
                       severe or you cannot keep fluids down.


      4.​ Physical Aches And Pain
        ​Pregnancy hormones loosen ligaments to prepare the body for birth.
              ​The growing uterus also shifts posture and adds strain to
               muscles and joints.
        ​This can show up as round ligament pain, leg cramps, backaches, hip
         discomfort, and general soreness.

         ☆ Tips To Ease Physical Aches And Pain
              ​Use a lumbar pillow for lower-back support.
              ​Try a maternity belt if belly weight is making your pelvis / back
               feel strained.

304

               ​Use a heating pad carefully if your provider says that is okay.
               ​Get a gentle massage if available.
               ​Wear comfortable, low-heeled shoes.
               ​Practice gentle exercise and use good body mechanics when
               bending, lifting, or standing.
               ​Keep up with your prenatal vitamin, and ask your provider
               whether you need extra calcium, magnesium, or other support.


      5.​ Swelling And Varicose Veins
        ​Increased pressure on blood vessels can lead to fluid retention,
         swelling, and visible veins, especially in the legs and feet.
               ​This tends to become more noticeable later in pregnancy.

         ☆ Tips To Ease Swelling And Vein Pressure
               ​Wear comfortable shoes.
               ​Try compression socks if they feel helpful.
               ​Stay hydrated.
               ​Elevate your legs and feet whenever possible.
               ​Avoid long stretches of sitting or standing in one position.


      6.​ Bladder Changes And Incontinence
        ​Increased urination is common in pregnancy.
        ​In the third trimester especially, the growing fetus puts more
         pressure on the bladder.
               ​Some women also notice incontinence, meaning leaking a little
               urine when laughing, coughing, or sneezing.
        ​Pregnancy can also raise the risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs).

         ☆ Tips To Support Bladder Comfort
               ​Practice Kegel exercises to strengthen the pelvic floor muscles.
                     ​As mentioned in previous sections, think of your pelvic
                      floor muscles as the ones you would use to stop urine or
                      prevent passing gas!
               ​Do not practice Kegels while actively urinating.

305

              ​Do not hold the contraction so long that you start straining.
              ​Stay hydrated even if frequent urination is annoying.
                      ​Watch for UTI warning signs such as pain or burning
                      with urination, frequent urination with discomfort, cloudy
                      urine, foul-smelling urine, or blood in the urine.


      7.​ Heartburn And Constipation
        ​Hormonal changes and the physical pressure of pregnancy can slow
         digestion.
              ​That can lead to heartburn, constipation, bloating, and general
               digestive discomfort.

         ☆ Tips To Ease Heartburn And Constipation
              ​Eat small, frequent meals instead of large heavy ones.
              ​Avoid foods that are especially spicy or greasy if they trigger
               symptoms for you.
              ​Do not lie down for two to three hours after eating.
              ​Increase fiber intake, including foods like dried fruit if they
               work well for your body.
              ​Keep fluids up throughout the day.


      8.​ Skin Changes
        ​Pregnancy hormones and skin stretching can cause stretch marks,
         melasma, linea nigra, and acne.
              ​Melasma     is   the brown-to-gray-brown facial pigmentation
               sometimes called the mask of pregnancy.
                      ​Acne can also flare because of hormonal shifts.

         ☆ Tips To Support Pregnancy Skin
              ​Stick with a gentle skincare routine.
              ​Use gentle cleansers and moisturizers.
              ​Wear sunscreen regularly, especially if melasma is showing up.
              ​Stay hydrated.

306

                     ​Avoid acne medications that are not pregnancy-safe, including
                     isotretinoin.


         9.​ Trouble Sleeping
            ​Sleep problems are very common in pregnancy, especially in the third
            trimester.
                     ​Discomfort, bladder trips, heartburn, anxiety, and trouble
                     getting physically comfortable can all pile on at once.

            ☆ Tips To Sleep Better While Pregnant
                     ​Adjust your sleep position with supportive pillows.
                           ​Try C-shaped or wedge-shaped pillows for belly, hip, and
                            back support.
                     ​Do light stretches before bed if they feel good.
                     ​Warm milk may be soothing for some women.
                           ​Avoid taking sleep medications during pregnancy unless
                            your provider specifically recommends something!

Okay, symptom management: check. ( ^ ___ ^ ) ‫ و‬Now, let me pivot the
conversation for a second. Your intuition matters. I cannot stress this enough. If
your gut is telling you something is up, please make sure to listen to it! You don’t
need to prove how tough you are by waiting too long to get help.


      ☆ Warning Signs Not To Ignore
            ​Severe vomiting.
            ​Sudden, severe swelling.
                     ​Severe headache, vision changes, chest pain, trouble breathing,
                     or swelling of the face/hands.
            ​Symptoms that are intense, persistent, or rapidly worsening.
            ​UTI symptoms such as burning, blood in urine, or cloudy foul-smelling
            urine.
                     ​Any discomfort that feels far outside your normal or comes
                     with fear that something is off.

307


Conclusion ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

Pregnancy discomforts can be frustrating, but many of them respond really well to
gentle daily support, practical adjustments, and paying attention to what your
body is asking for! The goal is not to have a perfectly symptom-free pregnancy. It
is to feel more equipped, more comfortable, and less thrown off when your body
does what pregnant bodies so often do! A little gentleness, a little strategy, and a
willingness to call your provider when something feels truly off can do some
serious heavy lifting at the end of the day! ( ˘ᴗ˘ )

Easing Childbirth Fears With Info
Look, staring down labor in the face can make a woman bounce between being
totally ready for this and wanting to sprint in the opposite direction. ( ｡﹏｡"ᵕ ) A lot
of fear around birth is not due to any personal flaw. Instead, it is due to the fact
that birth comes with uncertainty, intensity, and a whole lot of outside stories that
are not always helpful (like the ones you stumble across while doom-scrolling on
pregnancy forums … I see you (^_−)☆ ). If any of this hits home, this section is
for you!

Fear of childbirth is common, understandable, and usually much more manageable
when it is met with real information, flexible preparation, and support instead of
radio silence. Here, we will delve into research-backed facts that’ll make birth
feel less mysterious, less doom-filled, and a whole lot more navigable. Not because
every birth goes exactly to plan, but because understanding the common paths can
help take the monster out from under the bed! ( o ^ _ ^ o )

As always, this section is for education only, not medical advice.

309


Main Content ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

One of the biggest reasons childbirth feels nerve-wracking is that so many women
hear fragments of information instead of getting a clear, grounded overview. And,
to be perfectly honest, vague fear usually packs a bigger punch than specific fear.
Once you know what you are actually afraid of without somersaulting to the worst
case scenario, it becomes much easier to respond with something useful! ദ്ദി ´⌣` )


      ☆ What Childbirth Fear Really Is
            ​Childbirth fear is the fear, dread, or intense anxiety some women
             feel about labor and delivery.
                   ​It exists on a spectrum.
                          ​Some women have normal worries, which are extremely
                           common.
                          ​Some women have more intense fears that may need
                           extra support or clinical attention.
            ​Fear can show up even before pregnancy, not just during it.

According to the cited research, about 80% of pregnant women report more
general worries, around 20% experience more specific and intense worries, and
around 10% deal with severe childbirth fear. Clinically relevant childbirth fear has
also been reported in non-pregnant women, which goes to show that fear can start
long before labor ever enters the picture.


      ☆ Why Birth Can Feel So Scary
            ​Birth involves uncertainty.
                   ​You do not know exactly when labor will start.
                   ​You do not know exactly how long it will last.
                   ​You do not know how intense it will feel in your own body.
            ​You may worry about pain, tearing, interventions, making decisions
             quickly, or losing control.

310

                   ​And keep in mind: media, social media, and exaggerated birth
                   stories can make birth look more dangerous or chaotic than it
                   usually is!

A lot of fear grows in the space where information is fuzzy. That is why naming the
exact fear is so important. Fear of pain needs a different kind of support than
fear of the unknown, fear after trauma, or fear of medical intervention.


      ☆ The Most Common Types Of Birth Fear
            ​Fear of the unknown.
            ​Fear of pain.
            ​Fear of tearing or birth injury.
            ​Fear of medical interventions.
            ​Fear of pooping or peeing during labor.
            ​Fear of not making it to the hospital in time.
            ​Fear after a previous difficult or traumatic birth.

Each of these fears has its own emotional texture, which means each one is eased a
little differently. A generic pep talk usually does not do much. Specific fear tends
to need a specific response.

One of the subtlest fear reducers is simply knowing that labor often takes time.
It is a process. Many women imagine a panicked race from first contraction to
immediate delivery, when in reality there is usually more time to think, call, move,
and assess than fear first tells you.

      ☆ What To Expect: The General Reality Of Birth
            ​Birth doesn’t usually unfold in one dramatic movie-style moment!
                   ​For first-time mothers, labor commonly takes much longer than
                   people expect.

311

                   ​Average labor for first-time mothers is often described
                   in the range of about 8—17.5 hours. Now, that does not
                   mean every woman labors for that exact amount of time,
                   but it does mean labor is usually a process rather than an
                   instant emergency.
      ​Birth can begin with contractions, a gush of amniotic fluid, slow
      leaking fluid, or discharge of mucus from the vagina.

      ☆ What The Beginning Of Labor May Look Like
            ​Contractions may start gradually and become stronger, more
             regular, and closer together.
            ​Your waters may break as a gush or as slow leaking fluid.
            ​You may notice mucus discharge.
                   ​Not every sensation means the baby is arriving that
                   exact second.

             This is why it helps so much to ask your provider or midwife in
             advance what they want you to do when labor begins. Knowing
             who to call, what to time, and when to come in can make those
             first hours feel a lot less chaotic.

      ☆ What Happens During Labor And Birth
            ​Labor involves the cervix opening, also called dilating, so the
             baby can move down and be born.
                   ​Cervical dilation may be checked vaginally by a midwife or
                   provider to feel how open the cervix is.
                         ​Monitoring may include CTG, where a belt with
                          ultrasound plates is placed around the abdomen.
            ​In normal labor, a woman is not automatically locked into one
             position.
                   ​Movement and position changes can help the birth
                   process!

312

                                 ​Women can often choose different labor positions
                                  rather than staying flat on the back the entire
                                  time.

            ☆ What Happens After The Baby Is Born
                  ​Birth is not over the instant the baby comes out.
                         ​The placenta still needs to be delivered afterward.
                                 ​This is called the afterbirth.
                  ​A healthy newborn may be placed with the mother soon after
                   birth.
                  ​The umbilical cord doesn’t always have to be cut immediately.
                  ​The cervix is not sutured shut again. That takes time, no
                   matter what kind of bizarre internet myths try to tell you
                   otherwise. (￣^￣ )ゞ

Now, fear is not only reduced by facts. It is also reduced by how birth is framed
in the mind. A more natural, flexible mindset tends to be linked with lower fear,
while facts alone do not always do the whole job.

      ☆ The Two Birth Mindsets
            ​A natural birth mindset sees birth as generally a natural event the
            body can manage in normal circumstances.
            ​A medical birth mindset sees birth mainly as a medical event that
            needs to be managed through medical care.
                  ​Medical care can absolutely be life-saving and important.
                         ​But the way a woman mentally frames birth may influence
                            how fearful it feels to her!

            ☆ What Makes Birth Feel Less Scary
                  ​Seeing birth as something the body is designed to do, while still
                   respecting that support may be needed sometimes.
                  ​Feeling involved in decisions.
                  ​Knowing that labor can have multiple normal paths.

313

                  ​Having realistic expectations instead of horror-story
                   expectations or fantasy expectations.
                  ​Building self-efficacy, which means the belief that you can
                   cope with the process.


Okay, let’s get into the most common anxieties and look at some practical ways to
work through them! (^▽^)


      ☆ Fear Of The Unknown: Tips And Tricks
           ​Ask your doctor or midwife what labor usually looks like in normal
            situations.
           ​Ask what changes the plan and what does not.
           ​Learn the general stages of labor.
                  ​Ask what happens if contractions start, if your waters break,
                   and when you should call or come in.
                          ​Ask your team, “What are the most likely scenarios, and
                           what would change the plan?”

      To supplement this, here is the kind of birth knowledge that can genuinely
      help, partially reiterated to paint a crystal clear picture.


           ​Birth can happen in different settings depending on location and your
            care situation, such as hospital, birth center, or home birth where
            appropriate.
                  ​First births often take longer than many people imagine.
                  ​Labor can begin with contractions, leaking fluid, or mucus
                   discharge.
                  ​Women can often move and change positions during labor.
                          ​There are different pain relief options, both medical and
                           non-medical.
           ​C-sections happen for specific reasons, not randomly.
           ​Having one C-section doesn’t automatically mean all future births must
            also be C-sections.

314

      ☆ Fear Of Pain: Tips And Tricks
           ​Talk to your provider in advance about pain relief options.
                 ​Ask what non-medical methods are available.
                 ​Ask what medical pain relief options exist and when each can be
                  used.
           ​Think in layers instead of extremes.
           ​Breathing, movement, position changes, massage, water, and
           medication can all be part of the same coping toolkit!
                 ​Replace “What if I cannot handle it?” with “I will handle one
                  contraction at a time.”

                  ☆ Non-Medical Coping Tools For Labor Fear
                          ​Slow breathing.
                          ​Guided relaxation.
                          ​Meditation.
                          ​Yoga.
                          ​Grounding practices.
                          ​Massage or firm touch.
                          ​Position changes.
                          ​Walking or movement if appropriate.
                          ​Shower or bath if available and permitted.
                          ​Calm music, low lighting, or familiar comfort items.

      ☆ Fear Of Interventions: Tips And Tricks
           ​Learn what common interventions are and why they are used.
                 ​Ask what situations most often lead to induction, epidural,
                  assisted delivery, or C-section.
           ​Ask what choices you usually still have if labor changes course.
           ​Ask how your team communicates if something needs to happen
           quickly.
           ​Go to antenatal / birth classes instead of relying only on online
           stories.

           ☆ A Few More Childbirth Facts

315

                 ​Episiotomy is not usually necessary by default just because
                  someone is a first-time mother.
                        ​It may be used to prevent uncontrolled tearing and is
                         generally performed only when medically necessary.
                 ​ Induction may be recommended if continuing the pregnancy
                  feels less safe than starting labor (e.g., 7-14 days past due
                  date, water breaking without labor, or complications).
                        ​ Epidural, assisted delivery, or C-section may be used
                         when extra support is needed for pain relief, labor
                         progress, or safety.

      ☆ Fear Of Tearing Or Birth Injury: Tips And Tricks
           ​Ask your provider what tears are, how common they are, and how they
           are managed.
           ​Ask what support your team uses during pushing and birth.
           ​Ask what healing usually looks like if a tear happens.
                 ​Learn about postpartum pain relief and recovery support ahead
                  of time.
                        ​Remind yourself that birth injury risk is taken seriously
                         and managed, not ignored.

      ☆ Fear Of Pooping Or Peeing During Birth: Tips And Tricks
           ​This is extremely common. It can happen.
           ​Your care team has seen it many times before.
                 ​It is usually cleaned discreetly.
                        ​You may not even know it happened! (⌒-⌒ )
           ​Plus, if it happens, it often means you are pushing in the right
           direction!

      ☆ Fear Of Not Making It To The Hospital In Time: Tips And Tricks
           ​Remember: first-stage labor often takes longer than people expect.
           ​Keep the delivery unit or maternity ward number saved in your phone.
           ​Ask in advance when they want you to call and when they want you to
           come in.

316

            ​Pack your hospital bag early.
            ​Know your route, backup route, parking situation, and who is driving.
                   ​If you live far away, ask your team ahead of time what to do if
                   labor starts early.

Another way to stay afloat? A birth plan, hands down. It works best when it gives
you a solid structure without making you feel like any sudden detour is a total
failure!
      ​It can include who you want present, pain relief wishes, positions you want to
       try, and what matters most to you.
            ​Keep it short and clear.
      ​To reiterate, think of it as preferences, not rigid demands.


       ☆ Who To Have With You
            ​Choose people who make you feel calmer, safer, and more respected.
                   ​Do not pick someone just because they “should” be there.
            ​Tell your support people what actually helps when you are anxious.
            ​Be specific about whether you want quiet presence, encouragement,
             hand-holding, advocacy, humor, massage, or reminders to breathe.
            ​Avoid people who make your stress spike.


Getting the right people in your corner is a big deal—especially when a whole
truckload of extra anxiety can pile on if your pregnancy has already been a rocky
ride. Without further ado, here are some practical steps you can take to manage
fears surrounding a previous difficult birth:
      ​Tell your provider and midwife early.
      ​Name what was hardest last time.
      ​Write down what you do not want repeated if possible.
      ​Write down what would help you feel safer this time.
            ​Do not wait until the last minute to bring up trauma, panic, or
             feeling ignored.

317

A huge part of fear reduction is not just learning facts, but learning how to trust
yourself inside the process. That inner steadiness matters just as much as
information does.

      ☆ What Helps Fear The Most, Emotionally
            ​Becoming well informed.
            ​Attending antenatal / birth classes.
            ​Visiting the maternity ward if that is an option.
            ​Preparing mentally and physically ahead of time.
            ​Practicing relaxation techniques before labor.
            ​Talking to a trusted provider, counselor, midwife, or calm, supportive
            parent.
            ​Avoiding people and media that make birth sound only terrifying.

To tap into your prefrontal cortex (the part of your brain responsible for calming
your emotional responses, rationalizing fears, and overriding stress), here are some
positive affirmations! These kinds of phrases help because they lower the
pressure by signaling to your nervous system that you are safe. (˘⌣˘)


      “I do not need to know everything to prepare well.”


      “I can make decisions one step at a time.”


      “Every contraction is one part of the process, not the whole story.”​


      “Flexible does not mean powerless.”


      “My team can explain options as we go.”


      “I can be afraid and still be capable.”


      “I do not need to be fearless to give birth.”

318


Conclusion ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

Childbirth can feel scary because it matters, because it is powerful, and because
there is so much we are told about it without always being taught how to feel
steady inside it. But fear does not have to run the whole show. When you
understand what birth commonly looks like, learn the facts that actually matter,
build a flexible plan, and practice calming your nervous system before labor begins,
birth often starts to feel less like a cliff edge and more like something you can
move through with support. :-) You do not need to be fearless. You just need to
feel informed, held, and gently reminded that your body and your support system
can work together.

Tending to Postpartum Emotions
Postpartum emotions can be the internal equivalent of a category 5 hurricane.
(๑/////๑ " ) Unpredictable, random, and possibly intense. One minute you might
feel like you’re wrapped in a warm, fuzzy blanket—totally relieved, proud, deeply
enshrouded by love. Next, you might feel overwhelmed, weepy, anxious,
touched-out, or very unlike yourself. And it all checks out! Because becoming a
parent is a huge physical, hormonal, emotional, and identity-level shift. ( っ , -)

This era can hold joy and struggle at the same time, which is part of why it can
feel so perplexing. But know this: these emotional shifts are common and
understandable, help is out there, and you don't have to go through it alone. This
section is here to help you understand what is normal, what deserves closer
attention, and how to care for yourself without having a nagging storm cloud of
shame over your head!

321

And, as always, this section is for education only, not medical advice.


Main Content ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

The postpartum period isn’t only a physical recovery. Nope. Not by a long shot. It
is an emotional adjustment too! Hormone shifts, sleep disruption, body changes,
feeding stress, and the constant responsibility of caring for a newborn can all hit
at once, which is a lot for one nervous system to hold.


☆ Why Postpartum Emotions Can Feel So Intense
      ​Hormones shift quickly after birth.
            ​Sleep often becomes broken, short, and unpredictable.
                    ​Your body is recovering while you are also learning how to care
                    for a baby!
      ​Body image changes can feel emotionally tender.
            ​Pressure to feel grateful, happy, and instantly confident can make
             harder feelings feel even lonelier.

You know, a lot of new mothers underestimate just how emotional they can get
during this season! ( つ ╥ ﹏ ╥ )つThat surprise alone can make things feel far more
worrisome than they need to.

      ☆ What Emotional Changes Can Show Up Postpartum
            ​Joy.
            ​Stress.
            ​Anxiety.
            ​Sadness.
            ​Mood swings.
            ​Irritability.
            ​Feeling overwhelmed.
            ​Crying more easily than usual.
            ​Feeling disconnected from yourself for a little while.

322

Please know that these feelings can exist together. You can be full of love for your
baby and still feel exhausted, emotional, frightened, or unlike yourself. Those
things are not polar opposites.

Now, knowing the difference between a standard case of the baby blues and
something more serious is very crucial. Here is how you can tell them apart!
      ​Baby blues usually involve tearfulness, mood swings, sadness, and emotional
      sensitivity that last for a few days up to about two weeks.
            ​More serious postpartum mental health conditions, such as postpartum
             depression, postpartum anxiety, or postpartum psychosis, are more
             intense, more persistent, and more likely to need professional care.
                  ​Duration matters.
                  ​Severity matters.
                  ​How much it affects daily functioning matters.

      ☆ What Baby Blues Can Look Like
            ​Crying easily.
            ​Feeling extra sensitive.
            ​Mood swings that seem to come out of nowhere.
            ​Feeling overwhelmed or emotionally raw.
            ​Sadness that comes and goes.

             ☆ Signs It May Be More Than Baby Blues
                  ​Symptoms feel severe.
                  ​Symptoms last longer than a couple of weeks.
                  ​You are struggling to function.
                  ​Anxiety feels constant or hard to control.
                  ​Sadness feels heavy, persistent, or numbing.
                  ​You feel unable to care for yourself or bond in a way that
                   worries you.
                  ​You feel frightened by your thoughts or emotional state.

☆ Postpartum Depression, Anxiety, And Psychosis: The Basic Difference

323

      ​Postpartum depression can involve ongoing sadness, hopelessness, emptiness,
      guilt, low motivation, and difficulty feeling like yourself.
      ​Postpartum anxiety can involve racing thoughts, constant worry, panic,
      dread, or feeling unable to relax.
            ​Postpartum psychosis is much more serious and urgent and requires
             immediate professional help.
                   ​Sitting and waiting for any of these conditions to disappear is
                    not the way to go!（￣へ￣）

Alright, now that we’ve covered symptoms, let’s jump right into what actually helps!

☆ Build A Strong Support Network
      ​Do not suffer in silence.
      ​Talk to your partner, family, or trusted friends about how you are feeling.
      ​Join a support group with other new parents if that feels comforting.
      ​Let other people help you feel less alone.
      ​Use community spaces that feel safe and judgment-free.

      Sometimes one of the most healing things postpartum is hearing, “Me too.”
      Not because it makes the struggle fun, obviously :,), but because it reminds
      you that you are not broken or uniquely failing.

      ☆ Practical Support Counts Too
            ​Ask for help with meals.
                   ​Ask for help with dishes, laundry, or tidying up.
            ​Ask someone to hold the baby while you shower, nap, or eat.
            ​Let people help with errands or childcare support if that is available.
            ​Accept help without feeling like you need to earn it first.

             Emotional recovery gets harder when basic needs are constantly
             pushed to the bottom of the list. Practical help is mental health
             support too.

☆ Seek Professional Help Early
      ​Perinatal mental health conditions are serious, but treatable.

324

      ​Talk to your doctor, midwife, therapist, or another qualified mental health
      professional.
      ​Bring up symptoms directly instead of minimizing them.
            ​Ask for help recognizing what is normal adjustment and what may
             need treatment.
      ​Work with a provider to create a treatment plan that fits your needs!

      ☆ Treatment Options Can Include
            ​Talk therapy or counseling.
            ​Medication prescribed by a qualified healthcare professional.
            ​Support groups.
            ​Ongoing follow-up with a healthcare provider.

             ☆ Crisis And Support Lines Matter
                  ​Keep information for postpartum and maternal mental health
                      support lines somewhere easy to find.
                           ​E.g., the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline &
                            Postpartum Support International helpline.
                                 ​If there is immediate danger, thoughts of harm, or
                                  a crisis, call emergency services or 988 right away.
                  ​Save support contacts before you need them if possible.
                  ​Reach out immediately if symptoms feel urgent, frightening, or
                      unsafe.

☆ Self-Care
      ​Self-care postpartum does not need to look pretty to count.
      ​It can be very basic and still be very potent! ᕙ(⇀‸↼‶)ᕗ

      ☆ Self-Care That Actually Helps
            ​Prioritize rest as much as realistically possible.
            ​Eat regularly and keep meals simple if needed.
            ​Drink water throughout the day.
            ​Step outside for a short walk if that feels good.

325

             ​Make a little time for something that reminds you that you are still a
             person, not only a caregiver.

             Sometimes self-care is a nice hot shower. Sometimes it is ten quiet
             minutes. Sometimes it is asking someone else to take over while you lie
             down and stare at the ceiling. All of that counts.

☆ Rest And Nutrition
      ​Sleep matters, even if it comes in short bursts.
      ​Balanced meals can support energy and emotional steadiness.
      ​Skipping food and running on fumes can make emotional vulnerability feel
      worse.
             ​Rest is not laziness.
             ​Fuel is not optional.
                    ​No one feels emotionally regulated on empty, fragmented sleep
                    and random leftover crackers alone!

☆ Gentle Activity And Mindfulness
      ​Go outside for fresh air.
      ​Try a gentle walk if your body feels up for it.
      ​Return to simple hobbies you enjoy, like baking, drawing, or another calming
      activity.
      ​Use mindfulness practices if they help you feel more grounded.

☆ Self-Compassion
      ​Be kind to yourself.
      ​Let go of the pressure to be perfect.
      ​Do not interpret every hard feeling as proof that something is wrong with
      you.
      ​Remind yourself that transition is hard, even when it is wanted and
      beautiful.
      ​Refuse shame wherever possible.

☆ Set Realistic Expectations
      ​New parenthood is a major adjustment.

326

      ​Some days will feel sweet and manageable.
      ​Some days will feel messy and hard.
            ​Both can be true in the same week, or even the same hour.
      ​Progress does not have to look polished.

      Realistic expectations are protective. A lot of postpartum suffering gets
      worse when women think they should already be handling everything better!
      Now, expecting some chaos doesn’t mean you’re going to be stuck feeling this
      way forever, of course. ^___^ It just means that going in with your eyes
      open is a very strong buffer.

☆ Tips And Tricks For Coping Day To Day
      ​Name what you are feeling instead of just saying “I’m fine.”
      ​Tell one trusted person the honest version.
      ​Keep snacks and water near where you feed or rest.
      ​Make a short list of people you can text when you are having a rough day.
      ​Reduce pressure to host, perform, or respond quickly to everyone.
      ​Let low-priority things stay low priority for a while.
      ​Use online community spaces only if they genuinely feel supportive and safe
      for you.

      ☆ When To Speak Up Right Away
            ​If sadness feels heavy and persistent.
            ​If anxiety feels relentless or panicky.
            ​If you feel emotionally unsafe.
            ​If you feel detached in a way that scares you.
            ​If you are having thoughts of harming yourself or the baby.
                   ​Seek urgent help.
            ​If you feel like you cannot cope.

327


Conclusion ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

Postpartum emotions can be tender, intense, confusing, and, overall, very human.
Feeling joyful sometimes does not cancel out feeling overwhelmed at others, and
struggling does not make you a bad mother. The biggest thing to remember is this:
you do not need to hide, minimize, or power through postpartum mental health
changes. With support, honesty, self-compassion, and professional care when
needed, this time of your life can become much safer, warmer, and more
manageable. ( っˊᗜˋ)(ᵔ ᵕ ᵔ˶) ♡

Postpartum Recovery
Those first six weeks after giving birth are such a tender, completely upside-down
kind of era! Your body is trying to heal, your hormones are resetting, and your
normal routine? Totally out of the window! It’s actually so wild that people act like
the baby arriving means the hard part is over. It’s definitely not over. You’re just
entering a different phase. And, of course, you deserve the utmost support and
recovery time while you move through it. ( ˶˘ ³˘)♡

Postpartum healing is not one quick six-week checkpoint and a gold star for
surviving. (˶ᵔ ᵕ ᵔ˶)ゞ It is an ongoing recovery period that deserves rest, monitoring,
nourishment, and early help when something feels off. In this section, we will
tackle what is normal, what deserves attention, and what small practical things can
make those first weeks feel more manageable. (b~_^)b

And, as always, this section is for education only, not medical advice.

329


Main Content ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

The postpartum period begins right after birth and usually lasts about 6–8 weeks,
though some parts of healing can take longer. In those early weeks, your body is
recovering from pregnancy and birth while also adjusting to feeding, broken sleep,
and huge hormonal shifts. That is a lot for one body to hold at once. ( ¬ ▵ ¬ ) ~ 3


      ☆ What Is Normal In The First 6 Weeks
            ​Vaginal bleeding and discharge called lochia.
            ​Uterine cramping called afterpains.
            ​Vaginal or perineal soreness after a vaginal birth.
            ​Incision tenderness after a C-section.
            ​Night sweats, temporary hair shedding, and hormonal emotional shifts.
            ​Breast fullness or engorgement as milk comes in.
            ​Constipation, hemorrhoids, bladder weakness, and deep fatigue.

Sore, swollen, tired, crampy, sweaty, tender, and emotionally all over the place can
all be part of early healing. The best question to ask yourself mentally is “Am I
healing in the expected direction?”

☆ Lochia: What Postpartum Bleeding Usually Looks Like
      ​Lochia is the normal vaginal discharge that happens as the uterus sheds
      extra blood and tissue after pregnancy.
      ​It can last up to about 6 weeks.
      ​It changes over time instead of staying exactly the same.

      ☆ Lochia Stages To Expect
            ​Lochia rubra: first 3 to 4 days, dark or bright red, heavier like a
             period, sometimes with small clots.
            ​Lochia serosa: around days 4 to 10, thinner and more pinkish-brown.
            ​Lochia alba: by around day 12, and sometimes lasting up to 6 weeks,
             lighter and more yellowish-white.

             ☆ Bleeding: Tips And Tricks

330

                  ​Use sanitary pads or disposable underwear, not tampons.
                  ​Avoid inserting anything into the vagina for at least 6 weeks
                   unless your provider says otherwise.
                  ​Track whether bleeding is gradually lightening over time.
                  ​Rest more if bleeding increases after activity, because that can
                   be your body telling you to slow down!
                         ​Call early if bleeding suddenly gets much heavier
                          instead of better.

                          ☆ Urgent Bleeding Red Flags
                               ​Soaking through a pad in 1 hour, or bleeding that
                                feels suddenly heavy or hard to control.
                               ​Heavy bleeding that keeps going instead of easing
                                up.
                               ​Feeling dizzy, faint, or like your blood pressure is
                                dropping.
                               ​Foul-smelling discharge.
                               ​Fever with bleeding or uterine tenderness.
                               ​Severe headache that does not go away.
                               ​Vision changes.
                               ​Chest pain.
                               ​Trouble breathing.
                               ​Fever of 100.4°F or higher.
                               ​Severe belly pain.
                               ​Extreme swelling of the hands or face.
                               ​Calf pain, redness, or swelling.

Now, a quick heads-up about postpartum cramps: they can definitely come out of
left field if nobody warned you about them! While they can be pretty
uncomfortable, they are a normal part of the process and usually settle down
within a few days. Here’s what you need to know about them!
      ​As the uterus shrinks back toward its pre-pregnancy size, it contracts.
      ​Those contractions are called afterpains.

331

            ​They can be more noticeable during breastfeeding because oxytocin is
             released, which makes the uterus contract more.


      ☆ Tips For Afterpains
            ​Expect them to be strongest in the first few days.
            ​Use approved pain relief if your provider says it is okay.
            ​Rest when you can instead of pushing through extra activity.
            ​Use a heating pad only if your provider says it is appropriate and safe
             for you.
                   ​Remind yourself that these cramps usually mean the uterus is
                    doing its job.

☆ Perineal Healing After A Vaginal Birth
      ​The perineum is the area between the vagina and anus.
      ​It may feel sore, swollen, tender, or stingy after birth.
      ​If you had a tear or an episiotomy, healing can take longer.

      ☆ Perineal Recovery Tips And Tricks
            ​Use ice packs in the early days for swelling and soreness.
            ​Try a sitz bath, which is a shallow warm bath for the perineal area.
            ​Use a peri bottle with warm water after using the bathroom.
            ​Pat gently instead of wiping harshly.
            ​Sit on a padded surface or ring if that feels better.
                   ​Do not ignore severe or worsening pain.

☆ C-Section Incision Healing
      ​If you had a C-section, the incision will usually feel tender and sore at first.
      ​You may feel pulling, weakness, or discomfort with movement.
      ​Healing takes time, even if the incision looks small from the outside!

☆ C-Section Recovery: Tips And Tricks
      ​Keep the incision clean and dry.
      ​Avoid lifting anything heavier than your baby for the first 6 weeks.

332

      ​Move carefully but regularly, because gentle movement can support
      circulation and recovery.
      ​Hold a pillow against your abdomen when coughing or laughing if that feels
      more supportive.
      ​Wear loose, comfortable clothing that does not rub the incision.
            ​Call if you notice redness, swelling, pus, or worsening pain.

☆ Breast Engorgement And Milk Coming In
      ​A few days after birth, your milk may come in and your breasts may feel
      swollen, firm, warm, and painful.
      ​This is called engorgement.
            ​It can happen whether you are breastfeeding or not, though it is
             managed a little differently depending on your feeding plan!

      ☆ Engorgement Tips If You Are Breastfeeding
            ​Feed frequently.
            ​Offer both breasts regularly.
            ​Use a warm compress or warm shower before feeding to help milk
             letdown.
            ​Use cool packs between feeds for comfort.
            ​Ask someone to assess latch, swallowing, nipple condition, and
             positioning.

      ☆ Engorgement Tips If You Are Not Breastfeeding
            ​Use cold packs.
            ​Wear a supportive bra.
            ​Use pain relief if approved.
            ​Relieve pressure carefully if your provider recommends it.

333

Now, as for hormonal shifts, your estrogen and progesterone levels take a sudden
dive, which can throw your body for a bit of a loop! This sharp drop is the main
culprit behind those random night sweats, and it can also cause some temporary
hair shedding a few months down the road. Beyond the physical stuff, this huge
hormonal shift can leave you feeling emotionally reactive or just a little wobbly
while everything settles back down.

Okay, now let’s jump right into some less-talked-about body changes that come
with postpartum recovery!

☆ Constipation And Bowel Recovery
      ​Constipation is common after delivery.
      ​It can be worse if you are sore, dehydrated, scared to push, taking iron, or
      using certain pain medications.
      ​Hemorrhoids can also show up or flare after labor and postpartum straining.

      ☆ Constipation: Tips And Tricks
            ​Drink plenty of water.
            ​Eat more fiber, including dried fruits, fresh fruit, vegetables, and
             other high-fiber foods.
            ​Do not wait too long to respond to the urge to go.
            ​Try not to strain.
            ​Ask about stool softeners or mild laxatives if you have not had a
             bowel movement within a few days and are uncomfortable.

☆ Bladder Changes And Pelvic Floor Recovery
      ​Frequent urination and some bladder leakage are common postpartum.
      ​The pelvic floor has been stretched and stressed by pregnancy and birth.
      ​Incontinence is common, but common does not mean untreatable.

      ☆ Bladder And Pelvic Floor Tips
            ​Stay hydrated instead of cutting fluids too hard.
            ​Try not to hold urine for long stretches.
            ​Do Kegel exercises correctly and gently if they are appropriate for
             you.

334

            ​Do not practice Kegels while actually urinating.
            ​Ask for pelvic floor physical therapy if leakage is moderate, severe, or
             persistent.

☆ Rest Is Not Optional
      ​Rest is one of the biggest postpartum recovery tools.
      ​The early postpartum period is not the time to prove productivity.
      ​Your body is healing from pregnancy and delivery while also adjusting to
      feeding and disrupted sleep.

      ☆ Rest: Tips And Tricks
            ​Sleep when the baby sleeps whenever you realistically can.
            ​Nap before 3 p.m. if daytime sleep helps but does not ruin your
             nighttime rest.
            ​Lower household standards for a while.
            ​Ask friends and family for help with meals, chores, laundry, and
             holding the baby while you shower.
            ​Delegate before you get desperate.

☆ Nutrition And Hydration For Healing
      ​Recovery needs fuel.
      ​A balanced, varied diet supports tissue healing, hormones, milk production if
      breastfeeding, bowel regularity, and energy.
      ​Breastfeeding mothers generally need about 500 extra calories per day.

      ☆ Nutrition: Tips And Tricks
            ​Eat regularly, even if meals are simple.
            ​Keep easy snacks near wherever you feed or rest.
            ​Hydrate   throughout     the   day,   especially   if   breastfeeding   or
             constipated.
            ​Do not aggressively diet in the immediate postpartum period.

☆ Exercise And Returning To Movement
      ​Early postpartum recovery is not about jumping back into intense workouts.
      ​Strenuous activity is generally something to avoid early on.

335

      ​Rest is especially important in the first 2–3 weeks.
      ​Gentle walking and low-impact movement are usually the starting point!

      ☆ Movement: Tips And Tricks
            ​Start with short, gentle walks.
            ​Increase slowly instead of trying to make up for lost time.
            ​Stop if bleeding gets heavier or pain ramps up.
            ​Use supportive clothing or a belly binder only if it feels comfortable
             and your provider says it is okay.

☆ Sex, Libido, And Contraception
      ​Desire may be lower postpartum, especially with fatigue, soreness, hormonal
      changes, and breastfeeding.
      ​Lower estrogen during breastfeeding can affect lubrication and libido.
      ​Healing of the perineal area often takes about 4–6 weeks, sometimes longer.

      ☆ Sex And Contraception Tips
            ​Wait until healing has happened and you feel ready!
            ​Do not compare your timeline to anyone else’s.
            ​Use lubricant if dryness is an issue.
            ​Talk about contraception before resuming sex, not after.
            ​Remember that breastfeeding alone is not automatically reliable birth
             control.

☆ Postpartum Mood: Baby Blues Vs. Something More Serious
      ​Baby blues are very common in the first week after birth.
      ​They can include crying spells, irritability, anxiety, mood swings, and sleep
      difficulty.
      ​They usually improve within about 2 weeks.

      ☆ Mood: Tips And Tricks
            ​Watch the duration, not just the presence, of symptoms.
            ​Tell someone if you feel emotionally off.
            ​Ask directly for postpartum mood screening if needed.

336

            ​Get help promptly if symptoms continue beyond 2 weeks or make it
             hard to care for yourself or the baby.

             ☆ Mental Health Red Flags
                     ​Symptoms that continue beyond 2 weeks.
                     ​Struggling to care for yourself.
                     ​Struggling to care for the baby.
                     ​Thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, which deserve
                     urgent help right away.

☆ Medical Follow-Up Matters More Than One 6-Week Visit
      ​Postpartum care should be ongoing, not just one quick check.
      ​Early contact in the first few weeks matters.
      ​Ongoing care as needed matters.
      ​A comprehensive postpartum visit by 12 weeks matters too!

      ☆ Follow-Up: Tips And Tricks
            ​Set appointments up early.
            ​Do not wait until something feels like an emergency to reach out.
            ​Bring    up   blood pressure, bleeding, glucose follow-up, thyroid
             symptoms, pelvic floor problems, mood symptoms, breastfeeding
             issues, and contraception.
            ​Keep a note in your phone of questions as they come up.

      ☆ Other Important Postpartum Issues Not To Miss
            ​Pregnancy-related high blood pressure can still be dangerous after
             delivery.
            ​Gestational diabetes follow-up still matters after pregnancy ends.
            ​Thyroid issues can appear postpartum too.
            ​Persistent fatigue, palpitations, anxiety, unusual swelling, severe
             headaches, vision changes, or feeling very unwell deserve evaluation.

☆ Best Overall Postpartum Mindset
      ​Postpartum is a healing period.
      ​Recovery is not linear.

337

      ​Support is part of care, not an extra luxury.
             ​Remember: catching problems early is one of the kindest things you
              can do for yourself! (つ｡˃ ᵕ ˂)つ ⸝♡


Conclusion ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

The first six weeks after birth can feel raw, messy, emotional, and deeply physical
all at once. That does not mean you are doing it wrong! It means your body is
healing from something major. When you know what to expect, support your body
early, rest more than you think you should, and take red flags seriously,
postpartum recovery usually starts to feel just a bit more like a walk in the park!
So, please take your time, be gentle with yourself, and heal with all the care you
deserve. ( ´･ ᵕ･)ﾉ(´ ᵕ `˶)

Postpartum Nutrition
Think of your body right now as a house trying to rebuild itself right after a major
storm. Your body is healing from pregnancy and birth, your energy is being pulled in
about twelve directions at once, and if you are breastfeeding, you are also using
extra energy and nutrients to make milk. Your physical resources are being
stretched pretty thin, if I do say so myself! ( ˚ ∘ - ﹏ - )

That is exactly why postpartum nutrition is not about dieting, “snapping back,” or
trying to eat as little as possible, even if part of you is tempted to rush back into
shape. It is about rebuilding, replenishing, and keeping yourself steady. >___<
This is all about helping you heal, keeping your energy levels from crashing, and
making sure both you and your baby are well-nourished if you are breastfeeding.

And, as always, this section is for education only, not medical advice.

339


Main Content ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

A lot of women get very clear nutrition messaging during pregnancy, then
postpartum arrives and food support gradually comes to a halt. (｀_´)ゞ The fourth
trimester is a time of high metabolic demand, which is just a science-y way of
saying your body is working overtime. Even when you are sitting still, resting, or
feeding your baby, recovery is still happening. So yes, postpartum nutrition
deserves a lot more consideration than it usually gets!


      ☆ Why Postpartum Nutrition Matters So Much
            ​Your body is repairing tissue after pregnancy and birth.
            ​Blood loss during delivery can leave some women depleted.
            ​Hormonal shifts, and sleep disruption can make energy feel shaky.
            ​Breastfeeding increases calorie and nutrient needs.
            ​Regular nourishment helps support healing, stamina, and overall
             recovery.

             ☆ The Overall Nutrition Mindset For Postpartum
                  ​The general principles of healthy eating still apply!
                  ​What changes is that certain nutrient needs become more
                   important.
                  ​Postpartum eating should focus on recovery, consistency, and
                   nourishment.

                   ☆ Extra Calorie Needs, Especially If Breastfeeding
                         ​Breastfeeding mothers need roughly 2000 kilojoules
                          more per day, which is about 478 extra calories.
                                ​This is about 400–480 additional calories above
                                  normal intake.
                         ​These extra calories support milk production.
                         ​Non-breastfeeding mothers generally return closer to
                          their usual calorie needs, depending on activity level!

                   ☆ A Simple Calorie Picture

340

                                ​For breastfeeding mothers, think normal intake plus
                                 about 400–480 extra calories.
                                ​For non-breastfeeding mothers, general intake may be
                                 around 1800–2000 calories if sedentary, 2000–2200 if
                                 moderately active, and 2200–2400 if active.
                                ​Individual needs vary, so these are general guides rather
                                 than exact rules.
                                ​Appetite may also vary day to day.

With the general overview out of the way, we can now dive into the exact nutrients
that’ll bolster your healing process and help you make nutrient-rich milk if you are
nursing! (⁠⁠/⁠^⁠ω⁠^⁠)⁠/

        ☆ Protein For Healing And Rebuilding
                ​Protein is essential for tissue repair and healing.
                          ​This is especially important after a C-section, tearing, or any
                          physically demanding recovery.
                ​Good protein sources include lean meats, poultry, fish, eggs, beans,
                 and lentils.
                ​Including protein regularly can also help meals feel more satiating.

        ☆ Iron To Replenish After Blood Loss
                ​Postpartum women may be at risk of anemia because of blood loss
                 during birth.
                          ​Iron helps rebuild stores and supports energy.
                                ​Good iron-rich foods include red meat, dark leafy
                                 greens, and legumes.
                ​Iron matters even more if you are feeling especially depleted, weak,
                 or drained.

        ☆ Iodine For Thyroid Health And Baby’s Brain Development
                ​Iodine supports the mother’s thyroid function.
                          ​It also supports infant brain development through breast milk.

341

                         ​The recommended intake for breastfeeding women is 290
                          micrograms per day.
            ​Good sources include seafood, dairy products, and iodized salt.

      ☆ Vitamins B12 And D For Energy And Healthy Function
            ​Vitamin B12 supports energy and healthy body function.
                   ​It also matters for infant growth.
                   ​B12 is found in meat, fish, eggs, and dairy.
                         ​Vegetarians and vegans may need supplementation.
            ​Vitamin D also supports healthy function and infant growth.
                   ​Sources include fatty fish, fortified dairy products, and
                   sunlight exposure.
                         ​Some women may still need individualized guidance
                          depending on diet and levels.

      ☆ Water Is Not Optional
            ​Hydration is essential for energy.
                   ​It also helps support milk production for breastfeeding
                   mothers.
            ​Try to drink about 8 glasses of water.
                   ​Drinking regularly throughout the day is often easier than
                   trying to chug large amounts at once!

Okay, that wraps up the key nutrients you need to know about! Now, to make this
easier to remember, let us group these into simple categories. I have also included
a quick plate visual to help you meal prep!

342




☆ Food Groups To Emphasize Postpartum
      ​Vegetables and legumes.
      ​Fruit.
      ​Grains and cereals.
      ​Lean meats, or other protein-rich foods.
      ​Dairy, or other appropriate calcium-containing options.

      ☆ Daily Serving Guide
                ​Vegetables and legumes: about 7.5 serves if breastfeeding, about 5 if
                not breastfeeding.
                ​Fruit: about 2 serves whether breastfeeding or not.
                ​Grains and cereals: about 9 serves if breastfeeding, about 6 if not
                breastfeeding.

343

            ​Lean meats or poultry: about 3.5 serves if breastfeeding, about 2.5
             if not breastfeeding.
            ​Dairy:    about   2.5     serves   if   breastfeeding,   about   2   if   not
             breastfeeding.

             ☆ What To Actually Eat For Healing And Energy
                  ​Build meals around a protein, a carbohydrate, and some color
                      when possible.
                           ​E.g., eggs with toast and fruit, yogurt with oats and
                            berries, lentils with rice, chicken with vegetables and
                            potatoes, or salmon with grains and greens.
                  ​Keep simple snacks around so you are not waiting until you are
                      shaky to eat.
                  ​Think easy, frequent, nourishing, and realistic.

                      ☆ Helpful Foods By Goal
                           ​For healing: protein-rich foods like eggs, poultry, beans,
                            lentils, fish, and lean meats.
                           ​For iron repletion: red meat, legumes, and dark leafy
                            greens.
                           ​For thyroid and breastfeeding support: seafood, dairy,
                            and iodized salt.
                           ​For steady energy: grains, fruit, dairy, beans, and
                            balanced meals rather than random snacking alone.
                           ​For hydration: water, plus water-rich foods and regular
                            fluids throughout the day.

☆ Tips And Tricks To Make Postpartum Eating Easier
      ​Eat before you get ravenous.
      ​Keep one-handed snacks nearby for feeding sessions.
      ​Accept meal help from friends and family.
      ​Batch simple staples if you can, like boiled eggs, cut fruit, yogurt cups,
      soups, or grain bowls.
      ​Do grocery delivery or ask someone else to shop if possible.

344

      ​Pair iron-rich foods with vitamin C foods when you can for better
      absorption.
           ​Do not shame yourself for repeating easy meals.

      ☆ If You Are Breastfeeding
           ​Expect hunger to increase.
           ​Make space for extra calories rather than fighting them.
           ​Prioritize hydration consistently.
           ​Include iodine, protein, and overall balanced meals regularly.
                    ​Remember that feeding a baby through breast milk also means
                     feeding yourself well.

      ☆ If You Are Not Breastfeeding
           ​Recovery nutrition still matters.
           ​You still need enough protein, iron, hydration, and overall balanced
            meals.
           ​Postpartum healing does not only apply to breastfeeding mothers.
                    ​Your   calorie   needs   may    be   lower   than   if    you   were
                     breastfeeding, but nourishment is still a priority! :-)


Conclusion ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

Postpartum nutrition is about much more than calories on a page! It is about
helping your body heal, protecting your energy, supporting milk production if you
are breastfeeding, and giving yourself the nutrients needed for this intense
transition. Forget about a perfect meal plan. Seriously. All your body really needs
right now is a consistent, gentle commitment to keeping yourself fed, hydrated,
and cared for. ◠ ‿ ◠
