Healthy Weight in Midlife Women
Gaining unwanted weight or seeing your body change in ways you don’t want is never
a fun experience, especially during postpartum or midlife, and it makes total sense
why! These are two major chapters where your hormones, sleep, stress, appetite,
and daily routine all decide to switch up at the exact same time. ( @ ‸ @ ) So, if
you’ve been feeling a bit more sensitive, more hungry, or less like yourself lately,
please know that it doesn’t mean you lack discipline or are necessarily doing
anything wrong.

Getting to a healthy weight does not have to involve heavy restriction, extremes,
or any of that tiresome diet-culture nonsense. (ᵕ — _ — ) The best approach is
merely setting realistic goals, eating enough of the good stuff, and focusing on
adopting habits that actually support your body instead of fighting it. And, even
though we are honing in on postpartum and midlife specifically here, these same
habits can help women feel their best at pretty much any stage of life!

396

As always, this section is for education only, not medical advice. Please always
talk with your doctor, a registered dietitian, or your trusted healthcare team
before making any big changes to your diet or health routine.


Main Content ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

Weight management is not just about the number that pops up on the scale.
(´ ◡ ` ) It is also about protecting blood sugar, blood pressure, cholesterol,
energy, hormones, muscle, and long-term health. An efficient, more structured
approach usually works better than severe restriction, especially in bodies already
moving through major transitions!


      ☆ Why Weight Changes Often Happen In Postpartum And Midlife
            ​Postpartum and midlife are both periods where weight retention or
             weight gain can become more common.
                   ​This is influenced by hormonal, biologic, psychological, and
                    lifestyle changes.
            ​In postpartum life, sleep disruption, recovery, feeding demands, and
             routine changes can all affect eating and movement.
            ​In midlife, hormonal shifts, changes in body composition, and
             metabolic risk can make weight feel more stubborn.
                   ​Excess weight during these stages may increase risk for type 2
                    diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, stroke, and some
                    cancers, including breast and ovarian cancers.

Now, when it comes to managing what you eat, there is genuinely no need for a
perfect super-strict meal plan to see real progress. That’ll only serve to burn you
out. (｡ᵕ ◞ _◟) What you actually need is just a realistic rhythm and a flexible
pattern that you can easily live with day in and day out.
      ​Dietary management is one of the most effective strategies for achieving
      and maintaining a healthy body weight.
      ​Nutrition affects energy balance, metabolism, and body composition.
      ​Dietary advice should be realistic and personalized.

397

      ​It should take into account BMI, activity level, breastfeeding status,
       lifestyle, and eating habits.
             ​In real life, not everyone has easy access to a dietitian, so basic,
              practical nutrition guidance matters a lot.

       ☆ A Smart Stepwise Approach Works Best
             ​Helpful steps include setting realistic weight goals, estimating calorie
              needs, balancing macronutrients, meeting micronutrient needs, and
              considering culture, routine, and food preferences.
             ​This kind of approach tends to be more sustainable than copying
              someone else’s diet from the internet.
             ​It also helps women make choices based on their body’s needs instead
              of panic.

Alright, let’s switch gears slightly and talk about what healthy, sustainable weight
loss in women actually looks like in real life!
      ​Women who are overweight or obese are encouraged to pursue gradual
       weight loss.
             ​Even women with a normal BMI may still benefit from weight
              management if they have a waist circumference above 80 cm, body
              fat above about 30–38%, or postpartum weight retention of at least
              4.5 kg.
      ​A 5—10% reduction in body weight is considered clinically meaningful.
      ​That level of change can improve blood glucose, blood pressure, and blood
       lipid levels.

       ☆ The Safest Pace Is Usually The Most Effective One
             ​A recommended rate of weight loss is about 0.5—1 kg per week.
             ​This gradual pace helps preserve lean muscle mass.
             ​It also supports fat loss while lowering the risk of under-eating or
              burning out.
                       ​Slower progress is not failed progress. It is often the kind that
                       actually lasts.

398

Speaking of making things last, let’s talk about calories for a second. Figuring out
how to fuel your body properly can really help you understand what your system
actually needs to get through the day!
      ​Calorie needs depend on basal metabolic rate, physical activity level, and
      total energy expenditure.
            ​Basal metabolic rate, or BMR, is the energy your body uses for basic
             functions like breathing, circulation, and cellular activity.
            ​Total energy expenditure is the broader estimate of how much
             energy you need in a day.
      ​Activity level changes this a lot, which is why one person’s intake will not
      automatically fit another person’s body.

      ☆ Special Calorie Needs In Postpartum Life
            ​Breastfeeding women need additional calories.
                   ​During the first 6 months postpartum, needs may increase by
                   about 600 kcal per day.
                   ​From 7–12 months postpartum, needs may increase by about
                   520 kcal per day.
            ​If a postpartum woman is overweight, intake may still be reduced by
             around 500 kcal per day to support gradual weight loss while
             maintaining nutrition.
            ​The key word here is gradual. Postpartum bodies still need fuel,
             especially when healing and possibly producing milk.

      ☆ Energy Reduction For Midlife Women
            ​For weight loss in midlife, a 500–1000 kcal per day deficit is
             commonly used by clinicians.
            ​This typically supports about 0.5–1 kg of weight loss per week.
            ​The goal is to reduce energy intake enough to create progress without
             making eating feel obsessive or nutritionally thin.
                   ​More restriction is not always better. Often it is just harder
                   to sustain.

399

It’s important to remember that it’s not just about numbers. To avoid feeling
totally depleted, you need the right mix of fuel.
      ​A balanced eating pattern should generally include carbohydrates, protein,
      and fat.
      ​A common distribution is about 50–60% of energy from carbohydrates,
      15–25% from protein, and less than 30% from fat.
      ​The goal is to choose better-quality versions of each and keep the overall
      pattern balanced.

      ☆ Carbohydrates Are Not The Enemy
            ​Complex carbohydrates are preferred over simple sugars.
            ​They tend to provide more fiber, lower glycemic impact, slower
            digestion, and better blood sugar control.
            ​Helpful sources include whole grains, millets, fruits, vegetables, and
            legumes.
            ​Foods to limit include refined flour products, sugary beverages, and
            heavily processed snacks.
                  ​Not all carbohydrates need to be avoided. Some can be very
                   good for you!

      ☆ Protein Helps With More Than Muscle
            ​Protein supports muscle maintenance, satiety, metabolic health, and
            recovery.
            ​This is especially important in postpartum healing and in midlife, when
            preserving lean mass becomes even more valuable.
            ​During lactation, protein needs also rise.
            ​Protein needs may increase by about 16.9 g per day during the first
            6 months postpartum and about 13.2 g per day during months 7–12.
                  ​Helpful sources include low-fat dairy, eggs, fish, lean chicken,
                   soy foods, nuts, and legumes.

      ☆ Fat Quality Matters Too
            ​Recommended fat intake is about 20–30% of total calories.
            ​Saturated fat should stay below 10% of calories.

400

            ​Trans fat should stay below 1%.
            ​Cholesterol intake is often suggested at around 200–300 mg per day.
                  ​Better      fat     choices    include   monounsaturated        and
                   polyunsaturated fats from olive oil, nuts, seeds, and fatty
                   fish.

☆ Micronutrients Women Especially Need
      ​Certain nutrients are especially important during postpartum and midlife.
            ​Iron matters for preventing anemia.
            ​Calcium matters for bone health and lactation.
            ​Vitamin A supports immunity, vision, and breast milk nutrient content.
            ​Vitamin C supports immune function, antioxidant protection, and iron
             absorption.
            ​Vitamin D supports calcium absorption and bone health.

             ☆ Iron Support
                  ​Iron targets may be around 23 mg per day in postpartum
                   women and 29 mg per day in midlife women.
                  ​Food sources include poultry, fish, legumes, green leafy
                   vegetables, nuts, and seeds.
                           ​Iron matters even more if fatigue is an issue or blood
                           loss has been significant.
                  ​Pairing iron-rich foods with vitamin C sources can help
                   absorption!

             ☆ Calcium And Vitamin D Support
                  ​Calcium needs are often around 1000–1200 mg per day.
                           ​Good sources include milk, yogurt, paneer, leafy greens,
                           and fish.
                  ​Vitamin D supports calcium absorption and bone health.
                           ​Sources include sunlight exposure, fortified foods, and
                           fatty fish.
                                 ​This is especially important in midlife, when bone
                                  density protection becomes more urgent.

401

Once you have those core nutrients locked in, the next big building block is how
you actually space out your food. Proper meal preparation helps reduce both
overeating and undereating, making you feel more satisfied from morning to night!
      ​A helpful pattern is 3 main meals with 2–3 smaller snacks.
      ​This structure can help stabilize blood sugar.
      ​It may also reduce cravings and lower the chance of arriving at meals
      absolutely starving.
            ​For many women, this feels much more manageable than skipping meals
             and hoping for the best.

      ☆ The Healthy Plate Method
            ​A practical plate method is:
            ​1/2 plate vegetables
            ​1/4 plate protein
            ​1/4 plate complex carbohydrates
            ​This can support fullness, balance, and portion awareness without
             obsessive tracking.
            ​It is also flexible enough to work across many cuisines and routines.

      ☆ Hypocaloric Diets
            ​A hypocaloric diet usually reduces intake by about 500–750 kcal per
             day.
            ​Typical ranges may be about 1200–1500 kcal per day for midlife
             women and 1200–1800 kcal per day for overweight postpartum
             women.
            ​These are structured ranges, not a reason to under-eat recklessly.
            ​Food quality still matters just as much as total calories.

             ☆ Managing Cravings And Emotional Eating
                    ​Hormonal shifts during postpartum and midlife can increase
                    mood changes, cravings, and stress eating.
                         ​Helpful   strategies    include   small   frequent   meals,
                          high-fiber foods, and nutrient-dense snacks.

402

                        ​Better snack examples include sprouts, roasted nuts,
                         vegetable soups, and fruit yogurt.
                  ​This can help reduce the cycle of restriction, craving, and
                   rebound overeating.

            ☆ Cooking Methods Can Make All The Difference
                  ​Preferred    cooking   techniques       include   steaming,   boiling,
                   grilling, baking, and sautéing.
                  ​Deep frying and heavy-oil cooking are better used less often.
                        ​This does not mean food has to become bland or joyless.
                         It simply means the everyday baseline can be made
                         lighter and more supportive.

            ☆ Food Labels Are Worth Learning
                  ​Women are encouraged to look at calorie content, added sugars,
                   fat levels, sodium, and portion size.
                  ​This helps make packaged foods feel less misleading.
                  ​It also helps women notice when a “healthy” product is mostly
                   marketing.
                        ​Label reading is not obsessive. It is informed.

Okay, now that we’ve established the facts, let’s look at a few common myths that
deserve to be debunked so you don’t waste your energy on things that don’t
actually work.（￣へ￣）
      ​Myth #1: Eating very high-fat foods improves milk production.
            ​Fact: Milk production depends on nutrient-dense eating, not excess
            fats or sugars.
      ​Myth #2: Weight gain after pregnancy is unavoidable.
            ​Fact: Healthy lifestyle practices can support postpartum weight loss
            and recovery.
      ​Myth #3: Skipping meals helps with weight loss.
            ​Fact: Skipping meals often leads to overeating later and can make
            energy regulation worse.
      ​Myth #4: All carbohydrates should be cut out.

403

             ​Fact: Complex carbohydrates support energy, satiety, and better
             blood sugar control.

It’s also important to note that taking care of your weight actually pays off across
your whole body! ( ∩ ˃ ᵕ ˂ ∩ )
      ​In diabetes, even 2–5% weight loss can improve blood glucose control.
      ​In   dyslipidaemia,   5–10%    weight    loss can improve cholesterol and
      triglycerides.
      ​In hypertension, helpful eating patterns include fruits, vegetables, whole
      grains, and low-fat dairy, while sodium is ideally limited to about 1500–2000
      mg per day.
      ​In PCOS, 2–10% weight loss may improve ovulation and hormonal balance.
      ​In hypothyroidism, balanced meals, adequate fiber, and lean protein can
      help, and calcium and iron supplements should be spaced away from thyroid
      medication.

      ☆ Midlife Women Need Special Attention To Prevention
             ​Midlife often brings increased metabolic risk, hormone changes, and
             bone density loss.
             ​Preventive strategies include adequate calcium, adequate vitamin D,
             regular physical activity, and sunlight exposure.
             ​Weight management during this stage should support both metabolic
             health and long-term strength.

             ☆ A Realistic Mindset Makes The Whole Thing Work Better
                    ​Sustainable    dietary    prescriptions   should   be   realistic,
                    personalized, culturally appropriate, and workable long-term.
                    ​Women do better when the plan fits their real life.
                    ​Perfection is not required for meaningful progress.
                    ​Consistency matters much more than intensity.

☆ Practical Weight-Management Tips That Actually Help
      ​Aim for gradual, not rushed, change.
      ​Build meals around vegetables, protein, and complex carbohydrates.

404

      ​Keep regular meal timing instead of skipping meals.
      ​Include enough protein to support fullness and muscle.
      ​Choose higher-fiber foods more often.
      ​Use simple cooking methods most of the time.
      ​Keep healthy snacks visible and easy to reach.
      ​Read labels instead of trusting front-of-package wellness language.
      ​Adjust intake thoughtfully if breastfeeding rather than aggressively
      slashing calories.
      ​Think in patterns, not extremes.


Conclusion ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

Weight management does not have to be extreme to be effective. Especially in
postpartum and midlife, the body usually needs stability more than severity. When
women focus on realistic goals, balanced meals, enough protein and fiber,
thoughtful calorie support, and long-term health instead of short-term panic,
progress becomes much more sustainable. That is the heart of it: letting go of
restriction and perfection, and instead giving yourself the kind of smart support a
real woman can actually live with. ( ´ ▽ ` ʃ♡ƪ )

F luid Balance ; Lymphatic System
If you’ve ever woken up thinking that you feel heavy, puffy, or just completely
waterlogged in your own body, you are definitely not getting in your own head. So
many women deal with this, whether it’s right before their period, after a long
flight, on a smotheringly hot day, during pregnancy, or just when life gets
incredibly stressful and perimenopause hormones start causing a scene. And, yes,
you can get that tight, full feeling even if you are completely healthy and nothing is
medically wrong.

This is where your lymphatic system chimes in, and it’s pretty interesting how it
works! ( ⌒ ‿ ⌒ ) It essentially keeps your fluids balanced and supports your
immune system by moving lymph around to clear out waste and proteins. Giving
yourself a gentle lymph drainage massage is a great, relaxing way to get things
moving and knock down that temporary puffiness, but it works best when you have
a clear idea of what it actually can and cannot do. And that is exactly what this
section is all about! ( ´ ∀ ｀ )b

And, as always, this section is for education only, not medical advice. If you are
pregnant, breastfeeding, recently postpartum, or recovering from a procedure, ask
a provider before using more intensive facial or body drainage routines.

407


Main Content ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

The lymphatic system is separate from the blood vessel system, and unlike blood
circulation, it does not have a heart pumping it forward. Its movement depends
much more on things like muscle activity, breathing, hydration, and the state of
the nervous system. That is one reason you may feel more fluid retention when you
are stressed, sedentary, hormonal, overheated, or under-rested.


      ☆ What The Lymphatic System Actually Is
            ​The lymphatic system is a fluid-circulation network that is separate
             from blood vessels.
                   ​It moves lymph, which contains fluid, proteins, immune cells,
                      and waste products.
                   ​It    helps   support immune    function,    fluid   balance, and
                      inflammation regulation.
            ​Lymph movement depends on muscle movement, breathing, hydration,
             and nervous-system regulation rather than a central pump like the
             heart.

Okay, now that we know how it functions behind the scenes, let’s look at a popular
tool people use to get that fluid moving again: lymphatic drainage massage. >___<
      ​Lymphatic drainage massage is a gentle manual technique designed to
      encourage lymph movement.
            ​It uses slow, rhythmic, superficial strokes.
            ​It is intended to guide flow toward drainage areas.
            ​It is not supposed to feel like deep tissue work.
            ​It should not feel harsh or painful.

Fluid sluggishness can hit at the most inconvenient times, so it is super helpful to
know what this looks like in your day-to-day life so you can spot it early!
      ​Many women describe feeling puffy or swollen.
      ​Others notice heavy legs, body fatigue, cyclical water retention, bloating, or
      morning facial swelling.

408

      ​Hormonal shifts can make fluid changes feel more noticeable.
      ​These sensations may become especially obvious during the luteal phase,
      pregnancy, postpartum, or perimenopause.

      ☆ The Hormonal Connection
            ​Estrogen influences fluid retention and vascular permeability.
            ​Progesterone also affects smooth muscle tone and circulation.
            ​Because of this, fluid shifts can feel more noticeable during the luteal
             phase, pregnancy, and perimenopause.
            ​Hormonal states do not create the same experience in every woman,
             but they can absolutely change how swelling and retention feel.

Giving your lymphatic system a little extra love can bring some seriously welcome
relief! Here are the common benefits:
      ​Women commonly report feeling lighter in the body.
      ​Many notice less sensation of swelling or heaviness.
      ​Some feel a temporary reduction in heaviness, tightness, or bloating
      sensation.
            ​Others experience more comfort during PMS, after long sitting
             periods, after travel, or after workouts.
      ​Relaxation and nervous-system calming are also commonly reported.
      ​Facial work may also temporarily support a more defined or less puffy
      appearance.

      ☆ What Lymphatic Drainage Does Not Do
            ​It does not melt fat.
            ​It does not permanently change body size.
            ​It does not make organs detox faster than they already do.
            ​It does not replace medical treatment.
            ​It does not fix endocrine disorders.
            ​It is not a cure for chronic edema conditions.


             ☆ Who May Benefit The Most
                    ​Women with sedentary routines may feel more benefit.

409

                  ​Women who notice hormonal water retention may also find it
                   helpful.
                  ​It may feel especially supportive for high-stress women,
                   because stress can affect both perceived swelling and
                   nervous-system tone.
                  ​Mild post-travel swelling, long sitting days, PMS-related
                   bloating, and general recovery routines are also common use
                   cases.
                  ​It can be a comfort tool, not just an aesthetic one!

              ☆ When Results May Feel Strongest
                  ​During the luteal phase.
                  ​After long sitting periods.
                  ​During high-salt periods.
                  ​In heat or humidity.
                  ​In postpartum recovery.
                  ​In perimenopause, when fluid variability may feel more
                   noticeable.

Now, it’s important to note that there is no such thing as a tool that works
identically on every face or body. We all get different results, and here’s the real
reason why:
      ​Hormonal state matters.
      ​Hydration status matters.
      ​Body composition and vascular tone matter.
      ​Baseline lymphatic efficiency may differ.
      ​Nervous-system regulation matters.
      ​Underlying medical conditions matter.

While these medical and biological details are integral, your daily habits matter
just as much!

            ​Some women report emotional release after lymphatic-style sessions.

            ​Deep diaphragmatic breathing.
            ​Good hydration.
            ​Stretching.
            ​Gentle bouncing or rebounding.
            ​Adequate sleep.
            ​Lowering chronic stress.

☆ Safety Matters

☆ The Most Realistic Takeaway On Body Lymphatic Drainage
      ​Lymphatic drainage is best understood as a supportive comfort tool.
            ​It may help women feel lighter, less puffy, and more regulated.

            ​Both approaches showed significant improvement in facial contour

                    and skin elasticity.
            ​If the goal is gentle de-puffing, superficial support, or a light
             preventive routine, the roller may make more sense.
      So, basically, if a woman mainly wants that fresh, less-puffy, lightly sculpted
      look, the roller is the cleaner choice.


      ☆ What Gua Sha Seemed To Do Best
            ​Gua sha is more strongly connected with deeper tissue manipulation,
             reduced muscle tone, and reduced dynamic stiffness.

When you look at the actual benefits, both tools do a pretty good job of giving
your face a beautiful, sculpted lift. The main difference is that a roller is your
go-to for gentle lymphatic drainage and moving fluid, while gua sha reaches a bit
deeper to ease muscle tension and work out those tight, stubborn spots in your
face. So, if you’re just trying to de-puff, the roller might be the way to go!

The lymphatic system is one of those body systems that women often feel before
they fully understand. Puffiness, heaviness, bloating, and facial swelling can be
influenced by hormones, stress, heat, immobility, and fluid shifts, so there is
nothing silly or vain about wanting support in that area. Gentle lymphatic system
care, facial rollers, and gua sha can all have a place, as long as we keep things
realistic: they are supportive tools, not cure-alls. Used well, they can help a woman
feel lighter, calmer, more comfortable, and a little more at home in her body.

Health Benefits of Yoga & Pilates
Movement is so much more than just burning calories or stretching a tight muscle.
The right kind of movement can actually protect your bones, fix your balance,
support your pelvic floor, and simply help you feel like you can trust your body
again. That is a big deal, especially if you are moving through postpartum recovery,
midlife, or the postmenopausal years. Those are the core life stages when things
like bone loss, weird pressure, leakage, and out-of-the-blue physical changes can
turn your world upside down! ( ︶︿︶ )

You know that old saying “work smarter not harder?” Well, it applies perfectly to
workouts too! ( ⌒▽⌒ ) Things like Pilates, yoga, and pelvic floor-friendly
exercises are the perfect example of movement that is incredibly effective
without needing to wear you out. However, the real magic comes down to how you
do them: with consistency, breathing, coordination, and a sprinkle of patience.

And, as always, this is for education only, not medical advice. If you have
significant pelvic symptoms, pain, prolapse concerns, or osteoporosis-related
medical restrictions, it is important to check in with your healthcare provider or a
pelvic floor physical therapist.

418


Main Content ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

When you hear about bone health, you may instantly think calcium and maybe
vitamin D, which are important, yes. But bones also respond to mechanical stress,
meaning they need regular physical loading and movement to stay stronger. At the
same time, the pelvic floor needs a very different approach: not constant
squeezing, but coordinated strength and release, as we discussed in earlier
sections.
      ☆ How Exercise Helps Bones In The First Place
              ​Exercise creates mechanical strain on bone tissue, which triggers
              bone-building, or osteogenic, effects.
              ​It also increases blood flow to bone tissue, which supports the
              creation of new bone cells.
                    ​Bone is constantly remodeling, meaning old bone is being
                     replaced by new bone.
                          ​That remodeling cycle is slow and usually takes about 4–6
                           months.
              ​Because of this, exercise needs to be maintained for at least about 1
              year to show substantial measurable benefits in bone mass.

Since bone density is a long-term project, you’ll want a routine that actually feels
good to stick with. And that is exactly where Pilates makes a grand entrance.
٩( ˊᗜˋ )‫♡ و‬
      ​Pilates may be slightly more effective than Yoga for bone mineral density.
              ​One reason is that Pilates emphasizes co-contraction of the
              lumbo-pelvic and trunk stabilizer muscles.
                    ​That core co-contraction creates direct mechanical forces on
                     the spine.
      ​Stronger core stabilizers are directly correlated with higher bone density in
      the vertebrae.
      ​Mat Pilates is especially helpful for body composition and physical
      performance.

419

            ​Research shows Pilates significantly improves bone mineral density in
               the lumbar spine and the trochanter, which is the upper part of the
               thigh bone.
                    ​It also improves reaction time and muscle strength in women
                     over age 65.

While yoga sometimes shows a smaller effect on bone mineral density compared to
Pilates, that does not make it unimportant! ˃ ᴗ ˂
      ​Yoga uses weight-bearing postures and balance-focused movement, which
      create a different type of strain on the body.
            ​A standard routine often includes Ashtanga-based              Yoga and
               Yogasanas.
      ​Evidence indicates that a consistent 12-minute daily Yoga routine can be
      enough to reverse osteoporotic bone loss in the spine, hips, and femur.
      However, the evidence is promising, not conclusive.
      ​Yoga is also associated with a reduced risk of hip and lower-limb fractures
      because it improves balance, helping women stay upright and avoid falls!

      ☆ The Dosage Of Movement That Seems To Work Best
            ​Most successful routines use 2–4 sessions per week.
            ​Sessions usually last about 45–60 minutes.
            ​Shorter programs may help balance and function, but routines longer
               than 24 weeks are much more effective for real tissue adaptation.
            ​Long-term commitment matters far more than intensity spikes.

Now, building strong bones won’t matter much if you can’t stay on your feet.
(ᵕ — ᴗ — ) Therefore, balance training cannot be treated as optional fluff!
      ​Most fragility fractures happen because of falls.
      ​Balance training is one of the main ways to reduce that risk.
      ​Experts recommend multicomponent training, meaning movement that
      combines strength and balance.
      ​These programs also support independence, self-management, and active
      aging.
      ​There are psychological and social benefits too, not just physical ones.

420

Drumroll, please… we’re bringing the pelvic floor back into the spotlight! ( ദ്ദി ˙ᗜ˙ )
Once again, if you’re dealing with postpartum recovery, leaking, heaviness, or
tension, this is a major puzzle piece. It really comes down to how these movements
impact your core, which is exactly why pelvic floor-friendly yoga & Pilates come in
clutch!
      ​The pelvic floor works together with the diaphragm, deep abdominals, and
      back muscles.
      ​Together, these form the body’s internal core support system.
      ​When this system is balanced, movement tends to feel more fluid, stable,
      coordinated, and powerful.
      ​You are not aiming for anything along the lines of constant gripping.
      ​The goal is coordinated support.

      ☆ Why This Approach Feels Different From Traditional Fitness Cues
            ​Many     workouts    overemphasize    gripping,   tucking,   and   holding
             everything in.
            ​That can increase pelvic floor tension.
            ​It can also worsen leaking, discomfort, pelvic heaviness, and pain.
            ​Pelvic floor-friendly movement focuses more on breath, coordination,
             gentle activation, and release when needed.
            ​It teaches the body to respond well, not to brace nonstop.

             ☆ The Breath And Pelvic Floor Connection
                    ​On the inhale, the diaphragm moves down and the pelvic floor
                    should lengthen and soften slightly.
                    ​On the exhale, the diaphragm rises and the pelvic floor gently
                    recoils and lifts.
                    ​Many people accidentally hold their breath, push downward, or
                    reverse this pattern.
                          ​That can increase downward pressure on the pelvic
                           organs.
                    ​Learning this breath pattern can reduce strain and improve
                    pressure management.

421

                    ☆ Major Benefits Of Pelvic Floor-Friendly Yoga And Pilates
                          ​Improves core support without over-bracing.
                          ​Helps reduce excess pelvic floor tension.
                          ​Supports better breath mechanics.
                          ​May help with urinary leakage during exercise when
                          symptoms are related to poor coordination or pressure
                          management.
                          ​May reduce pelvic heaviness or pressure.
                          ​Can help with pelvic pain or low back pain.
                          ​Improves flexibility and mobility in the spine, hips, and
                          pelvis.
                          ​Can support postpartum recovery.
                          ​Builds confidence in movement.
                          ​Teaches both strength and relaxation.

Now that we know why these practices work wonders, let’s look at how to actually
do them! To help you picture everything, I’ve put together a useful little diagram
of all the poses below!

422




☆ Exercise 1: Diaphragmatic Breathing
      ​Goal: coordinate and relax the pelvic floor with the diaphragm.
      ​Benefits: calms the system, improves breathing mechanics, teaches pelvic
      floor softening on inhale and gentle recoil on exhale, and reduces
      unnecessary tension.

423

      ​How to do it: lie on your back with knees bent. Place one hand on your chest
      and one on your belly. Inhale through your nose and let your ribs and
      abdomen expand. Imagine your pelvic floor gently widening or blooming.
      Exhale through your mouth, feel the ribs close, and let the pelvic floor lift
      naturally.
      ​Repeat for 1–2 minutes.
            ​Important cue: do not force a hard pelvic floor lift. Think gentle
                recoil.

☆ Exercise 2: Supine Bridge
      ​Goal: strengthen the glutes and core without bearing down.
      ​Benefits: activates glutes, supports hip and pelvic stability, trains core
      support without excess strain, and reduces overreliance on the pelvic floor
      itself.
      ​How to do it: lie on your back with knees bent and feet hip-width apart.
      Inhale to prepare. Exhale and gently roll your hips off the mat one vertebra
      at a time. Pause at the top and keep breathing steadily. Inhale to lower
      slowly back down.
            ​Modification: place a small yoga block between the knees for gentle
                inner-thigh and core connection.
                      ​Important cue: lift with control, not with gripping.

☆ Exercise 3: Cat-Cow
      ​Goal: improve spinal mobility and pelvic floor rhythm.
      ​Benefits: improves spinal movement, helps coordinate breath with pelvic
      floor lengthening and lifting, reduces torso and pelvic rigidity, and helps the
      core system move more naturally.
      ​How to do it: start on hands and knees. Inhale as you drop the belly and lift
      the chest into Cow. Let the pelvic floor lengthen. Exhale as you round into
      Cat and gently lift through the lower abdominals.
      ​Repeat 5–8 times.
            ​Important cue: move with the breath rather than rushing through
                the positions.

424

☆ Exercise 4: Child’s Pose
      ​Goal: encourage release and lengthening.
      ​Benefits: promotes pelvic floor relaxation, reduces guarding and tension,
      encourages deep breathing into the back and side ribs, and helps calm the
      nervous system.
      ​How to do it: kneel with big toes touching and knees apart. Fold forward
      and rest your forehead on the mat or on a pillow. Inhale deeply into the back
      and side ribs and let the pelvic floor soften downward.
      ​Stay for 5–10 slow breaths.
      ​Modification: place a bolster between the thighs and torso for comfort.
              ​Important cue: this is a release pose, not a force-the-stretch pose.

☆ Exercise 5: Tabletop Leg Lifts
      ​Goal: train lower abdominals with controlled breath.
      ​Benefits: strengthens the deep core without over-bracing, improves
      single-leg control, supports pelvic stability, and teaches engagement without
      flattening or gripping.
      ​How to do it: lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat. Inhale to
      prepare. Exhale and lift one leg to tabletop so the hip and knee are each
      around 90º. Inhale and lower it back down. Alternate sides.
      ​Repeat 8–10 times each side.
              ​Important cue: avoid flattening your back hard into the mat and avoid
              gripping your abs. Think light, connected lift.

☆ Exercise 6: Supported Deep Squat
      ​Goal: encourage pelvic mobility and opening.
      ​Benefits: helps the pelvic floor lengthen, improves hip and pelvic mobility,
      and supports coordination between relaxation on inhale and activation on
      exhale.
      ​How to do it: stand with feet wider than hips and toes slightly turned out.
      Hold onto a sturdy surface or doorframe. Lower into a squat with the spine
      tall and chest lifted. Inhale to relax the pelvic floor and exhale to gently
      rise.
      ​Modification: place a yoga block or folded towel under the heels if needed.

425

              ​Important cue: do not force depth if it causes pressure or
               discomfort.

Now, unnecessary struggle is a big no-no in movement, especially when it comes to
exercising your pelvic floor muscles. So, to keep things feeling good, here is a
quick guide on what to watch out for, how to move safely, and who benefits the
most.

☆ Movements To Be Cautious With
        ​Deep abdominal crunches or roll-ups.
        ​Double leg lifts.
        ​Long breath holds or heavy bracing.
        ​Inversions.
        ​Heavy bearing down.
        ​High-impact movements without proper exhalation control.
              ​These can increase pelvic pressure or strain.
                       ​The issue is not that strength is bad for you. It’s more so that
                       pressure management is crucial.

        ☆ Main Technique Rules For All Pelvic Floor-Friendly Movement
              ​Breathe continuously.
              ​Do not hold your breath.
              ​Exhale on effort, especially when lifting, standing, or working against
               gravity.
              ​Avoid bearing down.
              ​Do not over-grip the abs, glutes, or pelvic floor.
              ​Strengthen and release. Both matter.

☆ Who This Kind Of Movement May Help Most
        ​Women with mild pelvic floor dysfunction.
        ​Postpartum women easing back into movement.
        ​Women with chronic pelvic floor tension.
        ​Women who leak with exercise.
        ​Women who feel pelvic heaviness.

426

      ​Women with pelvic or low back discomfort.
      ​These are often safe starting points, but more specific symptoms deserve
      individualized support.

      ☆ When To Seek Extra Guidance
            ​If you are not sure whether your pelvic floor is too tight, too weak, or
            poorly coordinated.
            ​If you have pain, persistent leakage, heaviness, prolapse symptoms, or
            pressure that worsens with movement.
            ​If you want help with breathing mechanics, posture, or pressure
            management.
                  ​A pelvic floor physical therapist can assess what your body
                   actually needs rather than guessing.


Conclusion ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

Pilates, Yoga, and pelvic floor-friendly movement can be such wonderful tools for
women because they support more than one thing at once. They can help protect
bones, improve balance, build core support, reduce excess tension, and make
movement feel safer and more empowering again. The real secret is not intensity.
It is consistency, breath, and thoughtful technique. Done that way, these practices
become less about working out and more about helping the female body feel
strong, supported, and at ease. :-)

Makeup / Beauty Presentation
You know, I’ll never forget the day I got my first eyeshadow palette. I mean, I’m
pretty sure it was a cheap one from a retail store that chipped within two days,
but I treasured it with all my heart … for the time being. ( ＾ ｖ ＾ ) Makeup is one of
those things that can be fun, expressive, polished, soft, glamorous, corrective,
or all of the above. But underneath the products, trends, and tiny little “wait, what
even is contour and where does it actually go?” moments, the real underlying
message is much simpler: makeup changes how the eye reads the face.

It can bring certain features forward, soften others, create balance, add warmth,
and return life to the skin after coverage. The best makeup does not just sit on
top of the face. It works with facial structure, undertone, light, shadow,
texture, and proportion.

There is also a true psychological layer here. Research on makeup and face
perception found that makeup-enhanced faces were rated as more attractive and
pleasant, while also triggering stronger attention- and reward-related brain
responses. So yes, makeup can be playful and artistic, but it can also vividly shape
self-perception, confidence, and visual impact. (^ ‿ ^)b

      ​The smartest way to think about makeup is not product-first. It is

      ​Beauty makeup works by asking what should come forward, what should

          ​Makeup can increase facial contrast, especially around the eyes and

Okay, now let’s delve into the specifics of different makeup products and how they

      ☆ Undertones: Warm Vs. Cool
            ​Warm-toned skin has more golden, yellow, peachy, or olive warmth.
            ​Cool-toned skin has cooler, pinker, rosier, or bluish undertones.
            ​The easiest way to assess undertone is in bright natural daylight.
            ​Hold warm and cool colors near the face and notice which family
             makes the skin look healthier, clearer, and more vibrant.
                   ​If the color family is wrong, the skin may look gray, dull, muddy,
                    orange, or washed out.

             ☆ General Color Families That Often Work:
                   ​Warm      undertones     usually    suit   golds,   warm   peaches,
                    yellow-based beiges, bronze, copper, and warm browns.
                   ​Cool   undertones usually suit taupes, rosy pinks, mauves,
                    red-violets, plums, and cooler browns.

      ☆ Foundation: How To Make It Look Like Skin
            ​Match foundation at the jawline, not only the cheek.
                   ​Blend below the jaw and slightly under the chin.
                           ​Choose foundation by both depth and undertone.
            ​Use the thinnest layer that gives the effect you want, then build only
             where needed.
            ​Full coverage usually works better for glamorous, polished, or
             camera-ready looks.
            ​Lighter, thinner application usually looks better for natural makeup.

             Foundation should even the complexion, not erase the face. Once the
             skin is evened out, the face often needs color and dimension added
             back in through blush, lips, brows, bronzer, or subtle eye definition.

433

      ☆ Custom-Correcting Complexion Color
           ​If the base needs more gold, add yellow.
           ​If the base needs less yellow, add violet.
           ​If the skin needs less pink or has visible rosiness, add green.
           ​If the skin needs less peach, add mint first, then violet.
                   ​This same corrective color logic can also apply to powders.
                         ​A “wrong shade” is not always too light or too dark.
                          Sometimes the depth is right, but the undertone is off.

      ☆ Concealer Tips That Make A Difference
           ​Use concealer only where it is actually needed, especially for dark
           circles, blemishes, redness, and discoloration.
           ​Avoid over-powdering corrected areas.
                   ​Too much powder can make concealed areas look dry, heavy,
                   creased, or more textured.
           ​After concealing, add life back with blush or lip color if the face looks
           flat.
           ​Concealer can visually flatten the face if nothing else is added
           afterward!

      ☆ Powder And Finish Control
           ​Powder helps set makeup, control movement, and reduce shine.
           ​Use only as much as needed.
           ​Too much powder can make skin look dry, flat, or lifeless.
           ​Powder is especially useful when reshaping lips, setting concealer, or
           creating a more glamorous base.
                   ​Anti-shine products can help when certain areas are catching
                   light in a way you do not want.

                   ☆ A Helpful Way To Think About Finish:
                         ​Matte or satin gives more control and often photographs
                          cleaner.
                         ​Soft dew can look fresh, healthy, and youthful.

434

                         ​Gloss and shine work best when used intentionally, not
                          spread everywhere with no plan.

☆ Matte Vs. Dewy: How To Choose
      ​Matte works well when you want cleaner structure, less shine, longer wear,
      and a more controlled finish.
      ​Dewy or glossy finishes work well when you want softness, fullness, glamour,
      freshness, or a more stylized look.
            ​Oily or textured skin often does better with matte or satin finishes.
            ​Drier skin or more glamorous looks can usually handle more dew or
             gloss.
      ​The whole face does not need to be shiny for the skin to look healthy.

☆ Contour Vs. Bronzer Vs. Highlight
      ​Contour changes shape.
      ​Bronzer changes warmth.
      ​Highlight changes projection.
            ​Contour should mimic shadow.
            ​Bronzer should mimic warmth from the sun.
            ​Highlight should mimic light hitting a raised plane.

The easiest mistake is using bronzer as contour. Bronzer is usually too warm to
create a believable shadow, which can make the face look orange instead of
sculpted.

      ☆ Face Shape Guide: Placing Product With Intention

435




          ​Oval faces usually need balance maintained rather than dramatically
           corrected.
          ​Round faces often benefit from added length and gentle structure.
          ​Square faces often benefit from softened angles and reduced visual
           width.
          ​Heart faces often need the wider upper face balanced with the
           narrower lower face.
          ​Diamond faces often need cheek width softened while the forehead
           and chin are brought into harmony.

      ☆ Nose Shaping Basics

436




           ​Contour the outer sides of the nose if the nose appears wider than
           desired.
           ​Keep the center highlight slim if you want a narrower effect.
           ​If the nose is long, contour the tip and keep the highlight shorter.
           ​If the nose is short, use a longer center highlight and keep tip contour
           minimal.
           ​Shade around the nostrils if they look wider than desired.
           ​Use light and shadow subtly.


      ☆ Blush: The Step That Brings The Face Back To Life
           ​Blush restores healthy-looking color after foundation and concealer.
                 ​Pinks and roses often flatter cool undertones.
                 ​Peaches and apricots often flatter warm undertones.
                        ​Deeper skin tones can look beautiful with tiny amounts
                         of richer reds, berries, corals, or warm terracotta
                         shades.
                 ​Cream blush often looks especially natural on the skin.

437

                        ​Powder blush layered over cream can improve longevity.

                  Blush placement can also help shape the face:
                        ​Round face: pull blush slightly up and out.
                        ​Square face: use a rounder placement to soften.
                        ​Heart face: keep blush slightly lower to balance the
                         forehead.
                        ​Diamond face: avoid exaggerating the outer cheek width.

      ☆ Brows: Framing The Face Softly
           ​Groom brows first, then fill only where needed.
           ​Use short strokes that mimic real hair.
                 ​Taupes and soft browns often photograph softer than overly
                  dark brow colors.
           ​A soft arch adds lift.
           ​A straighter brow can look calmer, broader, or more youthful.
           ​A fuller tail can help elongate the eye area.
           ​A lifted tail can open the eye visually.

438

☆ Eye Makeup: Corrective Logic That Actually Helps




      ​Light shades advance.
      ​Dark shades recede.
      ​Medium shades help transition.
      ​Eye makeup should be adjusted to eye shape, not copied exactly from every
      trend.


      ☆ Wide-Set Eyes
            ​Use more depth toward the inner corner to visually bring the eyes
               closer together.
            ​Avoid over-highlighting the inner corners if the goal is balance.


      ☆ Deep-Set Eyes
            ​Keep the lid lighter.
            ​Use medium tones softly in the crease.
            ​Avoid very dark crease work that pushes the eyes back even further.

439

      ☆ Large Eyes
          ​Darker lid and crease shades can help contain size.
          ​Smokier placement usually works beautifully.


      ☆ Round Eyes
          ​Emphasize the outer corners to create more elongation.

      ☆ Small Eyes

           ☆ Eyeliner Tips
                ​For natural makeup, softer browns, taupes, and grays often look

                       ​Keep the liner close to the lash base.
                       ​Dotting color into the lash line can define the eyes
                        without creating an obvious stripe.
                       ​Outer lift can make the eyes look more almond-shaped.
                ​Thick all-around liner tends to make the eyes look smaller.
                ​Softer smudging usually looks more natural.

                 ☆ Eyeshadow Tips
                       ​Cool undertones often suit taupes, mauves, cool browns,
                        and plums.
                       ​Warm undertones often suit bronze, warm brown, peach,
                        copper, and gold.
                       ​For natural makeup, soft creams, beiges, pinks, taupes,
                        and browns usually work beautifully.
                       ​For glamour, stronger shape, stronger contrast, and
                        bolder color can make sense.
                             ​Choose shadow based on what the eye shape needs,
                              not just what is trending.

440



                                ☆ Lash Tips
                                      ​Individual lashes are often the softest and
                                       most natural-looking.
                                      ​Half lashes can create a lifted soft-glam
                                       effect.
                                      ​Outer-corner lash focus lifts and elongates
                                       the eyes.
                                      ​Center-heavy     lashes create more of a
                                       doll-eye look.
                                      ​Brown-black can look softer than jet black.
                                      ​For natural looks, curled lashes and light
                                       mascara may be enough.

      ☆ Lip Reshaping Tips




           ​To make lips look smaller, line just inside the natural lip border.

441

           ​To make lips look fuller, line just outside the natural border very
            carefully and symmetrically.
                 ​A thin upper lip can be balanced by lining slightly above the top
                     lip only.
                 ​A thin lower lip can be balanced by slightly enlarging the
                     bottom lip instead.
           ​Light to medium lip colors and classic reds can make lips look fuller.
           ​Medium to deeper tones can make lips look smaller or more contained.
                 ​When changing lip shape, setting with powder can help the new
                     line last better.


      ☆ Highlight Rules
           ​Highlight goes where you want the face to come forward.
           ​Good zones often include the tops of cheekbones, cupid’s bow, parts
            of the brow bone, and sometimes the nose bridge.
           ​More shimmer means more attention.
                 ​Strong shimmer can emphasize texture, acne, or enlarged
                     pores.
           ​Use highlight with purpose, not everywhere all at once.

      ☆ Bronzer Rules
           ​Bronzer adds warmth, not shadow.
           ​Good bronzer zones include the forehead perimeter, temples, upper
            cheek perimeter, and sometimes lightly along the jaw.
           ​Warm skin often handles golden bronzers well.
           ​Cool skin often looks better in neutral bronzers rather than orange
            tones.
           ​Use bronzer to warm the skin, not carve out hollows.

442

Now that we’re past the general rules, let’s settle this right here and now. Natural
or glam? Well, neither one is “better” than the other. ╮(￣▽￣””)╭ They’re just
completely different design choices. Natural makeup keeps things on the down low
with soft edges, light coverage, and subtle definition. Glamour makeup goes all out
with more coverage, sculpting, stronger contrast, bold lashes, and defined lips. The
right move depends solely on the occasion, the lighting, your outfit, and whatever
mood you’re in!

      ☆ Natural Makeup
            ​Lighter base.
            ​Minimal visible liner.
            ​Softer lids.
            ​Subtle cheek color.
            ​Groomed brows with only a little fill.
            ​Fresh-looking lips rather than obviously overdrawn lips.
            ​Less gloss and less shine.
            ​Softer edges overall.

      ☆ Glamour Makeup
            ​Fuller coverage base.
            ​Stronger contour and highlight.
            ​Bolder brows and eyes.
            ​False lashes.
            ​More sculpting.
            ​More defined lips.
            ​Shine or gloss can be part of the look.
            ​Strong blending matters.

             ☆ Beginner Mistakes That Make Makeup Look Heavier
                   ​Choosing the wrong undertone.
                   ​Using too much powder.
                   ​Making brows too dark.
                   ​Using bronzer as contour.
                   ​Overlining lips without symmetry.

443

                   ​Making small or deep-set eyes too dark.
                   ​Leaving an unblended foundation line at the jaw.
                   ​Forgetting to add color and life back in after base makeup.

☆ A Simple Makeup Cheat Sheet
      ​Want something to look slimmer or farther back? Use shadow.
      ​Want something to look fuller or more forward? Use light.
      ​Want the face to look healthier? Add cheek and lip color back in.
      ​Want natural makeup? Use softer edges, softer browns, lighter coverage,
      and less shine.
      ​Want glamour? Use fuller coverage, more sculpting, lashes, gloss, and
      stronger definition.
      ​Warm undertone? Think gold, peach, bronze, copper, and warm browns.
      ​Cool undertone? Think taupe, rose, mauve, plum, and cooler browns.
      ​Small eyes? Keep the lid lighter.
      ​Large eyes? Darker lid and crease can help.
      ​Wide-set eyes? Add more depth toward the inner corner.
      ​Deep-set eyes? Use a light lid and softer crease.
      ​Thin lips? Slight overline with careful setting.
      ​Full lips too dominant? Line slightly inside.


Conclusion ☆ ‧ ₊ ˚

The most flattering makeup is rarely the heaviest or the trendiest. It is the
makeup that understands the face in front of it. When you learn how undertone,
placement, shadow, light, finish, and proportion work together, makeup starts to
feel much less like smearing on random products and hoping they blend, and much
more fulfilling. Not because you are covering the face up, but because you are
learning how to enhance what is already there with intention, balance, and a hint
of artistry! ☆～（ ゝ 。 ∂ ）

      A Glimpse Into the World of Surrogacy (っᵔ◡ᵔ)っ
